title: feat(rs,ts): SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution defence, the freshness bound it needs, and the §10.4 message leaks
body:
SPEC §7.2 item 11 makes duplicate-execution protection a normative consumer requirement for a *consequential Trust Task*. **No runtime implemented it.** There was no id-keyed store anywhere in the repo, and `StandardCode::IdConflict` was emitted by nothing.

Every transport binding delegates the defence to the consumer and says so in writing — `bindings/https/0.2` §5: "Freshness / replay: None", with `didcomm/0.2` §6, `didcomm-v1/0.2` §6 and `tsp/0.1` §7 identical. So the consumer was the only layer that could do it, and it did not. A captured envelope, or a bearer-authenticated body, re-sent, executed `acl/grant` or `vault/release` a second time — and an ordinary mediator retry did it by accident. §10.1 is explicit that the two are indistinguishable at the document layer, which is why the rule does not try to tell them apart.

This lands the seam in `trust-tasks-rs`, mirrors it in the TS runtime, and adds the freshness bound without which the record could not be bounded at all.

## The seam

```rust
#[async_trait]
pub trait ReplayGuard: Send + Sync {
    async fn claim(&self, id: &str, digest: &DocumentDigest,
                   retain_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, now: DateTime<Utc>)
        -> Result<ReplayVerdict, ReplayGuardError>;
    async fn record_response(&self, id: &str, response: Option<&Value>) -> Result<(), ReplayGuardError>;
    async fn release(&self, id: &str, digest: &DocumentDigest) -> Result<(), ReplayGuardError>;
}
```

Object-safe and async, so a deployment hands `consume_inbound` a `&dyn ReplayGuard` over Redis, Postgres, or DynamoDB. `InMemoryReplayGuard` is the batteries-included LRU default, documented as **not** correct behind a load balancer — two replicas hold separate maps, so a document accepted by A is fresh at B and the effect happens twice, which is the exact failure the rule exists to prevent.

`ReplayVerdict` is three-valued: `Fresh` (execute), `Duplicate { prior_response, in_flight }` (do **not** execute; return the prior result), `Conflict` (`idConflict`). §7.2's *Disposition of a duplicate* is why `Duplicate` carries a cached response and why `ConsumeOutcome::Duplicate` is a separate outcome from `Rejected`: "In no case is a duplicate reported as `taskFailed`; the task did not fail, it already happened." A caller that folded it into `Rejected` would report a failure that did not occur.

## Why the key is a digest of the canonical form, not the received bytes

§7.2's keying paragraph fixes both halves. The key is the document `id` **alone** — "Transport request identifiers, transport message identifiers, and execution handles **MUST NOT** substitute" — and the comparison is over the canonical serialization, because "an `id` alone cannot distinguish the retry it must absorb from the conflict it must reject".

Keying on the octets as received would break the retry rule rather than enforce it. A body re-indented in transit, a member order chosen by an intermediary, or a gateway that re-serializes are all the *same document* under RFC 8785 — and §8.4 defines the safe resend as exactly that document. A byte-keyed consumer answers a legitimate retry with `idConflict`, or, if it keyed on something looser, executes it. Canonicalizing first is what makes "the same document" a property of the document rather than of the pipe it arrived through.

**The digest covers `proof`.** That is a deliberate departure from the §4.9.3 *task digest* over `JCS(document ∖ proof)`, and the spec draws the line itself:

> **This is not the document identity of §7.2 item 11.** The two answer different questions and are deliberately computed differently. Item 11 and §8.4 ask *which serialization arrived*, so a re-signed `proof` over identical content makes a different document — that is the `idConflict` case, and the distinction is the whole point of the rule.

§8.4 says it from the producer's end too: "A *producer* that 'retries' by re-signing, re-stamping `issuedAt`, or otherwise altering the bytes has not retried — it has issued a different document under a reused `id`, which item 11 requires the *consumer* to reject with `idConflict`." Stripping `proof` before hashing would silently absorb precisely that case as a retry, which is the one disposition both sections rule out. There is a test for it in each language.

The canonicalizer and SHA-256 are written in-crate rather than pulled in: this crate is deliberately dependency-light, the TS package ships no runtime dependencies, and the digest is consumer-local content identity, never a signature, a MAC, or a published citation value. Both hashes are pinned to the FIPS 180-4 / NIST CAVP vectors. The Rust canonicalizer's two documented deviations from literal JCS (member ordering by Unicode scalar rather than UTF-16 code unit; `serde_json`'s exponent spelling) are confined to the bytes and cannot change the equality relation JCS induces — which is the only load-bearing property here, since the value never leaves the process. `trust-tasks-proof` still uses a real RFC 8785 implementation for the `eddsa-jcs-2022` proof input, and §4.9.3 task digests are unaffected.

## Freshness — and why it is the same feature

`validate_basic` checked `expiresAt` and nothing else. `issuedAt` was parsed and looked at by nobody. So a document stamped a year in the future was accepted, and accepted *again* for the whole of that year; and a document whose `expiresAt` sat at or before its own `issuedAt` — a validity interval containing no valid instant — was accepted whenever the clock happened to sit before the expiry.

It is also what makes item 11 implementable. §7.2's *Bounding the record*: the consumer "**MUST** retain the record for at least as long as it remains willing to execute that document", and "the two bounds are the same bound". `FreshnessPolicy::record_expiry` computes that instant — `expiresAt` where present, otherwise `issuedAt + max_age` — and it is what `claim` receives as `retain_until`. That is why the two travel as one argument: separating them lets a deployment configure a five-minute record and an unbounded acceptance window, which reads as a working replay defence and is not one.

`FreshnessPolicy::default()` enforces only the two internal-consistency rules, which no conforming producer can fail. `FreshnessPolicy::consequential()` is the posture the bounding paragraph describes: `issuedAt` required, five-minute window. Where the policy can place a document in no window at all, `consume_inbound` refuses rather than pretending to guard it — §7.2: a consumer "that can establish neither an `expiresAt` nor an age for a document has no window in which to place it, and **MUST NOT** execute a *consequential Trust Task* on it".

The mechanism is unconditional and configurable; it is not gated on the framework-spec change that will require `issuedAt` for consequential tasks.

## Ordering, and the two ways to get it wrong

The claim is taken **last**, after every other §7.2 check. Claiming first would burn the `id` on every malformed or unauthorised arrival, so a corrected resend would come back `idConflict` forever — and an observer could pre-burn any `id` it had merely seen.

A **retryable** refusal releases the claim: §8.4 has just told the producer it MAY re-send this document bit-for-bit, and holding the claim would answer that invited retry with the cached failure forever. A **non-retryable** refusal is final for that document, so the record stands and a replay is answered with the same determination rather than re-evaluated. A guard whose store is unreachable fails **closed** → `unavailable`, `retryable: true`, which is the honest answer: the resend is absorbed correctly once the store is back.

## Error-message leaks (SPEC §10.4)

`wire_message` sanitised only `IdentityMismatch` and `WrongRecipient`, so `ProofInvalid { reason }` passed the verifier's own error text to the wire. Real strings a cryptosuite backend produces include `resolve did:web:x: <error>`, `verificationMethod … not present in DID document`, and `verificationMethod is controlled by {vm_did}, not the document issuer {issuer}`. The party receiving that message is by construction **unauthenticated** — the proof did not verify — so it is a resolver-reachability and DID-document-content oracle, answered at the sender's chosen rate. §10.4 states the rule for `identityMismatch` and then generalises it to every standard code.

`ProofInvalid` now carries a constant. `trust-tasks-https`'s `proof_invalid_when_verifier_rejects` asserted the leak (`msg.contains("signature")`) — it was pinning the vulnerability, so it is renamed `proof_invalid_wire_message_withholds_the_verifier_description` and now asserts both halves: the constant on the wire, and the description still present on `RejectReason`'s `Display`, which is the operator's log line. A change that dropped the reason outright would satisfy the first assertion and leave operators debugging blind. So do `Unavailable` (which would otherwise name a backing store) and the new `Stale` (which would otherwise disclose the size of the acceptance window, inviting a probe for its boundary). The detail stays on the `Display` impl, which is what the operator logs. `RejectReason::malformed_from_serde` categorises deserializer failures — syntax / EOF / data / IO — instead of echoing `serde_json`'s member path and byte offset, which describe the consumer's internal type layout to anyone willing to send malformed JSON. The TS side already used a constant for `proofInvalid`; it is now a named export so the two can be compared.

One existing Rust test asserted the leak (`assert!(msg.contains("signature"))`). It now asserts its absence, with a comment saying why it flipped.

## `trust-task-error` version drift

Four answers were in circulation: `0.5` from `trust-tasks-rs`, `0.5` from the TS runtime, `0.2` from the HTTPS server, `0.1` in both READMEs. A producer could not tell from the documentation which schema an error response would validate against, and a bump had to be found in four places. `trust_task_error_type_uri()` is now `pub` and documented as the one definition on the Rust side — which is what `CLAUDE.md` already assumed — and `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI` is its TS counterpart, with its stale "`0.3`, because…" comment corrected (the value had moved to `0.5`; the prose had not).

**The HTTPS server now uses it too**, closing the drift entirely. `synthesise_error` and `suppressed_error_response` spelled `trust-task-error/0.2` out for themselves while every *other* error response that server emits already carried `0.5` — those are built by `reject_with` in `trust-tasks-rs` — so the version a producer saw depended on which branch of the rejection path its request hit. `0.5` is a forward-minor move from `0.2`, and §5.2 says a `0.2` consumer SHOULD accept it. `trust-tasks-https` goes `0.11.0` → `0.11.1` with a CHANGELOG entry; nothing depends on that crate, so it does not cascade.

## READMEs that did not compile

The `trust-tasks-rs` README showed `consume_inbound` with 7 arguments against a function taking 8 (`payload_policy` was added later, and is now 9). The TS README omitted the non-optional `payloadPolicy`. Both are corrected, along with the rs README's "`0.1.0` — tracks `SPEC.md` version `0.1`" status line, which the CHANGELOG's own versioning note had superseded.

## ⚠ Behavioural break, and the version number

This change is breaking in character:

- `consume_inbound` takes a new required argument (`ConsumeChecks`), and requires `R: Serialize`.
- `RejectReason` gains `IdConflict` and `Stale`; `ConsumeOutcome` gains `Duplicate`. Exhaustive matches need new arms.
- **A conforming consumer now rejects documents it previously accepted**: a future-dated `issuedAt`, and an `expiresAt` at or before `issuedAt`. Neither is emitted by a conforming producer, but a deployment whose producers are not conforming will see refusals it did not see before. `consumeInbound` in TS additionally throws on a missing `checks` option, as it already did for `payloadPolicy`.

Under the rules at the top of `trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md` — which say plainly that a behavioural break counts even against an unchanged wire format — **this earns `0.12.0`.** It ships as **`0.11.18` / `0.12.18`**, a non-leading bump, because moving the leading component means editing the `version = "0.11"` requirement in six dependent crates and releasing them in `publish.yml`'s order. Those crates are owned by concurrent work and this change touches none of them. The CHANGELOG entry opens with a call-out saying so; **the release manager should cut this as `0.12.0` with the six dependent releases.** `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` is clean at `0.11.18`, so nothing is broken in the interim.

## Follow-ups the binding crates need

Deliberately not done here — those crates are owned by concurrent work.

1. **`trust-tasks-https`** — the server pipeline in `src/server.rs` runs its own §7.2 checks and never reaches `consume_inbound`, so it gets neither the replay guard nor the freshness bound. It needs a `ReplayGuard` on its server config, threaded into the handler path. It also still maps a `serde_json::Error` with `format!("{e}")` when deserializing a payload — that is the raw-path leak this PR fixed elsewhere, and `RejectReason::malformed_from_serde` is exported for it. (The `trust-task-error` version drift in that crate *is* fixed here; see above.)
2. **`trust-tasks-didcomm` / `-didcomm-v1` / `-tsp`** — a mediator redelivering a queued message is the single most likely source of an accidental duplicate, and these are the crates that see it. Each needs the guard applied to the unpacked document, keyed on the *document* `id` and never on the DIDComm `@id` or `thid` — §7.2 forbids substituting a transport message identifier.
3. **Binding specs** — `bindings/https/0.2` §5 and the DIDComm/TSP equivalents say "Freshness / replay: None" and point at the consumer. That text is still accurate but should now name `ReplayGuard` as the thing the consumer is expected to have, rather than leaving it as an unnamed obligation.
4. **`trust-tasks-capability-client`** — as a producer, it should not reuse an `id` across attempts; §8.4's retry rule now has a consumer that enforces it.

## Tests

New, in both languages: identical resend absorbed and the handler invoked exactly once; differing content under a reused `id` → `idConflict`; a re-signed `proof` over identical content → `idConflict`, not an absorbed retry; the record released when the acceptance window closes; a document refused before the claim does not burn its `id`; an unboundable document refused rather than executed; a store outage fails closed with no store detail on the wire; a retryable refusal releases the claim while a non-retryable one keeps it; future `issuedAt` rejected (and its message free of the consumer's clock); `expiresAt <= issuedAt` rejected; `max_age` window; LRU eviction and the conflict-does-not-displace property; `ProofInvalid`'s wire message carrying no resolver detail; SHA-256 against the published vectors; canonical form independent of received whitespace and member order.

```
cargo build -p trust-tasks-rs   Finished
cargo test  -p trust-tasks-rs   475 lib + 9 replay_guard + 47 other integration; 0 failed
cargo clippy -p trust-tasks-rs --all-targets   no warnings
cargo fmt --check -p trust-tasks-rs            clean
cargo check --workspace --all-targets          clean (no sibling crate needed an edit)

npm test  (trust-tasks-ts)      73 pass, 0 fail   (50 before)
npm run build / npm run smoke   OK — 451 exports, pipeline reachable
npm run check-bindings          349 specs vs 349 TS / 344 Rust modules — all agree
```

title: feat(rs,ts): SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution defence, the freshness bound it needs, and the §10.4 message leaks (#274)
body:
feat(rs,ts): SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution defence, the freshness bound it needs, and the §10.4 message leaks (#274)

* feat(rs): implement SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution defence and the freshness bound it needs

No runtime implemented item 11. Every transport binding delegates replay
defence to the consumer — bindings/https/0.2 §5 says "Freshness / replay:
None", and didcomm/0.2 §6, didcomm-v1/0.2 §6 and tsp/0.1 §7 say the same —
so a captured envelope or bearer-authenticated body, re-sent, executed
acl/grant or vault/release a second time, and an ordinary mediator retry
did it by accident. StandardCode::IdConflict existed and was emitted by
nothing.

ReplayGuard is the seam: an object-safe async trait keyed on the document
id, holding a SHA-256 digest of the canonical serialization of the whole
document. Not the received octets — a re-indented body or a member order
chosen by an intermediary would make a legitimate §8.4 retry look like a
different document, and the consumer would answer it with idConflict or
execute it. The digest covers proof, deliberately unlike the §4.9.3 task
digest over document∖proof: §4.9.3 and §8.4 both require a re-signed proof
over identical content to be idConflict rather than an absorbed retry.
InMemoryReplayGuard is the LRU default, documented as not correct behind a
load balancer.

FreshnessPolicy is what makes the record droppable. validate_basic checked
expiresAt and nothing else; issuedAt was parsed and looked at by nobody, so
a document stamped a year in the future was acceptable for a year, and one
whose expiresAt sat at or before its own issuedAt was accepted whenever the
clock happened to sit before the expiry. §7.2 (Bounding the record) makes
the acceptance window and the record's retention the same bound, and forbids
executing a consequential task on a document that fits in no window at all —
consume_inbound refuses that case rather than pretending to guard it.

consume_inbound takes ConsumeChecks as a required fourth argument, for the
reason PayloadPolicy is required: whether a task is consequential is a
decision only the consumer can make. The claim is taken last, after every
other §7.2 check, so a refused document does not burn its id. A retryable
refusal releases the claim — §8.4 has just invited a bit-for-bit resend, and
holding it would answer that invited retry with the cached failure forever.

ConsumeOutcome::Duplicate is separate from Rejected because §7.2 says so:
"In no case is a duplicate reported as taskFailed; the task did not fail,
it already happened."

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(ts): mirror the replay guard and freshness bound in the runtime pipeline

The two reference implementations must reach the same verdict on the same
document, which is a property this repo maintains deliberately — consume.ts
already says so at the top of the file, and the test sets mirror each other.
Landing item 11 in Rust alone would have made a TypeScript consumer the
non-conforming one.

Same seam, same shape: ReplayGuard as an interface (so a replicated
deployment backs it with a shared store), InMemoryReplayGuard as the LRU
default over a Map, documentDigest over canonicalJson of the whole document
including proof, and consumeInbound taking `checks` as a required option
with the same runtime TypeError guard payloadPolicy has — a JavaScript
caller gets no compile-time check, and defaulting to "keep no record" would
silently reproduce the defect the option exists to remove.

canonicalJson is closer to literal RFC 8785 here than on the Rust side,
because JavaScript's own primitives are what JCS was written against.
sha256Hex and its UTF-8 encoder are hand-rolled rather than reaching for
node:crypto or TextEncoder: the package ships no runtime dependencies and
must typecheck under lib: ["ES2022"] for Node, browsers and workers alike.
Both are pinned to the published FIPS 180-4 vectors.

Also fixes the TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI doc comment, which explained why
the value was 0.3 while the value said 0.5 — the value moved and the prose
did not.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs: correct the README examples and the three trust-task-error versions; bump to 0.11.18 / 0.12.18

The trust-tasks-rs README showed consume_inbound with 7 arguments; it took
8 (payload_policy was added later) and now takes 9. The TS README omitted
the non-optional payloadPolicy. Neither example compiled.

Both READMEs described `trust-task-error/0.1` while both libraries emit
0.5 and the HTTPS server emits 0.2 — three answers on the wire and a fourth
in the docs, with no way for a producer to know which schema an error
response would validate against. trust_task_error_type_uri() is now pub and
documented as the one definition on the Rust side, matching what CLAUDE.md
already assumed; TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI is its TypeScript counterpart.
The HTTPS crate still spells 0.2 out for itself and must adopt the constant
— that crate is owned by concurrent work and is left untouched here.

The rs README's status line claimed "0.1.0 — tracks SPEC.md version 0.1",
which the CHANGELOG's own versioning note had already superseded.

Version: this change is breaking in character — a required argument, two
new enum variants, and a check that refuses documents a consumer used to
accept — and under the rules at the top of CHANGELOG.md it earns 0.12.0.
It ships as 0.11.18 because moving the leading component means editing the
version requirement in six dependent crates and releasing them too, which
is a workspace event and out of scope for a change that touches none of
them. The CHANGELOG entry says so at the top, for the release manager.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(https): stop asserting the proofInvalid leak, and adopt the one trust-task-error constant

Two CI failures against the newly-rebased main, both of them the correct
change meeting stale code.

clippy: CI's toolchain (1.98) has chunks_exact_to_as_chunks, which my local
per-crate run did not. Both call sites in canonical.rs use as_chunks with
the constant sizes now, which is the lint's own suggestion and lets the
compiler see the block and word shapes; the FIPS 180-4 vectors still pass.
A rustdoc redundant-explicit-links error in replay.rs is fixed the same way
— by taking the suggestion, not by allowing the lint.

end_to_end.rs: proof_invalid_when_verifier_rejects asserted
msg.contains("signature") — that the verifier's own error description
reaches the wire. That is the SPEC §10.4 leak the ProofInvalid constant
closes, so the test was pinning the vulnerability. Renamed to
proof_invalid_wire_message_withholds_the_verifier_description, and it now
asserts both halves: the constant on the wire with none of the verifier's
vocabulary in it, and the description still present on RejectReason's
Display, which is what the operator's log renders. Keeping the second half
matters — a change that dropped the reason outright would satisfy the first
and leave operators debugging blind.

server.rs: synthesise_error and suppressed_error_response spelled
trust-task-error/0.2 out for themselves while every other error response
this server emits carries 0.5, because those are built by reject_with in
trust-tasks-rs. So the version a producer saw depended on which branch of
the rejection path its request hit. Both now call
trust_task_error_type_uri(), closing the last of the three-way drift. 0.5
is a forward-minor move from 0.2 and §5.2 says a 0.2 consumer SHOULD
accept it.

trust-tasks-https 0.11.0 -> 0.11.1 with a CHANGELOG entry: CI requires a
version bump for every changed publishable crate, and nothing depends on
this crate, so it does not cascade.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(release): cut trust-tasks-rs 0.12.0 and carry the six dependent crates

The replay guard and freshness bound are breaking under the rules at the top
of trust-tasks-rs/CHANGELOG.md: consume_inbound gains a required argument,
RejectReason and ConsumeOutcome gain variants, and a consumer now refuses
documents it used to accept. Behaviour changed against an unchanged wire
format, which the library version has to say so.

Moving the leading component is a workspace event. The six crates that
depend on trust-tasks-rs each pinned version = "0.11" and re-export its
types, so each moves its requirement to "0.12" and its own leading
component with it, following the shape of the 0.6.5 -> 0.7.0 release in #223:

  trust-tasks-rs                0.11.18 -> 0.12.0
  trust-tasks-https             0.11.1  -> 0.12.0
  trust-tasks-didcomm           0.11.0  -> 0.12.0
  trust-tasks-didcomm-v1        0.10.0  -> 0.11.0
  trust-tasks-proof             0.10.0  -> 0.11.0
  trust-tasks-tsp               0.10.0  -> 0.11.0
  trust-tasks-capability-client 0.10.0  -> 0.11.0
  @openvtc/trust-tasks          0.12.18 -> 0.13.0

The TypeScript runtime mirrors the same seam and breaks the same way, so it
takes its leading component too. Publish in the dependency order publish.yml
uses.

Each dependent CHANGELOG records that its binding still has no ReplayGuard
wired: the HTTPS server runs its own SPEC 7.2 checks and never reaches
consume_inbound, and the DIDComm and TSP bindings are where mediator
redelivery actually produces duplicates.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: chore(scripts): remove the authoring friction that shipped the registry's front-matter monoculture
body:
Removes authoring friction from the registry build tooling, and closes three defect classes that had already shipped. Every change leaves the build green; where a new lint would fail existing content it ships as a counted warning with an explicit allowlist rather than as a broken CI.

`npm run validate`, `npm run build` and `npm run check-bindings` all pass — output at the bottom.

## Before / after

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Spec-discovery implementations | 4, following 2 different rules | 1 module, 2 `.mjs` consumers wired |
| Version folders with one of `spec.md` / `payload.schema.json` | silently half-published | build failure |
| Specs with a conforming `## Security & Privacy` | 0 of 349 | 0 of 349, all 349 enumerated as countable debt |
| Specs with no `## Security & Privacy` at all | 14, unreported | 14, on the allowlist and counted |
| Front-matter template in `CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md` | fails `npm run validate` (omits required `sideEffects`, `exposure`) | validates |
| Scaffold script | none | `npm run new-spec -- <slug>`, output validates unmodified |
| `## Authorization` coverage | 208 consequential specs, 70 specs carry the section (58 of them consequential) | scaffold emits the stub whenever the declared classes make the task consequential |
| Depth-relative `SPEC.md` links | 754 across 218 files | 0 — rewritten to `/SPEC.md#…` |
| Root-relative links checked by the build | not at all (the check only matched `..`) | resolved from the repository root |
| `targetFrameworkVersion` | `M.N` only — a spec written to the canonical text fails the build | `M.N` and `M.N.P` |
| `SPEC.md` header | Document version 0.3 (Appendix B documents 0.4; 23 specs target it) | 0.4, with a canonical-source note |
| `authors` / `keywords` | required; `authors` byte-identical in 345 of 349 | optional, derived from CODEOWNERS/git and slug+category |
| `proofRequirement` / `sideEffects` / `exposure` rationales rendered | nowhere — zero hits in `pages.jsx` and `components.jsx` | a "Why this task is classified as it is" section on every spec page |

## What is in each commit

1. **`chore(scripts): one spec-discovery rule`** — `scripts/lib/specs.mjs`. Discovery was implemented four times under two rules: the registry build and the bindings check found a spec by `spec.md`, the Rust codegen and `build-ts-bindings.mjs` found one by `payload.schema.json`. Those agree only while every version folder carries both, and nothing reports the moment one does not. Now one rule: **both** files required, one without the other **fails the build**, and a slug directory nested among another slug's version siblings **warns** (`vtc/auth/recognise` and `witness/session` both do this today — that ambiguity is what made an earlier review's "missing `spec.md`" reading plausible; the file was in fact present and the spec registered, and the consolidation stands on its own merits).

   This is **not** the `expectedPolicy()` duplication `CLAUDE.md` protects. That one is a deliberate independent derivation of the §7.2 policy; "which directories are specs" has one right answer and two implementations of it can only agree or be a bug. A note in the module says so.

2. **`chore(scripts): lint the Security & Privacy section`** — requires the section plus four sub-headings (**Data carried**, **Correlation**, **Retention**, **Consent/purpose**). A **warning** today, with all 349 non-conforming specs listed in `scripts/lib/security-privacy-allowlist.json`. The list may only shrink: a spec **not** on it warns by name, an allowlisted spec that starts conforming is reported as a stale entry to delete, and an entry naming a spec that no longer exists is reported too. `TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY=1` turns every warning into a build failure — that is the documented switch, and when the allowlist empties it becomes the default. Template added to `CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md`.

3. **`fix(specs): three-part targetFrameworkVersion, SPEC.md header 0.4`** — the pattern now accepts `M.N.P`, and `checkExampleDocuments()` truncates to the `M.N` prefix when picking the envelope schema, so a spec written to the canonical text is still example-validated rather than landing in the silent "NOT validated" bucket (verified: 533 example documents before and after). `SPEC.md`'s header is corrected with a note recording `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec` as canonical. **Nothing restructured, generated or deleted** — whether this copy should be generated from the canonical repo or dropped is a working-group decision that is still open, and the note says so.

4. **`feat(specs): framework 0.5.0 declarations`** — companion to **trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#2**, added at the coordinator's request. All three are SHOULD, so all three are OPTIONAL and none is added to `required`; no existing spec is newly invalid.
   - `retention` — `{class, rationale}`, class `transient | exchange | durable`. Absent reads as `durable`. Carried into `registry.json` and rendered on the spec page.
   - `exposure.ingests` — `none | metadata | personal | secret`. The enum deliberately differs from `discloses` (no `personal`) and the two are **not** merged. Making `exposure.rationale` required for `personal`/`secret` extends the `if/then` the object already uses for `discloses: secret` — with a `required: ["ingests"]` guard, without which the branch would match every spec that omits the member and demand a rationale from all 349.
   - `parties[].identifierScope` — `pairwise | public | any`. `checkIdentifierScopeJustification()` warns when a `public` declaration is never discussed in the prose. It asks only that the body discuss it: a lint cannot tell a justification from a sentence, but it can tell one from silence.

   Nothing under `specs/trust-task-discovery/` is touched — re-issuing it to declare `proof: RECOMMENDED` is a separate spec-authoring change.

5. **`feat(registry): optional authors/keywords, rationales on the page`** — derived defaults (CODEOWNERS → git; slug + category), `authorsSource` / `keywordsSource` carried so a derived value cannot be mistaken for an editorial claim, and the three `rationale` fields finally rendered. Also fixes the Metadata row's blank **Proof requirement** for the per-variant `{request, response}` form. `TT_CATEGORIES` and the category enum are untouched, so the `data.js` lockstep trap is not in play.

6. **`chore(scripts): npm run new-spec`** — `npm run new-spec -- <slug> [--version 0.1] [--no-response]`. Output passes `npm run validate` unmodified (verified for the request/response, fire-and-forget, and destructive + secret + acts-as-subject variants). It derives `proofRequirement` from the declared classes so it cannot emit something `checkProofFloor()` rejects, refuses reserved slugs (**both** `trust-task*` and `trust-ceremony*`), and carries commented stubs for the three 0.5.0 declarations. `CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md`'s template is fixed, its reserved-slug text now says `trust-ceremony*` as well, and `payload.invalid-examples.json` — which 254 specs carry and the file-layout section never mentioned — is documented, including that it is the only thing in the toolchain that tests a schema's negative space.

7. **`chore(scripts): root-relative /SPEC.md links + codemod`** — renderer resolves `/SPEC.md#anchor` (and any surviving `../` chain) onto the SPA's `/specification` route, which is a better destination than the relative form ever reached: that one downloaded a raw markdown file. The build's link check now validates root-relative links from the repository root.

8. **`docs(specs): rewrite 754 links`** — the codemod's output, on its own, 736 changed lines across 218 files, no prose touched.

## Things I deliberately left alone

- **The Rust codegen and `scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs` still carry their own spec walkers.** `trust-tasks-codegen` is owned elsewhere; `build-ts-bindings.mjs` is a generator whose output tree is owned elsewhere and which I was asked not to regenerate. Both should adopt `scripts/lib/specs.mjs` (the Rust one by porting the rule). Noted in the module header.
- **No bindings were regenerated.** Nothing here requires it: the codegen reads neither `targetFrameworkVersion` nor `authors`/`keywords` nor any of the three 0.5.0 fields, and `npm run check-bindings` passes unchanged (349 specs vs 349 TS and 344 Rust modules, all agreeing). If a reviewer disagrees, regeneration is a follow-up, not a hidden edit in this PR.
- **The 349 non-conforming Security & Privacy sections.** Rewriting them is spec-authoring work owned per slug by CODEOWNERS; this PR makes the debt countable and gives it a burn-down path.
- **`specs/trust-task-discovery/`**, per the coordinator's instruction.
- **The two nested-slug layouts** (`vtc/auth/recognise/challenge`, `witness/session/submit`). Both are legal and the registry handles them; they now warn so the ambiguity is visible, but restructuring them is a spec-owner decision.
- **`SPEC.md`'s structure.** Only the version header and the canonical-source note changed.

## One caveat worth a reviewer's attention

GitHub's markdown renderer does **not** resolve a root-relative link against the repository root, so `/SPEC.md#anchor` works on the registry site and in the build's link check but not when browsing `spec.md` on github.com. The trade was taken deliberately — the rendered site is where specs are read, and the depth-relative form was silently broken *there* for 135 links across 65 files. Recorded in `CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md`. Say the word and the codemod is trivially reversible.

## Verification

```
$ npm run validate
Trust Tasks build (validate-only)
  warn: specs/vtc/auth/recognise: holds version folder(s) [0.1, 0.2] alongside nested slug directory [challenge]. …
  warn: specs/witness/session: holds version folder(s) [0.1] alongside nested slug directory [submit]. …
  warn: 1 fenced JSON block(s) did not parse and were skipped …
  validated 533 example documents against the framework envelope schema
  Security & Privacy: 0/349 spec(s) carry the section and all four sub-headings; 349 allowlisted as
    pre-existing debt, 0 not allowlisted (warning — set TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY=1 to fail the build)
  warn: vta/contexts/create/1.0/payload.schema.json: $defs.Response declares neither additionalProperties nor unevaluatedProperties
  … (7 more pre-existing $defs.Response warnings, unchanged by this PR)
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.

$ npm run build
… same, then:
  wrote website/assets/tasks.generated.js
  wrote website/registry.json
  synced specs/ → website/specs/
  synced bindings/ → website/bindings/
  synced ceremonies/ → website/ceremonies/
  synced SPEC.md → website/SPEC.md
Done.

$ npm run check-bindings
Bindings conformance: 349 specifications checked against 349 TypeScript and 344 Rust modules — all agree.

$ npm run codemod:spec-links
Rewrote 754 links across 218 files under specs/
```

New warning counts: **2** nested-slug warnings, **1** Security & Privacy summary line (0 conforming, 349 allowlisted, 0 unallowlisted offenders), **0** `identifierScope` warnings. The 8 pre-existing warnings are unchanged.

Both `website/assets/pages.jsx` and `website/assets/components.jsx` were syntax-checked through the same `@babel/standalone` version the site loads.

title: chore(scripts): remove the authoring friction that shipped the registry's front-matter monoculture (#273)
body:
chore(scripts): remove the authoring friction that shipped the registry's front-matter monoculture (#273)

* chore(scripts): one spec-discovery rule, so the build and the generators cannot describe different registries

Discovery was implemented four times with two rules: build-registry.mjs and
check-bindings-conformance.mjs found a spec by spec.md, while
trust-tasks-codegen and build-ts-bindings.mjs found one by
payload.schema.json. The two rules agree only while every version folder
carries both files, and neither side reports the moment one does not — a
folder with only payload.schema.json is a spec to the generators and does not
exist to the registry.

scripts/lib/specs.mjs states the rule once: a spec version directory contains
BOTH files, one without the other is a build error, and a slug directory
nested among another slug's version siblings warns (vtc/auth/recognise and
witness/session both do this today).

Wired into the two .mjs consumers. This is not the expectedPolicy()
duplication CLAUDE.md protects — that one is a deliberate independent
derivation; "which directories are specs" has one right answer.

trust-tasks-codegen/src/main.rs and scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs still carry
their own walkers and should adopt the same rule.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(scripts): lint the Security & Privacy section, with the 349-spec backlog enumerated rather than ignored

The section was optional in practice — CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md listed it under
"plus anything else useful" and nothing checked it. 14 of 349 specs carry no
such section, 206 of the 335 that do are three non-blank lines or fewer, and
corpus-wide two specs mention data minimisation.

checkSecurityPrivacySections() requires the section plus four sub-headings —
Data carried, Correlation, Retention, Consent/purpose — chosen as the questions
a task registry's reader needs and that free prose reliably skips. It prints a
summary count on every build.

It ships as a warning with every currently non-conforming spec listed in
scripts/lib/security-privacy-allowlist.json, so the build stays green and the
debt is one number in one file. The list may only shrink: a spec not on it
warns by name, an allowlisted spec that starts conforming is reported as a
stale entry, and an entry naming a spec that no longer exists is reported too.
TT_STRICT_SECURITY_PRIVACY=1 turns every warning into a build failure; when the
allowlist empties, make that the default and delete the file.

CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md gains the template and the burn-down instructions.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(specs): accept the three-part targetFrameworkVersion the canonical spec now requires, and correct SPEC.md's header to 0.4

Two data fixes with more effect than their size.

targetFrameworkVersion's pattern accepted only MAJOR.MINOR, so a spec written
to the framework spec repo's normative text — which now requires
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — failed `npm run build` outright. The pattern now accepts
both; three-part is preferred for new specs and two-part stays valid, because
349 published specs declare it and re-versioning them would be a wire-visible
change made for an editorial reason. checkExampleDocuments() truncates to the
MAJOR.MINOR prefix when selecting the envelope schema under specs/_framework/,
so a three-part declaration is still example-validated rather than falling into
the "no envelope schema compiled, NOT validated" bucket. A companion PR on
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec carries the normative text.

SPEC.md's header said "Document version 0.3" while Appendix B documents 0.4 and
23 specs target it. Corrected, with a note recording that
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec is the canonical source and this copy must
be kept in sync. Nothing restructured or generated: whether this copy should be
generated from the canonical repo or dropped is a working-group decision that
is still open, and the note says so.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(specs): accept framework 0.5.0's retention, exposure.ingests and parties[].identifierScope

Companion to trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#2, which adds three declarations
to SPEC §7.3. Without meta-schema support the build rejects any spec written to
framework 0.5.0.

All three are SHOULD, so all three are OPTIONAL: none is added to `required`,
and no existing spec is newly invalid.

* `retention` — {class, rationale}, class one of transient | exchange | durable.
  The third descriptive dimension beside sideEffects (integrity) and exposure
  (confidentiality and agency): how long what the recipient receives lives.
  Absent or unrecognized reads as `durable` — the only reading that cannot
  understate what a recipient is holding by omission. Carried into
  registry.json and tasks.generated.js, and rendered on the spec page.

* `exposure.ingests` — none | metadata | personal | secret, the inbound
  counterpart of `discloses`. The enums deliberately differ: `discloses` has no
  `personal` because what a task returns is assessed for whether the caller may
  hold it, while what a task accepts is assessed for what the recipient must now
  protect and minimise — and personal-but-not-secret data is exactly the class
  that changes those obligations without being secret. Not merged, on purpose.
  `exposure.rationale` becomes REQUIRED when ingests is personal or secret,
  expressed by extending the existing if/then the object already uses for
  `discloses: secret` — with a `required: ["ingests"]` guard, without which the
  branch would match every spec that omits the member and demand a rationale
  from all 349.

* `parties[].identifierScope` — pairwise | public | any. `public` forecloses
  pairwise identifiers for every producer of the task, so framework 0.5.0 asks
  the prose to justify it; checkIdentifierScopeJustification() warns when a
  `public` declaration is never discussed in the body. It asks only that the
  body discuss the declaration — a lint cannot tell a justification from a
  sentence, but it can tell one from silence, which is the failure mode.

Nothing under specs/trust-task-discovery/ is touched: re-issuing it to declare
proof RECOMMENDED is a separate spec-authoring change. No binding regeneration
is implied — the codegen does not read any of these fields.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* feat(registry): drop the front matter that carried no information, and put the three rationales on the page

Two findings, one change.

`authors` was byte-identical in 345 of 349 specs and 46% of declared keywords
were literally a slug segment or the spec's own category. Both become OPTIONAL
in the meta-schema and are derived when omitted: `authors` from CODEOWNERS —
which already names who reviews each slug and is kept current because GitHub
enforces it — falling back to the spec folder's git history; `keywords` from the
slug's segments plus the category, which is what 46% of hand-written lists
already were. A declared value always wins: the derivation removes ceremony, it
does not overrule an author with something to say. The registry carries
`authorsSource` / `keywordsSource` so a derived value cannot be mistaken for an
editorial claim, and the spec page labels it.

The three `rationale` fields — proofRequirement, sideEffects, exposure — are
REQUIRED, are the most carefully written security prose in the registry, and
were rendered NOWHERE: zero hits in pages.jsx and components.jsx. They reached
registry.json for machine consumers and never reached a human. A new "Why this
task is classified as it is" section sits between the Metadata grid and the
spec's own prose, which is where the question arises — the grid states the
levels, this says why. It renders framework 0.5.0's exposure.ingests and
retention too, and states the descriptive-not-prescriptive rule so the panel
cannot be read as a consent requirement.

Two fixes fall out: the panel renders the per-variant proofRequirement form
({request, response}), which the Metadata row's `.requirement` read leaves
blank, and the sidebar TOC gains the new section.

TT_CATEGORIES and the category enum are untouched, so the data.js lockstep
CLAUDE.md warns about is not in play.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(scripts): npm run new-spec scaffolds a spec that validates as generated

The documented path for a new spec was "copy the front-matter template from
CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md" — and that template omitted `sideEffects` and `exposure`,
both of which the meta-schema lists as required. Copying the official template
produced a spec that failed the build, so nobody copied it: authors copied a
neighbouring spec instead, inheriting its keywords, its error codes, its
Security & Privacy paragraph and its depth-specific ../../../../SPEC.md links.
Both halves of the registry's front-matter monoculture start there.

  npm run new-spec -- <slug> [--version 0.1] [--no-response]

emits spec.md + payload.schema.json that pass `npm run validate` unmodified,
with:

  * every required declaration, plus commented stubs for framework 0.5.0's
    retention / exposure.ingests / parties[].identifierScope so an author sees
    them without being made to fill them in;
  * an ## Authorization stub when the declared side-effect and exposure classes
    make the task consequential — 208 specs are, and only 70 carry the section;
  * the four ## Security & Privacy sub-headings the build now lints for;
  * a proofRequirement derived from those same classes, so the scaffold cannot
    emit something checkProofFloor() rejects;
  * root-relative /SPEC.md#... cross-references that do not depend on slug depth;
  * an example document that validates against the framework envelope schema.

It refuses reserved slugs (both trust-task* and trust-ceremony*) rather than
emitting something that cannot validate, and infers a category from the slug's
family.

CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md is corrected alongside it: the front-matter template gains
the two required declarations it was missing (and the three 0.5.0 optional
ones); the reserved-slug rule now says trust-ceremony* as well as trust-task*,
which is what SPEC §6.1 and the meta-schema have enforced since framework 0.4;
and payload.invalid-examples.json — which 254 specs carry and the file-layout
section never mentioned — is documented, including that it is the only thing in
the toolchain that tests a schema's negative space.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(scripts): support root-relative /SPEC.md links, and add the codemod that converts the corpus

A spec's prose links SPEC.md 754 times and the `../` count in each link is a
function of slug depth — four from auth/passkey/enroll/start/0.1, three from
acl/grant/0.1. That makes a link's correctness a property of where the file
sits rather than of what it says, so it breaks when a spec moves, when a slug
gains a segment, and above all when a paragraph is copied from a neighbouring
spec at a different depth — which is how specs get written here. 135 such links
across 65 files had drifted before build-registry.mjs grew a check for them, and
they were broken on the live site rather than merely wrong in the repo. The
check catches the next one; it does not remove the reason there is a next one.

Three parts:

* The renderer resolves both `/SPEC.md#anchor` and any surviving `../` chain
  onto the SPA's own /specification route — a better destination than the
  relative form ever reached, which downloaded a raw markdown file.
* The build's link check now validates root-relative links from the repository
  root, so the new form is verified rather than merely unchecked (the old check
  only ever matched links beginning `..`).
* scripts/codemod-spec-links.mjs converts the corpus. It rewrites only a chain
  that actually resolves to this repo's SPEC.md, skips fenced code, and reports
  what it declined to touch — normalising an already-broken link into a
  differently-broken one would destroy the evidence of the bug.

The codemod's output lands in the next commit, on its own, so this diff stays
readable.

Caveat recorded in CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md: GitHub does not resolve root-relative
links against the repo root, so these read correctly on the registry site and
in CI but not when browsing spec.md on github.com. The site is where specs are
read, and the depth-relative form was silently broken there for 135 links.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* docs(specs): rewrite 754 depth-relative SPEC.md links to the root-relative form

Mechanical output of `npm run codemod:spec-links` — 754 links across 218 files
under specs/ (216 spec.md plus the six family CONVENTIONS.md). No prose changed:
every hunk turns `](../../../../SPEC.md#anchor)` into `](/SPEC.md#anchor)`, with
the `../` count varying by slug depth and the anchor untouched.

The codemod rewrote only chains that resolve to this repository's SPEC.md and
skipped fenced code blocks; it reported nothing it declined to touch, so no
already-broken link was laundered into a differently-broken one.

`npm run build` is green and the link check — extended in the previous commit to
resolve root-relative links from the repository root — passes on all 754.

Kept as its own commit so the 736-line diff is skimmable and the tooling that
produced it is reviewable separately.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: test(vta): make the coverage figure stable, and cover the signing oracle (#1116)
body:
test(vta): make the coverage figure stable, and cover the signing oracle (#1116)

#1115's coverage figure jittered: 31 then 33, then 33/30/33, off identical code
with the same 28 suites and the same 1281 tests passing every run. The cause was
in the recording, and it was mine.

`writeln!` on an unbuffered `File` can issue the text and the newline as two
separate write syscalls. Test binaries run their tests on many threads, so two
threads interleaved *between* those calls and produced lines like
`…/acl/grant/0.1#response…/dids/get/1.0#response`. Both tasks were then lost,
because the reporter matches whole lines — three or four mangled lines per run,
and the count moving by exactly the tasks they swallowed.

`O_APPEND` makes a single write atomic against other appenders, so formatting
the newline into the buffer and issuing one `write_all` is what actually buys
the atomicity the append mode promises. Three consecutive runs now report 37
observed tasks with zero mangled lines.

Two further robustness fixes found on the way. Coverage files are now written
one per process rather than appended to one shared file, and are named for the
test binary so a number that moves is attributable. And `record_observed` no
longer lets the in-memory dedup gate the write: it marked a task seen and then,
if the write failed, never retried it — one transient failure silently lost the
task for the whole process, in the direction that under-reports.

Covers `keys/{show,sign,rename,revoke}/0.1`, which took coverage from 29 to 33.
The gate caught a real violation on the first newly-covered task: `KeyRecord`
emitted `contextId: null`, because `label`, `contextId` and `seedId` all lacked
`skip_serializing_if`. That component is returned by six tasks, so one fix
covers all of them — and it is direct evidence for why the coverage number
matters, since two tasks' worth of new coverage immediately found a defect.

Refs #1059

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(didcomm): close six fail-open paths in the DIDComm bindings and capability client
body:
Six fail-open paths across the two DIDComm bindings and the capability client. Each one below states the attack or failure it closes, the evidence, and the binding-spec clause the code is restored to.

Scope is `trust-tasks-didcomm/`, `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1/` and `trust-tasks-capability-client/` only. `bindings/` and `specs/` were read, not touched.

---

### 1. A bare JWS was accepted as an authenticated sender — MEDIUM

**Evidence:** `trust-tasks-didcomm/src/pack.rs:110-113` matched `UnpackResult::Signed { signer_kid: Some(..) }`, took the signer as the transport-authenticated peer, and set `local_did = None`.

**What that let through.** A JWS is signed but sealed to nobody. It has no recipient binding, so the *same bytes* verify for every party that holds the signer's key — one document can be fanned out to a whole deployment and each consumer accepts it as addressed to itself. And because `local` was `None`, SPEC §4.8.1's `recipient` cross-check was not *failed*, it was *skipped*: the one check that would have caught the misdelivery had nothing to compare against.

**Restored to:** `bindings/didcomm/0.2` §2 ("The DIDComm message **MUST** be encrypted using DIDComm's *authcrypt* algorithm") and §4 ("Envelope arrived as anoncrypt or plaintext … the message **MUST NOT** enter the framework pipeline"). Now `DidcommError::SignedNotAuthcrypted`.

The regression test asserts the fan-out rather than describing it: `agent.unpack` is shown returning `Ok(Signed { .. })` for the addressee *and* for an unrelated bystander who merely knows the signer, and `unpack_trust_task` is shown refusing both.

### 2. A fragment-less `kid` silently downgraded an authenticated identity — MEDIUM

**Evidence:** `trust-tasks-didcomm/src/pack.rs:176-178` — `did_from_kid` returned `None` when the `kid` carried no `#`.

**What that let through.** A DIDComm `kid` is a DID *URL*. Returning `None` for a malformed one is not a rejection: the peer became `None`, the pipeline fell back to the in-band `issuer`, and the transport cross-check was skipped — so a sender with a malformed `kid` could name any `issuer` it liked and be believed. An authenticated identity was reclassified as unauthenticated instead of raising an error.

**Restored to:** §3's identity mapping, which defines the transport-authenticated sender as "the verified `sender_kid` … normalised to its bare DID". A value that cannot be normalised is not a sender. Now `DidcommError::UnqualifiedSenderKid`.

The *recipient* `kid` deliberately keeps its passthrough: unlike the sender case that already fails closed, since a non-DID value simply fails §4.8.1's comparison and surfaces as `identityMismatch`.

### 2b. `expected_sender_did` was a lookup hint, never a check — found while fixing 2

**Evidence:** same match arm. The returned `sender_kid` comes from the JWE `apu`/`skid`, which is written by the sender; the DID that actually authenticated is the one whose public key opened the ECDH-1PU wrap. Nothing compared the two.

**What that let through.** A peer authenticates with its own key while labelling the envelope `skid: did:web:victim.example#key-1`. The consumer decrypts successfully — its own expectation of who this is was only ever used to pick a key — and hands `did:web:victim.example` to §4.8.1 as the *transport-authenticated* sender, which then confirms an in-band `issuer` of the same forged DID. The pre-fix run of the new test shows exactly this: `peer: Some("did:web:victim.example")`.

**Restored to:** §3 and §6's "Mapping to a VID" row — "`sender_kid` normalises to its bare DID **directly**. No external state is consulted". Now `DidcommError::SenderKidMismatch`.

### 3. The unknown-sender path was O(known peers), and an allowlist only by accident — LOW

**Evidence:** `trust-tasks-didcomm/src/pack.rs:65-71` documented the multi-peer pattern as looping over known senders, retrying on `IdentityNotFound` — one ECDH-1PU decrypt per candidate per inbound message.

That loop *was* the sender allowlist: a peer the agent had never been given could not be unpacked, so it could not be accepted. The property was real but incidental — invisible in the type signature, and lost to any refactor that made unpacking cheaper or the peer store broader.

**Fix:** `SenderAllowlist` + `unpack_trust_task_from` read the `skid` from the JWE protected header, check the DID it names against a *declared* list **before any decryption**, and unpack once. An empty allowlist permits nothing. `SenderAllowlist::from_agent_peers(&agent)` reproduces exactly the set the old loop could accept, so the migration is behaviour-preserving.

The `skid` is unauthenticated when read — it selects a key, it proves nothing — which is why 2b's re-check exists: the allowlist means something only because the verified sender is confirmed to be the DID that was looked up.

### 4. The capability client decided success from free text — HIGH

**Evidence:** `trust-tasks-capability-client/src/lib.rs:185-187` returned `WriteOutcome::IdempotentSuccess` for a `taskFailed` whose **`message`** contained `already_granted:` or `not_granted:`. And `:152-156` extracted the reply's `thid` and never compared it to anything.

**What that let through.** Two distinct failures.

*Free text as a control surface.* SPEC §8.2 defines `message` as non-normative, "intended for logs and operator UI". Keying on it means the client's behaviour hinges on wording the emitting service may reword, translate or drop — and in the other direction, a **genuine** `taskFailed` whose operator message merely quotes the phrase ("registry write aborted; **not** `already_granted:` the tuple was never written") is reported to the caller as a completed grant. A failed trust-registry write recorded as done.

*No correlation.* The reply was classified without ever being matched to the request. Any reply arriving on a shared inbound path could resolve a write the caller was still waiting on — including the `IdempotentSuccess` shortcut, which is precisely the outcome an attacker would want to forge.

**Restored to:** SPEC §8.5 extended codes, which the registry entries for these two tasks *already declare*: `specs/git-trust/grant/0.1/spec.md:34` (`git-trust/grant:already_granted`) and `specs/git-trust/revoke/0.1/spec.md:34` (`git-trust/revoke:not_granted`). The §4.10 lowerCamelCase spellings are accepted alongside them so a later registry re-casing is not a flag day; both are namespaced codes either way. Correlation is SPEC §4.9: `classify_git_trust_reply`, `parse_capability_reply` and `parse_envelope_reply` now take the expected thread and return `None` for a document belonging to another exchange.

`correlation_thread` gives the value to hold from the moment you send; `replies_to` is the bare predicate; `parse_envelope_document_for` is the correlating counterpart of `parse_envelope_document` — which is unchanged, and now documents that its `threadId` is a dispatch key, not a check.

**Deprecated compatibility path.** `ReplyPolicy::with_legacy_free_text()` restores the substring match for a peer that still emits nothing else. Opt-in, never the default, marked `// DEPRECATED:` at the call site, with its removal in the next MAJOR recorded in the crate's new CHANGELOG. The fix belongs on the emitting side.

### 5. The legacy basic-message carriage had no sunset — MEDIUM

**Evidence:** `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1/src/pack.rs:164` accepted any `basic-message` carrying a `trust-task` attachment.

**What that means.** `basic-message` is the Aries **chat** type. While that gate is open, any chat message from any established connection that happens to carry the attachment is a framework input — from every peer, with no end date. `bindings/didcomm-v1/0.2` §2.3 puts the contraction in a future MAJOR but left implementations no way to reach it early, and no way to see who still needed it.

**Fix:** the carriage sits behind the `legacy-basic-message` Cargo feature.

**Default: ON.** §2.3 is a **MUST** — "a `0.2` *consumer* **MUST** also accept the `0.1` carriage" — so default-off would ship a non-conforming default build. Nothing in this repo consumes the crate either way (checked: no reverse dependency outside the workspace member list), so the tie is broken by the spec. Turning it off is now a deliberate, documented departure available to a deployment that knows its peers have migrated (`default-features = false`), and §2.3's own contraction has a switch to land on when it comes. It is a genuine compile-out, not a runtime flag.

§2.3 also **SHOULD**s surfacing the superseded carriage "so an operator can see which peers have not migrated", which was not done at all. Every message on the legacy path is now logged at `warn` through the `log` facade — naming the sender — and reported as `Carriage::LegacyBasicMessage` on the handler, for callers that would rather meter it than grep logs.

### 6. Stale binding identifier — LOW

**Evidence:** `trust-tasks-didcomm/src/handler.rs:14` declared `didcomm/0.1`.

Bumped to `https://trusttasks.org/binding/didcomm/0.2` per `bindings/didcomm/0.2` §1. `ENVELOPE_TYPE` stays pinned at `.../didcomm/0.1/envelope` — §1 and §7.1 keep it deliberately unmoved so `0.1` and `0.2` implementations remain mutually intelligible on the wire; the README now says so, since the two differing versions read like a typo otherwise.

`trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` was checked for the same drift and had none — its `BINDING_URI` was already `didcomm-v1/0.2`.

---

## Versions

| Crate | | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.10.0 → **0.11.0** | **Breaking.** Envelopes it used to accept are now rejected (1, 2, 2b). A break in what a consumer observes, even though no wire format moved. |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.9.0 → **0.10.0** | **Breaking.** Signatures gain the expected thread, and the free-text path is no longer the default (4). |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | 0.9.0 → **0.10.0** | Minor. The legacy carriage is default-on, so the default build behaves as 0.9.0 did; the additions are `Carriage` and the handler accessor. |

`Cargo.lock` picks up `base64` (reading the JWE protected header) and `log` (the superseded-carriage warning), both already resolved in the graph — no new external crates.

## Tests

`trust-tasks-didcomm/tests/fail_closed.rs` is new; the rest are in-crate.

| Test | Covers |
|---|---|
| `signed_only_envelopes_are_rejected` | 1 — including the fan-out, asserted for a bystander |
| `a_fragment_less_sender_kid_is_an_error_not_an_absent_sender` | 2 |
| `a_skid_naming_a_different_did_than_the_key_that_opened_it_is_rejected` | 2b |
| `the_sender_allowlist_gates_before_any_decryption` | 3 |
| `anoncrypt_and_non_jwe_bytes_have_no_advertised_sender` | 3 — nothing to check is not a pass |
| `authcrypt_still_round_trips` | positive control for 1 |
| `idempotent_success_is_keyed_on_the_extended_code_not_the_message` | 4 — including the taskFailed that quotes the phrase |

title: fix(didcomm): close six fail-open paths in the DIDComm bindings and capability client (#272)
body:
fix(didcomm): close six fail-open paths in the DIDComm bindings and capability client (#272)

* fix(didcomm): a bare JWS and a fragment-less sender kid are rejections, not identities

Binding didcomm/0.2 §2 makes authcrypt a MUST and §4 states that an envelope
with no authenticated sender MUST NOT enter the framework pipeline. Three
inbound paths fell short of that, each failing open rather than closed.

A signed-only envelope was accepted as an authenticated sender with the local
DID set to None (pack.rs:110-113). A JWS is signed but sealed to nobody: it
carries no recipient binding, so one message delivered to every party in a
deployment verifies for each of them, and because the local DID was None the
§4.8.1 recipient cross-check was not failed but skipped. Now
SignedNotAuthcrypted.

A sender_kid with no #fragment reduced to None (pack.rs:176-178), which
downgraded an authenticated identity to an unauthenticated one: the pipeline
then fell back to the in-band issuer with the transport cross-check skipped, so
a sender with a malformed kid could name any issuer and be believed. Now
UnqualifiedSenderKid. The recipient kid keeps its passthrough — a non-DID value
there simply fails §4.8.1's comparison, which is fail-closed already.

expected_sender_did was used only as a key-lookup hint and never enforced. The
skid/apu is written by the sender, so the DID it carries is a claim; the DID
that authenticated is the one whose key opened the ECDH-1PU wrap. A peer could
authenticate as itself while labelling the envelope with another party's DID
and have the label handed to §4.8.1. Now SenderKidMismatch.

The multi-peer path also becomes explicit. The documented pattern was to loop
over known senders retrying on IdentityNotFound (pack.rs:65-71) — O(known
peers) ECDH-1PU decrypts per inbound message, and an allowlist only by
accident, since it held solely because an unknown peer could not be unpacked.
SenderAllowlist and unpack_trust_task_from state it: the skid is read from the
JWE protected header, checked against a declared list before any decryption,
and unpacked once. An empty allowlist permits nothing;
SenderAllowlist::from_agent_peers reproduces the old set exactly. The skid is
unauthenticated when read — it selects a key, it proves nothing — which is why
the verified sender is re-checked against it.

BINDING_URI moves to didcomm/0.2, matching the current specification.
ENVELOPE_TYPE stays pinned at 0.1/envelope — binding §1 and §7.1 keep it so
that 0.1 and 0.2 implementations remain mutually intelligible.

tests/fail_closed.rs asserts the fan-out the JWS path enabled rather than
describing it: the same bytes unpack for the addressee and for an unrelated
bystander who merely knows the signer.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(didcomm-v1): give the legacy basic-message carriage a switch and a log line

pack.rs:164 accepted any Aries basic-message carrying a trust-task attachment
as a Trust Task, per binding didcomm-v1/0.2 §2.3. basic-message is the Aries
*chat* type, so with that gate open, any chat message from any established
connection that happens to carry the attachment is a framework input — from
every peer, indefinitely. §2.3 places the contraction in a future MAJOR but
left implementations no way to reach it early, and no way to see who still
needed it.

The carriage now sits behind the `legacy-basic-message` Cargo feature,
default-on. Default-on because §2.3 makes accepting the 0.1 carriage a MUST for
a conforming 0.2 consumer and nothing in this repository depends on it either
way; turning it off is a deliberate, documented departure from that MUST for a
deployment that knows its peers have migrated. It is a real compile-out — with
the feature off the gate is a single equality against the dedicated type and
such a message is WrongMessageType.

§2.3 also SHOULDs surfacing the superseded carriage so an operator can see
which peers have not moved, which was not done at all. Every message arriving
on it is now logged at warn through the log facade, naming the sender, and
reported as Carriage::LegacyBasicMessage on the handler for callers that would
rather meter it than grep logs.

Tested both ways: the accept-and-report test compiles under the default
features, the refusal test under --no-default-features.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(capability-client): decide idempotent success from the error code, and match the reply to its request

lib.rs:185-187 returned WriteOutcome::IdempotentSuccess for a taskFailed whose
free-text `message` contained "already_granted:" or "not_granted:". SPEC §8.2
defines `message` as non-normative text intended for logs and operator UI, so
this made the client's behaviour depend on wording no emitter promised to keep
stable — and, in the other direction, silently reported a genuine taskFailed
whose operator message merely quoted the phrase as a completed write.

The control surface is now the namespaced extended code of SPEC §8.5, which the
registry entries for these two tasks already declare:
git-trust/grant:already_granted and git-trust/revoke:not_granted. Their §4.10
lowerCamelCase spellings are accepted too, so a later registry re-casing is not
a flag day. Both are codes either way; neither is free text.

Separately, lib.rs:152-156 extracted the reply's threadId and nothing ever
compared it to the outstanding request. Any reply arriving on a shared inbound
path could therefore resolve a write the caller was still waiting on —
including the IdempotentSuccess shortcut, which is the outcome an attacker
would most want to forge. classify_git_trust_reply, parse_capability_reply and
parse_envelope_reply now take the expected thread and return None for a
document belonging to another exchange (SPEC §4.9). correlation_thread gives
the value to hold, replies_to is the bare predicate, and
parse_envelope_document_for is the correlating counterpart of
parse_envelope_document — which is unchanged, and now says plainly that its
threadId is a dispatch key rather than a check.

The free-text form survives only as an opt-in compatibility path
(ReplyPolicy::with_legacy_free_text, marked // DEPRECATED: at the call site)
for a peer that emits nothing else. Its removal in the next MAJOR is recorded
in the crate's new CHANGELOG.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(release): trust-tasks-didcomm 0.11.0, -didcomm-v1 0.10.0, -capability-client 0.10.0

trust-tasks-didcomm and trust-tasks-capability-client are BREAKING: each now
rejects inputs it used to accept, which is a break in what a consumer observes
even though no wire format moved. trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 is a minor — the
legacy carriage is default-on, so the default build behaves as 0.9.0 did.

The didcomm README's multi-peer section recommended the retry loop that
unpack_trust_task_from replaces, and still carried the 0.1 binding URI and a
0.13-era MSRV; corrected. Cargo.lock picks up base64 (reading the JWE protected
header) and log (the superseded-carriage warning), both already resolved in the
graph.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>
