title: Migrate the Trust Tasks framework specification into Spec-Up-T
body:
Populates this repository — intended as the **canonical source** for the Trust Tasks framework — from `SPEC.md` in [`trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf), restructured onto the ToIP specification template.

The source is a single 1,476-line numbered markdown file. This splits it across the five Spec-Up-T sources declared in `specs.json`, drops the scaffolding the tooling now generates, and adds the sections the ToIP template requires.

**Individual Trust Task specifications are not part of this move.** `kyc-handoff`, `acl/grant`, `trust-task-error` and the rest stay in the registry repository, along with the transport bindings, the website, and the generated Rust and TypeScript client libraries. Only the framework document moves here.

## What went where

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `spec/header.md` | ToIP header block — version, document status, editors, abstract, IPR terms. Replaces the source's metadata table and its "Status of This Document" section. |
| `spec/intro.md` | Introduction, the status prose, Design Goals, Requirements Language. |
| `spec/terms-definitions/*.md` | The nineteen terms of the source's Terminology section, one file each, as `[[def: ...]]` entries with aliases. |
| `spec/body.md` | The normative body (Trust Task Documents … Task Control), then the template's considerations, conformance, and references sections. |
| `spec/appendix.md` | Appendix A (worked example), Appendix B (changelog), Appendix C (acknowledgements). |

## Mechanical changes

- **Section numbers removed from every heading.** Spec-Up-T generates the table of contents and the `§` anchors, so manual numbering would double up. All **380 in-page cross-references** were rewritten from `[§4.7](#47-proof)` to `[Proof](#proof)`. Every one resolves against a heading in the assembled document, and no two headings produce the same anchor — checked mechanically, not by eye.
- **Bibliography markers became links.** `[[RFC8259]]` is Spec-Up-T's term-reference syntax and would have been swallowed by the renderer; the eighteen occurrences now point at the RFC or W3C document directly.
- **Glossary references.** The first italicised occurrence of each defined term in every top-level section is now `[[ref: ...]]` — one route to the glossary from wherever a reader lands, without turning every paragraph into a link farm. `npm run render` reports no dangling definitions.
- A few headings were renamed to keep their anchors unambiguous: Discovery's `Request` / `Response` / `Privacy considerations` became `Discovery Request` / `Discovery Response` / `Privacy of Discovery Responses` (the last would otherwise have collided with the top-level Privacy Considerations section), and the ceremony subsections gained a `Ceremony` qualifier.

## Content changes

All of these are required by the template rather than chosen:

- **"Security and Privacy Considerations" splits in two.** The source's combined section becomes the template's separate Security Considerations (cross-recipient replay, parser hardening, schema-validation DoS, error-response identity leakage) and Privacy Considerations (data visibility, retention, plus pointers to the two subsections that carry privacy weight elsewhere).
- **Governance, Internationalization, and Accessibility Considerations are new.** Governance points at the registry policy, the stability commitment, and the framework's deliberate silence on authorization — all of which the source already stated, in scattered places. The other two record what the framework does and does not constrain today (UTF-8, ASCII lowerCamelCase identifiers; a data format rather than a user interface) and defer the rest until the document advances beyond Working Draft.
- **Conformance moves to the end**, as Conformance Targets (the three conformance classes from the source's §3) and Conformance Tests (none published yet; the registry repository's schemas and generated libraries are named as the expected basis).
- **References** are restated as Normative and Informative markdown lists, matching `dtgwg-cred-spec`.

**Every normative sentence is carried over unchanged.** The restructuring moves prose between files and rewrites references; it does not reword requirements. The one normative addition in this PR is the versioning change below, made deliberately rather than as a side effect of the move.

## This document now uses SemVer

The framework document's own version becomes three-part: **0.4.0**, and the framework is **published in the registry at that full version**. Its *Type URI* becomes `https://trusttasks.org/spec/trust-task/0.4.0`, and the `targetFrameworkVersion` a specification declares is that same three-part value.

**Why publish at the full version rather than keep `PATCH` off the wire.** Stability forbids altering the normative content served at a published *Type URI*. That left errata to a published framework version with nowhere to go: correcting `0.4` in place is precisely what that rule forbids for every other artifact in the registry, and minting `0.5` for a repaired example overstates what changed. A `PATCH` release now mints a new URI, exactly as every other registry artifact does.

A new **Versioning of This Framework Specification** subsection states the rule, adds a `framework-version` ABNF production alongside the existing one, and defines what each component means for this document: `MAJOR` for a change breaking for consumers or for the specification-authoring contract, `MINOR` for a backwards-compatible addition, `PATCH` for an errata-only correction that changes neither the wire format nor what a conforming specification must declare.

**The three-part form is confined to the exact reserved slug `trust-task`.** Individual Trust Task specifications keep the two-part `MAJOR.MINOR` of Version Scheme — and so do the framework-defined ones under the `trust-task-` and `trust-ceremony-` prefixes. `trust-task-error/0.4` is a Trust Task specification and versions like one. `https://trusttasks.org/spec/kyc-handoff/1.0` is untouched, as is the `specs/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>/` registry layout and everything generated from it.

**Nothing already published stops resolving.** `0.1` through `0.4` denote `0.1.0` through `0.4.0` — `0.4` and `0.4.0` are the same release, and the changelog entries stand as published. A two-part `targetFrameworkVersion` resolves as `M.N.0`, and the registry **MUST** continue to serve the two-part framework URIs `.../trust-task/0.1` through `/0.4` as aliases of the corresponding `.0` release. Specifications published or re-issued from this version onward declare the three-part form. **The document wire format is unchanged.**

Carried through Type URI (version-segment exception, reserved-slug note, bare-URL redirect), Schema Scope, Stability, Consumer Requirements item 1, Specification Requirements item 3, the Appendix A worked example, and the changelog. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 joins the normative references.

**Registry-side follow-up:** `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` needs `specs/_framework/0.4/` moved to `specs/_framework/0.4.0/`, with the two-part framework URIs kept resolving as aliases. Not in this PR.

## The version number itself

The source's header table said **version 0.3**, but its changelog documents a **0.4** release and the registry repository ships `specs/_framework/0.4/`. This PR records **0.4.0**, on the basis that the changelog and the published framework schema agree with each other and the header table does not. Say the word if that reads the wrong way.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

Syncing the framework back into `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` so the registry website keeps rendering it. Once this lands, that repository's `SPEC.md` should stop being the source and start being a copy — either a build step that pulls the rendered output, or a submodule. Worth agreeing the mechanism before wiring it up.

## Verification

```sh
npm install
npm run render     # clean: 19 terms indexed, no dangling definitions
```

The rendered `docs/index.html` has 217 anchors and no broken in-page links.

title: spec(auth): WebAuthn options may carry extensions, as the dictionary says
body:
`CredentialCreationOptions` and `CredentialRequestOptions` each say they mirror
a W3C dictionary, and each omits a member that dictionary defines. Both are
`additionalProperties: false`, so **a server emitting standard WebAuthn options
cannot conform.**

## The contradiction

> Server-issued options for `navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: ... })`.
> **Mirrors the WebAuthn Level 2 `PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptions`
> dictionary**; binary fields are base64url-encoded strings…

That dictionary defines `extensions`. These components did not. Closed objects
plus an incomplete mirror is a contradiction the schema cannot resolve in the
implementer's favour: the widely-used server libraries populate `extensions` by
default, so conforming meant **stripping a standard WebAuthn field on the way
out** — deleting a capability to satisfy a schema that only meant to describe
one.

Found by a reference implementation validating its real handler responses
against these schemas. It had been sending webauthn-rs's `{publicKey: …}`
wrapper, which failed for a different reason; unwrapping it to the shape this
component asks for exposed `extensions` underneath.

## Why the value is unconstrained

`{"type": "object"}`, nothing more. The set of extensions is open and
registered outside this framework, so enumerating them here would date the
schema against a registry it does not own — and a closed list would reproduce
the original defect one revision later, for whichever extension is registered
next.

## Scope

One shared file. Additive, so a patch bump, and `0.1` of the component is
edited in place rather than versioned — an added optional member leaves every
document that was valid before still valid.

Reaches `auth/passkey/enroll/start/{0.1,0.2}`, `auth/passkey/login/start/0.2`
and `auth/passkey/revoke/start/0.1`, which all `$ref` these components.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs, 65 shared schemas, 533 example documents
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — no drift
- `npm run check-bindings` — 349 specs against 349 TS and 344 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — 33 suites, no failures

The diff is **8 insertions, 0 deletions**. My first attempt reserialised the
file with a JSON library and produced 220 changed lines of pure reformatting;
this one is a surgical text insertion, because a hand-formatted schema should
not be rewritten to add two properties.

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.15 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.15.

title: fix(vtc): hex digests, and five ways round the extension slot
body:
Stacked on #1109. Closes `audit/*` and `policy/activate` — **68 → ~22
violations**, all remaining ones needing a decision rather than a fix.

## Hex digests where the schema requires multibase

`audit/list` sent `prevHash` / `entryHash` as bare hex; the canonical digest
pattern is `^(z[1-9A-HJ-NP-Za-km-z]+|u[A-Za-z0-9_-]+)$` — multibase-wrapped

which is the property that actually matters and is now what the test asserts.

**two internal** encodings while overlooking the third: the one the published
schema requires. A bare digest is also self-describing in neither its hash
function nor its encoding, which is what multihash and multibase each exist to
fix.

**The chain is untouched.** Stored envelopes still hold `[u8; 32]` and hash
over bytes; this is the wire view only.

ways** `ext` was worked around in this service, each locally reasonable and
none checked against SPEC §4.5.1:

|---|---|
| `policy/*` (#1109) | `org.openvtc.authorDid` — capital letter, invalid key |
| `audit/list` | `"vtc"` — one segment, where reverse-DNS needs two |

| `audit/verify` | `checkpoints` at the top level of a closed response |

now sit under `org.openvtc`.

store-level adversary cannot satisfy", so it is carried rather than dropped —
and it is worth proposing upstream so it need not live in an extension at all.

nobody owns, which is the collision reverse-DNS exists to prevent.

shape confirmed by whoever designed it.

title: spec(vtc): relationships 0.2 — an edge is a pair, and a digest says what it is
body:
Two `vtc/relationships` tasks whose published shape is weaker than what a
reference implementation has been serving. Both replace required members, so
both are new versions.

Found by validating **real handler output** against these schemas rather than
hand-written examples — the fixtures agreed with the schema and the service
did not, and nothing had compared the two.

## `graph/0.2` — an edge is a pair, not a credential

`0.1` called each credential an edge. That makes a DTG edge inexpressible.

Two directed halves between the same pair of identifiers are **one
relationship**. A flat list of credentials leaves every consumer to re-derive
that: sort the DIDs, group by pair, and decide for itself what "complete"
means. Two implementations doing that independently will disagree at the
margins — which is the reasoning a schema exists to settle once.

`0.2` makes an edge a pair:

| | |
|---|---|
| `endpoints` | the two DIDs, sorted, so the pair has one identity whichever half was published first |
| `halves` | every credential between them, oldest first |
| `complete` | whether both parties have asserted |

That last is the distinction worth having in the model rather than in each
client: **an edge asserted by one party is a claim; an edge asserted by both is
a relationship.**

`GraphHalf` also carries `personaDid`, the persona an issuer has asserted on
that half. It is the one place deliberate correlation becomes visible — two
pairwise halves carrying the same persona are the same party, said so by that
party. A consumer that cannot read it cannot honour a correlation its subject
chose to publish.

## `list/0.2` — `vrcSha256` becomes `vrcDigestMultibase`

A bare hex digest names neither its hash function nor its encoding. Two parties
comparing one must agree on both out of band, and the *member name* was the
only record of the function — which stops being true the moment anything but
SHA-256 is wanted.

A multihash says which function produced the bytes; multibase says how the
string is written. The value then carries its own interpretation, and a
mismatch is a mismatch rather than a guess.

This is also an internal inconsistency being closed:
`relationships/publish/0.2` already takes a multibase digest **on the way in**,
while `list/0.1` read back a different encoding from the one its sibling
accepts.

## Versioning

Both breaking — a required member replaced. Both `status: draft`, so released
as MINOR increments under SPEC §5.2, which permits that for draft artifacts.
The `0.1` pair moves to `retired` with `supersededBy` (§5.3).

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 349 specs, 65 shared schemas, 533 example documents
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — no drift
- `npm run check-bindings` — 349 specs against 349 TS and 344 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — 33 suites, no failures

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.14 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.14.

title: feat(vtc): implement the VPC as the deliberate-correlation mechanism on an edge
body:
Closes #1067.

Two commits. The first implements the VPC. The second fixes a regression found while doing so, on the function directly below the one the VPC work touches — it lands here rather than separately because it needs the same `check_authorization_envelope` helper, and a competing generalisation on main would conflict with this one.

---

# 1. `feat(vtc)`: the VPC as the deliberate-correlation mechanism

`PersonaCredential` appeared nowhere in this repo and `DTGCredential::new_vpc` was never called, so the P-DID had no implementation and the word "persona" drifted onto the membership DID for want of anything to anchor it.

## What the absence cost

After the publish proof-of-possession change (#1054) a member had exactly two settings: publish under a pairwise relationship DID and correlate with nothing, or publish under the membership DID and correlate with everything, permanently, for anyone who retains the credential. DTG Credentials §Privacy Considerations 3 says correlation "should occur only through the holder's deliberate assertion of a persona (via a VPC) or an M-DID". The precise instrument was missing, so members had only the blunt one.

## What this implements — and what it deliberately does not

**The VTC half only.** A VPC is self-issued by a person, exactly like a VRC: its `issuer` is a persona DID the member controls, and the VTC has no key that may legitimately sign one. So `credentials/dtg.rs` gained no `issue_persona`. What the VTC owns is verifying a presented VPC, deciding whether it may annotate an edge in this community's graph, and surfacing the correlation it asserts.

Minting the VPC, choosing when to assert a persona, and renaming `openvtc`'s `persona_did` — the field whose name is what made the word ambiguous — are all client-side and **not in this PR**.

New surface, both on `vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs`:

- `POST /v1/relationships/{id}/persona` — attach a VPC to a published edge.
- `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}/persona` — withdraw it, leaving the edge.

A VPC is an *annotation* credential — it creates no graph structure, it attaches to structure that already exists — so there is no "publish a VPC" collection endpoint, and the annotation is stored on the edge row (`vtc-service/src/relationships/mod.rs`, optional + `#[serde(default)]`, so pre-existing rows decode unchanged) rather than in a keyspace of its own. The P-DID surfaces on `GET /v1/relationships/graph` as `personaDid` and in the admin UI's connections view; an annotation nothing reads would leave #1067 in the state it describes.

## The binding assumption — please read this part

**trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#9 asks how a VPC binds to a specific relationship, and is open. Nothing here answers it, and nothing here should be read as a proposal that it be answered this way.**

A VPC names its persona (`issuer`) and the counterparty (`credentialSubject.id`), and *not* the relationship DID the persona used — so it does not identify an edge on its own. Rather than add a field to the credential and present that as the resolution, the binding is made at the **request** level:

1. the caller names the edge by id in the URL;
2. the caller proves control of that edge's `issuerDid`, with the same proof-of-possession construction publishing the edge required (`VpcAttachAuthorization` / `VpcDetachAuthorization`, envelope shared with `VrcPublishAuthorization`);
3. the VPC's `credentialSubject.id` must equal the edge's `subjectDid`.

(2) is what makes it safe: the only party who could have published this edge is the only party who can annotate it, so attaching a persona is exactly as authorized as publishing the edge was — no new trust is extended. (3) is a consistency check, not a binding. If #9 lands an in-credential binding (a `digest` over the VRC, as the VWC already has), this endpoint can require it *as well*, without changing the stored shape.

**Stated limitation.** The spec says a VPC's subject is "typically the R-DID **or M-DID** used in the relationship". A VPC naming the counterparty's M-DID, on an edge whose `subjectDid` is their R-DID, fails check (3) and is rejected. That case is real. Accepting it needs the same #9 answer; guessing would mean accepting a VPC that names a party the VTC cannot tie to the edge, which is the problem restated.

## Judgement calls, with reasoning

- **No uniqueness check on the P-DID**, in direct contrast to the R-DID rule the publish path enforces unconditionally a few lines away. A relationship DID that recurs across counterparties is a defect; a persona DID that recurs is the entire purpose of the credential. The contrast is deliberate and commented at the site.
- **Detach is in scope**, though it grows the change. A privacy mechanism that cannot be reversed is worse than none — a member who can correlate their edges but never stop is worse off than one who never could. It is gated identically, or anyone could strip another member's persona, and the two authorization `type` values are distinct so neither can be replayed as the other.
- **No `persona.rego`.** Attach is gated on a live member session plus proof of control of the edge's issuer. A community that already decides whether an edge may be published has not obviously earned a second, separate say over what its issuer calls themselves. Additive if that turns out to be wrong.
- **No P-DID secondary index.** "List every edge of persona P" is answerable from the admin graph. Falling into an enumeration surface as a side effect of an index write is not how that should get designed.
- **`new_vpc` is used in a wire-shape pin, not a mint path** (`vtc-service/src/credentials/dtg.rs`). The pin matters *more* here than for credentials the VTC mints: catalog drift on a minted credential changes what we emit and a consumer tells us, but drift on the VPC changes what we *accept*, and the failure is every conformant VPC in the ecosystem being rejected by a VTC that still compiles and still passes its own tests.
- **Audit** (`VpcAttached` / `VpcDetached`) records the P-DID with the authenticated member as actor. Same attribution decision, and the same explicitly-accepted residual, as VRC publish — set out in `docs/05-design-notes/vrc-publish-proof-of-possession.md` §Audit attribution. The `info!` on both paths carries the persona and not the member.
- **The 403s do not quote the row's DIDs.** Edge ids are unguessable UUIDs, but a member who has seen one should learn nothing from this endpoint about an edge they do not control.

## Trust Task registry

`vtc/relationships/persona/0.1` is bound ahead of its publication upstream, recorded in `UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK` (`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs`). This is the **first entry the `spec/vtc/` family has ever had**, so it deserves a reviewer's attention rather than a nod. The reasoning: the mechanism exists for exactly this (`vta/webvh/servers/reconcile/0.1` went up and back down the same way once the registry served it), and a payload schema authored now would have to encode this implementation's request-level binding as if #9 were closed. The endpoint can move first; the schema should not. It goes back to zero when the task is authored upstream.

Design note: `docs/05-design-notes/vpc-persona-annotation.md`.

---

# 2. `fix(vtc)`: let the issuer of a pairwise edge retract it

Found while implementing the above, verified independently by the coordinator.

`revoke` kept the identity equality `publish` replaced in #1054/#1061 — `auth.did == rel.issuer_did` — sitting one function below where it was fixed, in the same file. For an edge published under a pairwise relationship DID that compares a membership DID against an R-DID and is **false by construction**, so since #1061 a member could lodge an edge and then never take it back. Only an admin could.

`revoke_issuer_can_retract_own` (`vtc-service/tests/relationships.rs`) seeds `ISSUER_DID` as the session DID — the *attributed* form, where the equality still holds. That is why this shipped green, and it is why the new suite is written entirely against the pairwise form.

`DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` now takes an optional body carrying a `VrcRevokeAuthorization`: the shared `check_authorization_envelope` (`type`, `aud`, `sessionId`, `issuedAt`) plus the row `id`, then the same data-integrity check against the row's `issuerDid`. Bound to the row rather than to a credential digest, because the request names a row and carries no credential.

Three routes to authorization; the first two are unchanged:

- **attributed** — `auth.did == rel.issuer_did`. Still correct, still sufficient, no proof needed.
- **admin** — moderation, keys on row id. Untouched.
- **pairwise** — the new proof.

Every client sending this request today sends no body at all and keeps working: `Option<Json<_>>` yields `None` without a JSON content-type, and still rejects a malformed body when one is present. The authorization is verified and **discarded** — it carries `sessionId`, and this handler writes to the audit store, so it is the one place on the pairwise path where that linkage could plausibly become durable. Proving control of the issuing key is recorded as `revoked_by: "issuer"`, not "admin".

## Mutation testing — it found two tests that passed for the wrong reason

The suite was written first and **confirmed failing** against the unfixed handler (403 `only the issuer or an admin can revoke a VRC`). Four mutations were then applied to the new check:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `type` guard neutered | **survived** → new test |
| edge (`relationship`) binding removed | killed by `rejects_an_authorization_bound_to_a_different_edge` |
| signature check (`verify_di_proof`) removed | killed by `rejects_an_authorization_signed_by_another_key` |
| `sessionId` binding neutered | **survived** → new test |

- **Type guard.** `rejects_a_publish_authorization_replayed_as_a_revoke` was being caught by the *edge* binding — a publish authorization has no `relationship` field — so `type` was never exercised at all. Added `rejects_an_authorization_of_the_wrong_type`, valid in every respect except the one field under test. Mutant now killed.
- **Session binding.** Every test presented its authorization in the session it was minted for, so nothing exercised the binding the publish design note calls load-bearing. Added `rejects_an_authorization_replayed_in_another_members_session`: a second member replays a captured object whose signature is still the issuer's and still verifies, so `sessionId` is the only thing between them and an edge they do not control. Mutant now killed.

Neither gap was visible by reading the diff.

## Design-note correction

`docs/05-design-notes/vrc-publish-proof-of-possession.md` said "admin revocation is unaffected — it keys on row id, not issuer identity". True, and the wrong half to reassure the reader about; the sentence answers the question nobody needed answered and is silent on the one that mattered. It now states what happens to both halves and records the general lesson: **replacing an identity equality is not done until every sibling operation on the same resource has been checked for the same equality. Grep for the field, not for the function.**

---

## Testing

`cargo test -p vtc-service` fully green across all test binaries; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean; admin-UI build passes.

`tests/relationships.rs` goes 34 → 48 tests: eleven for the persona surface under `pairwise::persona` (happy path, one persona across two edges under two different R-DIDs, wrong signing key, missing authorization, wrong edge, a VRC posted to the persona endpoint, wrong counterparty, detach, attach-replayed-as-detach, absence of the session id and membership DID from the row and audit trail, 404), seven for revocation under `pairwise::revocation` as above, plus a storage test that rows written before the `persona` field still decode and the catalog wire-shape pin.

No `version =` edits, no changelog file.

title: fix(vtc): a null, and a revoke replying under the wrong task
body:
Three of the five VTC-family violations #1107's response layer found on real
handler output. The remaining two point at the specification rather than this
service, and are described at the end rather than guessed at.

## `join-requests` sent `extensions: null`

`JoinRequest.extensions` is `JsonValue` with `#[serde(default)]` and no
`skip_serializing_if`, so a request with no extensions serialised `null`. The
canonical component types it `object` and does not require it, so absent is how
"none" is spelled and `null` is a type error — the same shape as
`policyDecision` in #1099, and the third member of this family to have it.

## `personhood/revoke` replied under the *assert* task

This is the substantial one, and it was not a serialisation slip.

`POST` and `DELETE` shared one mount, with a comment saying the collapse was
"pending per-method selectors". **That workaround had outlived its reason.**
`task_routes` has supported one task per verb on a shared path since
`per_method_tasks_on_one_path_are_enforced_independently` landed in
`vti_common::trust_task::openapi`, and registering the path twice merges the
OpenAPI operations rather than overwriting them — which is what
`per_method_split_keeps_both_operations_in_the_spec` exists to prove.

The consequence was real. A revoke response went out labelled
`members/personhood/assert/0.1`, so a client was told the wrong task for the
document it received — and the response could not satisfy the schema it
claimed: assert requires `personhood: const true` plus `vmc` and `roleVec`,
while a revoke legitimately sends `false` with neither.

`members/personhood/revoke/0.1` has been published upstream the whole time, and
its shape matches `RevokeResponse` exactly: `personhood: const false`, both
credentials optional. Each verb now carries its own task.

### The witness knew, and that is the point

The assert entry's own comment said the DELETE answered under that URI with the
wrong shape, and called it "a shared-mount workaround, not a conformance defect
of this URI, so the witness carries the POST."

Every clause of that is true. It is also how the defect survived: the witness
was told to look at the POST, so nothing in the table ever saw the DELETE, and
a fixture cannot notice a response it was instructed not to examine. The
response layer had no such instruction — it validated whatever the handler
actually sent.

An honest note about a known gap is still a gap. This is the fourth time this
week the table's prose described something accurately and nothing acted on it.

## The census caught the follow-on

Binding a newly published URI made
`every_bound_published_uri_has_a_witness` fail, exactly as designed —
`personhood/revoke/0.1` had no entry. Added as `checked!`; the table is now 59
tasks, drift still 0.

## Not fixed here

Two remain, and both look like the **specification** being stale rather than
this service being wrong — which is the question this repository has now got
backwards three times, so I am not guessing:

- **`relationships/list`** sends `vrcDigestMultibase`; the schema requires
  `vrcSha256`. Multibase-wrapped multihash was a deliberate decision taken in
  this workspace; the service moved and the published schema never followed.
- **`relationships/graph`** returns `complete` / `endpoints` / `halves` — a
  materially richer shape than the schema's flat `id` / `issuerDid` /
  `subjectDid` / `createdAt`.

Both want an upstream `0.2` if the service's shape is the intended one, and
someone who knows the graph design should confirm that before a spec change is
proposed for it.

The eighteen shared-family tasks (`acl`, `audit`, `auth/passkey`, `policy`)
also remain, still pending the canonical-shape decision the witness header
names. One of those is worth surfacing early because it is a framework
violation rather than a shape mismatch: `policy/upsert` emits an `ext` key of
`org.openvtc.authorDid`, which fails the reverse-DNS namespace pattern in
SPEC §4.5.1 — the structure belongs *inside* `org.openvtc`, not flattened into
the key.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: feat(spec): migrate the Trust Tasks framework specification into Spec-Up-T
body:
feat(spec): migrate the Trust Tasks framework specification into Spec-Up-T

Populates this repository — the canonical source for the framework — from
`SPEC.md` in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf, restructured onto the ToIP
specification template.

The source is one 1,476-line numbered markdown file. This splits it across the
five Spec-Up-T sources declared in `specs.json` and drops the hand-maintained
scaffolding the tooling now generates:

* `spec/header.md` — the ToIP header block (version, document status, editors,
  abstract, IPR terms) replacing the source's metadata table and "Status of
  This Document" section. Version is recorded as 0.4, matching the changelog
  and `specs/_framework/0.4/` in the registry repository; the source's header
  table still said 0.3.
* `spec/intro.md` — Introduction, the status prose, and Design Goals, followed
  by Requirements Language.
* `spec/terms-definitions/*.md` — the nineteen terms of the source's
  Terminology section, one file each, as `[[def: ...]]` entries with aliases.
* `spec/body.md` — the normative body (Trust Task Documents … Task Control),
  then the template's required considerations, conformance, and references
  sections.
* `spec/appendix.md` — Appendix A (worked example), Appendix B (changelog),
  Appendix C (acknowledgements).

Mechanical changes applied throughout:

* Section numbers removed from every heading — Spec-Up-T generates the table of
  contents and the § anchors. All 380 in-page cross-references were rewritten
  from `[§4.7](#47-proof)` to `[Proof](#proof)`; every one resolves, and no two
  headings collide.
* Bibliography markers (`[[RFC8259]]`) became real links. The double-bracket
  form is Spec-Up-T's term-reference syntax and would otherwise be swallowed.
* The first italicised occurrence of each defined term in every top-level
  section is now `[[ref: ...]]`, so a reader landing anywhere has one route to
  the glossary. `npm run render` reports no dangling definitions.

Content changes, all required by the template:

* "Security and Privacy Considerations" splits into the template's separate
  Security Considerations and Privacy Considerations sections.
* Governance, Internationalization, and Accessibility Considerations are new.
  Governance points at the registry policy, the stability commitment, and the
  framework's deliberate silence on authorization; the other two record what
  the framework does and does not constrain today, and defer the rest until
  the document advances beyond Working Draft.
* Conformance moves to the end as Conformance Targets (the three conformance
  classes from the source) and Conformance Tests (none published yet).
* References are restated as Normative and Informative markdown lists.

Every normative sentence is carried over unchanged. Individual Trust Task
specifications stay in the registry repository; the README records the split
and the authoring workflow.

Renders clean with `npm run render`.

title: test(vtc): validate what handlers actually emit, not what fixtures claim
body:
**The conformance table's zero was measuring the wrong thing.** This adds a
layer that validates what handlers actually emit, and the first run found
**134 violations across 23 tasks** — five of them in the VTC family the table
calls fully conformant.

## What it does

One axum layer at `test_support.rs`, where all 35 integration-test binaries
build their router. It reads the `Trust-Task` header the tests already send,
looks up that task's `#response` schema (possible only since
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#265 indexed response schemas), and validates
the bytes the handler produced.

A layer rather than a helper per test file because each binary under `tests/`
is its own crate with its own `send` — thirty-five of them. One interception
point covers all of them and cannot be forgotten by the next test added.

## Why fixtures could not have found this

`trust_tasks::conformance` validates example documents typed by hand into the
witness table. That is a proxy, and it has now drifted **four** distinct ways:

| | |
|---|---|
| **stale** | `endorsements/revoke` described a response the handler had stopped sending six PRs earlier |
| **inventing** | a wrapper fixture carried a `totalEstimate` no producer ever sets |
| **omitting** | the profile fixture left out `personhood` — a **false green** on two routes |
| **over-populating** | `extensions` was hand-set to `{"org": "acme"}`, so the `null` real traffic sends was never seen |

The last is new here, and it is the one that survives the obvious fix.
`community_profile()` **was already derived from the real struct** — converted
in #1100 precisely to stop it lying — and it still hid this, because the
derivation was followed by `p.extensions = json!({"tier": "gold"})`. Deriving a
fixture from the real type only protects the members you do not then hand-set.

## Fixed here

- **`MemberResponse.extensions`** went out as `null` on `members/{list,show,update}`.
  The component makes it **required** and types it `object`, so `null` is a
  violation and omitting it would be too — an empty object is the only
  conforming spelling of "none". Now serialised as `{}`.
- **`CommunityProfile.extensions`** — same class on `community/profile/update`
  and `config/export`, but there it is *optional*, so it is now omitted when
  null.

## Not fixed here — the inventory

Reporting-only for now. Making the layer fail the build today would redden
every suite, and the remaining violations split into two groups that need
different decisions.

**Five VTC-family tasks the witness table calls conformant:**

| task | real output |
|---|---|
| `relationships/list` | sends `vrcDigestMultibase`; schema requires `vrcSha256` |
| `relationships/graph` | a different shape entirely — `complete` / `endpoints` / `halves` |
| `members/personhood/assert` | missing required `vmc` / `roleVec`; a `const` unsatisfied |
| `join-requests/list`, `show` | `null` where an object is required |

`relationships/*` looks like the **spec** being stale rather than the service
being wrong: multibase digests were a deliberate decision, and the graph shape
is richer than the schema's. The other three look like service bugs. Each needs
the "which side is wrong" question asked properly — the lesson this repository
has learned three times over.

**Eighteen shared-family tasks** — `acl`, `audit`, `auth/passkey`, `policy`.
The witness header states these 36 URIs are excluded by design, being "served
by both daemons, so witnessing them belongs with a decision about which
service's response shape is canonical". The layer needed no such decision to
*observe* them; acting on them still does.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 54 suites, no failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.13, for the response-schema index.

## The honest summary

I reported "drift 33 → 0" earlier today. That number was true of the fixtures
and false of the service. This is the tool that says so, and the count it
produces is the one worth trusting, because nothing in it was typed by hand.

title: feat(rs): index response schemas, not just requests
body:
`schema_for` answered only for requests. This indexes responses too, under the
same Type URI suffixed `#response` — **332 of them**.

## Why

A consumer could validate what it *received* and not what it *sent back*. A
producer's own output is the half it can actually fix, and it is the half that
drifts, because nothing on the wire pushes back on a response the way a
consumer pushes back on a request.

Without an index entry, an implementation that wants to check its emissions has
to hand-write a match arm per task. This function's own documentation already
says what that amounts to:

> It could only validate by hand-writing a match arm per task and remembering
> to add one with every new task — which is to say, it would validate whatever
> somebody remembered, which is not validation.

That argument was made for requests. It applies unchanged to responses.

## What it costs

Nothing at runtime — the schemas are `&'static str` constants that are already
compiled in, reachable only by naming the `Response` type, which a generic
dispatcher cannot do.

`#response` is not a convention invented here: it is what every generated
`Response` type already declares as its own `TYPE_URI`, so the index and the
types agree by construction rather than by discipline.

A task with no response side has no `#response` entry, and `None` stays a real
answer — the existing documentation on that point covers both sides unchanged.

## Tests

Four new, and two of them exist because the cheap wrong implementation would
pass a naive check:

- a producer can find the response schema for a task;
- **the response schema is not the request schema** — returning the payload
  schema for both would satisfy every "is it `Some`" assertion while validating
  responses against the wrong shape, which is worse than not validating them;
- **each side refuses the other's document** — `members/show` takes `{did}` and
  returns `{member: …}`, so each schema must reject the other, or the index is
  not really distinguishing them;
- an unknown `#response` URI is `None`.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 348 specs, 65 shared schemas
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — no drift
- `npm run check-bindings` — 348 specs against 348 TS and 343 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — 33 suites, no failures

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.13 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.13.

## What this unblocks

A reference implementation whose conformance sweep validates hand-written
example documents rather than real handler output. Forty-five of its fixtures
are hand-typed, and three separate defects this week came from one drifting
from what the service actually emits — including a fixture that *omitted* a
member and so reported two non-conformant routes as conforming. With responses
indexed, the integration tests can validate the bytes the handler really sent,
by the Type URI they already pass, and the fixtures stop being the thing under
test.

title: docs(vtc): retire four local tasks the index had already retired
body:
Four local task documents said `status: draft`. `trust-tasks/index.json` had
already recorded all four as `retired`, with correct `supersededBy` targets.
The index and the documents had disagreed, silently, for some time.

## What the audit found

The question was whether these four were genuinely VTI-specific tasks needing a
local home, or leftovers from the migration to published specs. They are
leftovers:

| local document | live route binds |
|---|---|
| `openvtc/vtc/policies/test/1.0` | `spec/vtc/policies/test/0.1` |
| `openvtc/vtc/admin/config/export/1.0` | `spec/vtc/config/export/0.1` |
| `openvtc/vtc/admin/config/import/1.0` | `spec/vtc/config/import/0.1` |
| `openvtc/vtc/website/files/delete/1.0` | `spec/vtc/website/files/delete/0.1` |

All four have published upstream equivalents, all four are in the conformance
table against those published specs, and **no route, test or client references
the local URIs** — the only mentions are the documents themselves, the index,
and one historical CHANGELOG line.

So there was nothing to publish. The migration finished in the code; four
documents were never updated to say so.

## The fix

Four one-line front-matter corrections, taking each `draft` to `retired` with
the `supersededBy` the index already names. Local task documents are now
**64 retired, 0 draft**.

## Why this matters beyond tidiness

A `draft` document is an invitation. Anyone reading `trust-tasks/` for the
shape of, say, config export would have found a live-looking local definition
that nothing implements, alongside a published one that everything does — and
no signal about which is real except the index, which is a different file.

It also settles a question worth recording: there are **no VTI-specific tasks
left that need a local definition**. The four candidates were the whole
remaining case for reintroducing locally-defined trust tasks, and none of them
survives inspection. Publishing upstream is what lets both sides validate
against one definition — which is how four defects were found in the specs
themselves this week, rather than in this service. A locally-defined task
cannot produce that: conformance against your own definition is a mirror.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast` — 54 suites, no failures
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

`tests/trust_task_manifest.rs`, which reads these documents, passes unchanged.

title: docs(vtc): retire four local tasks the index had already retired (#1106)
body:
docs(vtc): retire four local tasks the index had already retired (#1106)

Four local task documents said `status: draft`. `trust-tasks/index.json` had
already recorded all four as `retired` with correct `supersededBy` targets. The
index and the documents disagreed, silently.

The question was whether these were VTI-specific tasks needing a local home or
leftovers from the migration to published specs. They are leftovers: all four
have published upstream equivalents, all four are in the conformance table
against those published specs, and no route, test or client references the
local URIs. There was nothing to publish — the migration finished in the code
and four documents were never updated to say so.

Local task documents are now 64 retired, 0 draft.

Beyond tidiness: a draft document is an invitation, and anyone reading
`trust-tasks/` for the shape of config export would have found a live-looking
local definition that nothing implements beside a published one that everything
does. It also settles the case for reintroducing locally-defined trust tasks —
these four were the whole remaining argument, and none survives inspection.

title: Name the asymmetric edge: two halves may declare different correlation scopes
body:
## Summary

The specification assumes both halves of a DTG edge are the same kind of thing.
When two communities with opposite disclosure policies form an edge, they are
not: one half is published under an attributed, correlatable identifier and the
other under a pairwise one. The four VID types cannot name this edge, and
nothing states what an implementation should conclude about its privacy.

This is not the mixed-scope community case (a community that uses different
identifier kinds internally). It is two communities, two policies, and one edge
whose halves legitimately disagree.

## Detail

A DTG edge is two VRCs, one in each direction. Each party issues its own half
and chooses the identifier it appears under. Neither can impose that choice on
the other, and neither needs to.

Take a deliberately public community — an open-source project whose whole value
is that contributions trace back to named people — and a deliberately private
one, where members are known to each other only by per-counterparty identifiers.
A member of each forms a relationship with a member of the other:

- Half 1 is issued by the public member under an attributed identifier, into a
  graph anyone can read.
- Half 2 is issued by the private member under an R-DID that only their
  counterparty can map to them.

Both halves are conformant. The edge is one edge.

**1. The taxonomy has no word for it.** Under the four VID types, an implementer
must ask whether this is an R-DID edge or an M-DID edge. It is one of each.
There is no answer, because the question presumes both halves are the same kind.
This is a stronger argument for the structural change proposed in #22 than the
mixed-scope community case is: there, one authority chooses; here, no single
party is entitled to choose.

**2. Nothing says an edge's effective privacy is the minimum of its halves.**
The private member declared the scope of *their own* identifier, and that
declaration is honoured — only their counterparty can resolve it. But their
counterparty publishes the other half into a public, correlatable graph, so the
pairwise identifier now sits next to a named person in a place anyone can read.

The private member has no say in where the other half is published, and no way
to discover it. §Privacy Considerations 2 addresses R-DID uniqueness — reuse
across counterparties — which is a different failure. Nothing addresses the case
where a *correctly unique* R-DID is correlated by what the other party does with
its own half.

The rule that seems to be missing: **an edge's effective disclosure is the
maximum of its two halves; a declared scope binds only its own holder.** Neither
sentence appears in the specification, and an implementation that computed
privacy from one half alone would be wrong in a way nothing warns it about.

## Why it matters

Cross-community edges are the interesting case for a trust spanning layer — an
edge inside one community is governed by one policy and needs no reconciliation.
If the specification only describes edges whose halves agree, it describes the
case that does not need it.

An implementation reading the current text will reasonably conclude that a
pairwise-declared identifier stays pairwise. In the cross-community case it does
not, and the party who loses privacy is the one who followed the guidance.

## Requested clarification

1. Does the specification acknowledge that the two halves of one edge may
   declare different scopes, and is that a conformant edge?
2. Should it state that a declared scope constrains only its own holder's
   disclosure, and that an edge's effective disclosure is the maximum of its
   halves?
3. Should that appear as a Privacy Consideration, or normatively?

**Proposed answer**, for the group to react to rather than open cold: name it.
State that scope is declared per identifier and experienced per edge, that
halves may legitimately differ, and add the maximum rule as a Privacy
Consideration. Under the declared-scope model in #22 this falls out of the
vocabulary; under the four types it needs prose.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. The cross-community analysis is set
out in full, with the graph drawn from a single shared edge list, in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html) (items
X1 and X2). Related: #21 (edge verifiability), #22 (declared correlation
scope).

title: Relationship policy discovery: both communities must admit an edge, neither can find out
body:
## Summary

Forming an edge between two communities requires **both** communities' policies
to admit it, and there is no way for either side to learn the other's policy
before trying. The first signal that an edge is inadmissible is a rejection,
after one half has already been published.

Raising this as an interoperability question rather than a purely local one: the
failure is symmetric and neither party can fix it alone, which is the shape of
thing a specification usually settles.

## Detail

A cross-community edge needs two independent permissions:

- The **public** community must accept a half whose subject is an opaque
  pairwise identifier belonging to a non-member.
- The **private** community must permit its member to name an outsider in a
  credential at all.

Each is a reasonable policy position, and either may be "no". Nothing published
by either community says which.

A concrete instance from our implementation. Our default relationship policy has
two branches:

```rego
# Pairwise: membership comes from the session.
allow if {
    input.action == "publish"
    input.authenticated_member.is_current
    input.identifier_form == "pairwise"
}

# Attributed: both named parties are community members.
allow if {
    input.action == "publish"
    input.identifier_form == "attributed"
    input.issuer.is_current
    input.subject.is_current
}
```

The public member's half is *attributed* — that is the whole point of a public
community — and its subject is an outsider, so `input.subject.is_current` is
false and the publish is denied. The pairwise branch would admit an opaque
subject, but only when the publisher's own identifier is pairwise, which is
exactly what the public community has declared it does not use.

So the edge fails, correctly, under a policy that is defensible on its own
terms. What is missing is any way for the other party to have known that before
publishing their half — and by then the private member has already issued a
credential naming someone who cannot reciprocate.

## Why it matters

Both parties behave conformantly and the edge still fails, which makes this an
interoperability property rather than a local configuration choice. It also
fails asymmetrically in time: whichever party publishes first has already
disclosed something.

The information needed is small — whether a community accepts non-member
subjects, and which identifier forms it will publish under. Those are properties
a community can state without revealing anything about its membership, which
matters because the communities most likely to refuse are the private ones.

## Requested clarification

1. Should a community publish enough of its relationship policy for a
   counterparty to determine, before publishing, whether an edge is admissible?
2. If so, is that a discoverable field on the community profile, and is it in
   scope for this specification or for the Trust Task layer?
3. Is there an intended ordering for edge formation that avoids one party
   disclosing before the other's admissibility is known?

**Proposed answer**: publish the relevant predicates — accepted subject forms,
accepted issuer identifier forms — as a discoverable field on the community
profile. It is cheap, it reveals nothing about membership, and it turns a failed
publish into a pre-flight check. We will implement this locally either way; the
question for the group is whether it should be interoperable, since a
locally-invented field helps nobody else.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. Set out as item X4 in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html). Related:
#21, #22, and the two companion cross-community questions filed alongside this
one.

title: Edge verifiability across VTN contexts: different VTNs, or none at all
body:
## Summary

The VRC and VMC glossary entries make edge verifiability conditional on the
issuing VTCs being recognized as trust anchors *in a specific VTN*. Neither
entry says what happens when the two peers' VTCs anchor in **different** VTNs,
or when one anchors in **none** — which is the deliberate posture of a private
community. The condition is silent on precisely the case a spanning layer exists
to serve.

This is the fourth question in #21 seen from the cross-community direction. It
is filed separately because #21 asks whether the condition should exist at all,
while this asks what it means if it survives.

## Detail

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`):

> A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN if:
> a) it contains M-DIDs for both peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using
> their M-DID private keys, c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by
> VTCs, and d) **those VTCs are recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN**.

The VMC entry carries the same construction in one clause.

Condition (d) is stated as though one VTN context governs the whole edge. Three
cases it does not cover:

**1. The two VTCs anchor in different VTNs.** Each half traces to a VTC that
some VTN recognises, but no single VTN recognises both. Is the edge verifiable
in either context? In neither? The text gives no rule, and the natural readings
disagree — "in the context of a specific VTN" could mean *the verifier's* VTN or
*an* agreed VTN, and those produce different answers.

**2. One peer's VTC anchors in no VTN, deliberately.** A community that exists
precisely so its membership is not discoverable has no reason to seek anchor
status anywhere. Under condition (d) every edge it forms with the outside world
is, permanently and by construction, not a verifiable DTG edge — not because
anything is unproven, but because a party chose privacy.

**3. The verifier is outside both.** An external verifier can check that both
halves are authentic and that each traces to *some* VTC. Condition (d) does not
let it conclude anything, because it asks about recognition rather than about
what the verifier can check.

## Why it matters

Under condition (d) as written, verifiability is a property of the *network the
issuers joined*, not of what a verifier can establish. Two edges with identical
cryptography and identical proofs get different answers depending on registry
membership neither peer controls at verification time.

The cross-community case is where the spanning layer earns its name. If an edge
between two communities can never be a verifiable DTG edge unless both
communities' VTCs happen to anchor in the same VTN, then the answer for the
motivating case is "no", and that should be stated deliberately rather than
arrived at by silence.

## Requested clarification

1. For an edge whose peers' VTCs anchor in different VTNs, which VTN's context
   governs?
2. Is an edge with one deliberately unanchored peer intended to be permanently
   unverifiable as a DTG edge?
3. Should edge verifiability be defined **per verifier** — what this verifier
   can establish — rather than per VTN?

**Proposed answer**: resolve alongside #21 Q1 and Q2. If edge verifiability
survives as a defined property, define it per verifier and in terms of what must
be checkable, not which registry the issuers appear in. A verifier that trusts
both VTCs by any route should reach the same conclusion whether or not a VTN
mediated that trust.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. Set out as item X3 in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html). Directly
dependent on #21; related to #22.

title: chore(vtc)!: recognise and submit 0.2 — drift reaches zero
body:
Retargets `auth/recognise` and `join-requests/submit` to the `0.2` versions
published by trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#264.

**Drift 2 → 0.** Every Trust Task this service binds now speaks the schema it
publishes, on both sides. It was 33 when the sweep landed yesterday.

## Why these two moved the spec rather than the service

Both were recorded as "the service's shape is arguably stronger". Reading them
properly, one was not arguable at all.

**`auth/recognise/0.1` took `{vec, vmc}` — a replayable impersonation token.**
Both credentials are bearer artifacts, so anyone who obtained the pair from a
relayed join, an audit log, a backup or a compromised device held everything
the payload required, and the recognising community could not distinguish the
subject from someone holding a copy. No proof of key possession, no freshness,
no audience binding: one captured pair worked at every community that
recognised the issuer, indefinitely. This service has required a holder-signed
presentation — nonce, `domain`, holder-is-subject — since P0.2. `0.2` publishes
that.

**`join-requests/submit/0.1` returned `status: const "pending"`** where a
submission has four outcomes. `0.2` returns a verdict.

## One real find in the retarget

`VerdictEffect` serialised **`request_more`**, but I had specced `requestMore`
in #264, and SPEC §4.10 rule 4 is explicit that specification-defined decision
values are lowerCamelCase. So the wire was wrong.

The fix is not to change either vocabulary wholesale, because there are two of
them and both are correct in their own language:

- **Rego authors verdicts.** Operator-written policy returns
  `{"effect": "request_more", …}`, and snake_case is that language's idiom —
  `vtc-service/policies/default/join.rego` and every deployed policy alongside
  it. Re-casing there would break operator policies to satisfy a wire rule
  that does not govern them.
- **The wire publishes `requestMore`**, per §4.10 and the new
  `vtc/_shared/0.1/ceremony#VerdictEffect`.

`VerdictEffect` is the boundary: it now serialises camelCase and keeps
`#[serde(alias = "request_more")]` so anything producing the policy spelling
still deserialises. That is the same storage-versus-wire split `EndorsementRow`
(#1096) and `GenerationRow` (#1095) draw, applied to a policy vocabulary
instead of a keyspace.

The test that caught it now demonstrates the boundary instead of hiding it —
its inline Rego authors `request_more`, and it asserts the wire says
`requestMore`, with a comment saying why both are right.

## The table at zero

`KNOWN_DRIFT_COUNT` stays asserted at `0`. It can no longer shrink, so the only
thing it can do is catch a regression — which is what an asserted count is for.
A new task that diverges must add a `drift!` entry and raise it deliberately.

The `drift!` macro, `Side`, and `Conformance::KnownDrift` are now unconstructed
and kept with `#[allow(dead_code)]` rather than deleted. They are the
vocabulary for *recording* a divergence, and a table with no way to say "this
diverges, on this side, for this reason" invites the next author to leave a
real divergence unrecorded rather than write the machinery back. Deleting them
would make the zero look permanent instead of current.

## The header, rewritten

It described a 33-entry backlog. It now records how the 33 actually closed,
because the distribution is not what the sweep predicted:

| | |
|---|---|
| **10** | by correcting this service's wire shapes |
| **19** | on dependency bumps alone — the specs had moved and the notes had not |
| **4** | by correcting the **specification**, once the published shape turned out to be the weaker one |

That last group is the one worth remembering. A conformance table makes
divergence visible and says nothing about which side is wrong, and *"the schema
requires X and the service omits X"* reads as an accusation against the
implementation. Twice it was the schema. Once — `install/claim` — the
requirement had been built, found impossible in a browser, and removed two
months **before** the specification demanding it was written, and this table
recorded that as the service being behind on a security control.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

BREAKING CHANGE: `POST /v1/auth/recognise` and `POST /v1/join-requests` bind
the `0.2` task URIs; callers must send the new `Trust-Task` header values. The
verdict `effect` for a request-more outcome is now `requestMore` on the wire
instead of `request_more`; the snake_case form is still accepted on input, and
Rego policies are unchanged.

Refs #1059

title: VRC edge-verifiability conditions exist only in the glossary and contradict the body
body:
## Summary

The glossary definition of the VRC states conditions for edge verifiability that
appear nowhere in the body, contradict the body's Privacy Considerations, and
contradict the body's own bidirectional edge model. The VMC definition carries
half of the same construction.

The VRC entry (`spec/terms-definitions/verifiable_relationship_credential.md`)
has not been revised since the Working Draft 01 migration (#3), while the body's
treatment of R-DIDs, M-DIDs and the ZKP constructions has moved on. An
implementer reading the two together gets opposite instructions.

## Detail

The glossary entry reads:

> A VRC may contain either R-DIDs or M-DIDs. A VRC is only verifiable as a DTG
> edge in the context of a specific VTN if: a) it contains M-DIDs for both
> peers, b) both peers have signed the VRC using their M-DID private keys,
> c) both M-DIDs are verifiable via VMCs issued by VTCs, and d) those VTCs are
> recognized as VTN trust anchors in that VTN.

Three problems.

**1. It inverts the body's identifier guidance.** The body recommends the
opposite of condition (a):

- §VRC: "R-DIDs are RECOMMENDED for privacy; M-DIDs are allowed for
  bootstrapping (see Privacy Considerations)."
- §Unilateral Relationship Identification: "The valid application of this
  specification requires that each entity MUST generate a new, unique R-DID for
  every single entity they connect with, even within the same community."
- §Privacy Considerations 1: "Migration from M-DID-based to R-DID-based edges is
  recommended post-bootstrapping for enhanced privacy."

So the body tells an implementer to migrate to R-DID edges, and the glossary
tells the same implementer that an R-DID edge is not verifiable as an edge. Read
together, the privacy-preserving construction the body recommends is the one
that forfeits VTN-level edge verifiability.

**2. It is not reconciled with the Community-Anchored ZKP.** §Community-Anchored
Zero-Knowledge Proof states plainly that "Community membership is **not** a
precondition for issuing, holding, or presenting a VRC," and then defines a
construction in which the holder proves that "the VRC issuer possesses a VMC
from the *same* C-DID" *without revealing the specific DIDs*. That is the same
predicate the glossary's conditions (c) and (d) express by disclosure. If the
ZKP construction satisfies VTN-level edge verifiability, the glossary's
requirement for M-DIDs in the credential is unnecessary; if it does not, the
body should say so, because the ZKP section currently reads as though it does.
(Related: #9, on whether the linkages those constructions require are encoded at
all.)

**3. Condition (b) contradicts the bidirectional edge model** — and the first
sentence of the glossary entry itself. §VRC: "two VRCs (one each direction) form
a complete DTG edge," and the schema has a single `issuer` and a single `proof`.
The glossary entry opens by calling a VRC "one half of a bidirectional peer-to-
peer trust relationship" and then requires that "both peers have signed the VRC"
— which describes a single dual-signed credential, not two.

**4. The VMC entry carries the same unsourced construction.**
`verifiable_membership_credential.md`: "A VMC is only verifiable as a DTG edge in
the context of a specific VTN if the issuing VTC is recognized as a VTN trust
anchor on that VTN." Whether or not that one is correct, "only verifiable as a
DTG edge in the context of a specific VTN" is a normative-sounding constraint
that exists in no normative section. `grep` for it returns only these two
glossary files.

## Why it matters

This is not theoretical. In `OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054` we are
deciding whether relationship credentials published to a community should carry
pairwise R-DIDs or membership M-DIDs, and the current VTC policy requires both
parties to be identifiable current members — which is the glossary's rule.
Choosing correctly requires knowing whether an R-DID edge is a first-class DTG
edge or a degraded one, and the specification currently answers both ways
depending on which file is read.

## Requested clarification

1. Is VTN-level edge verifiability intended to be a defined property of the
   specification at all? If so, it belongs in a normative section, not only in
   the glossary.
2. If it is: does a VRC carrying R-DIDs, presented with a community-anchored
   ZKP, satisfy it? Our reading of §Community-Anchored ZKP is that it should,
   and that condition (a) is a bootstrapping-era artifact.
3. Should condition (b) be struck as inconsistent with the two-VRC edge model,
   or does it describe an alternative single-credential form that the body does
   not define?
4. Should the VMC entry's edge-verifiability sentence be moved to the body or
   removed?

Happy to open a PR against `spec/terms-definitions/` and the relevant body
sections once the group has a view on (1) and (2) — the answer to (2) in
particular changes what the fix looks like rather than just where it lands.

title: ci: name the semver job what it is — a report, not a gate
body:
Renames the `semver checks` job to **`semver report (informational — never
blocks)`**. One line of YAML; no behaviour change.

## Why

The job is `continue-on-error: true` and has been since it was written. It
compares each published crate's public API against crates.io and **reports** —
it cannot fail a build. Every crate here is `0.x`, where breaking changes are
expected, and `release-plz.toml` sets `semver_check = true`, so the actual
enforcement happens at release time from the same signal. This job is the
early copy, so the author sees it while the change is still in hand.

All of which the job's comment already said. But the check list is where most
people meet this job, and there it was a bare name beside a red cross on every
single PR.

I proposed deleting it. The reasoning was that a check failing on every PR
protects nothing, so it trains people to ignore red — which is true of a
broken gate, and this is not one. The premise came from the name, and the
name is what the check list shows.

So the fix goes where the problem is: a job whose red is expected should say
so **where the red is displayed**, not only in a comment nobody opens.

## What did not change

- Still `continue-on-error: true`; still cannot block a merge.
- Still runs on pull requests only.
- The eleven standing items are unchanged and are not rot — they are the
  *known* breaking changes across `vti-common`, `vta-sdk` and `vta-service`,
  and reporting them is what lets release-plz move the version instead of
  shipping a break as a patch.

Baselining them to green was the alternative. It would clear the report until
the next genuine break, which is arguably when you most want to see it — but
it changes published version numbers, so it is a release decision rather than
a CI one, and worth taking separately if wanted.

## Checks

`main` is not branch-protected, so the rename does not orphan a required
status check. The only other references to `semver-checks` in the repo are to
the *tool* (`cargo-semver-checks` in `publish.yml` and the run step), which is
unchanged. Workflow YAML parses.

title: chore(vtc): install/claim 0.2, and a drift note that blamed the wrong side
body:
Moves the install ceremony to `vtc/install/claim/{start,finish}/0.2`, which
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#263 published without the DID-binding
challenge and signature. Drift **4 → 2**.

## What this closes, and how the ledger got it backwards

Both entries were recorded — by me, yesterday — as *"the only place the
service is behind the spec on a security control"*, and I kept the requirement
out of #262 on that basis rather than deleting a required member so we could
conform.

That was the reverse of what happened:

| | |
|---|---|
| **2026-05-12** | implementation lands **with** `did_binding_signature` |
| **2026-05-15** | implementation **removes it** — *"test-passable but impossible to complete in a production browser"*, because WebAuthn never exposes the credential private key |
| **2026-07-21** | the **specification** is written, two months later, **still requiring it** |

Nothing in any repository has ever sent or read those members. Verified across
every local clone for all six spellings — `didBindingChallenge`,
`didBindingSignature`, both snake_case forms, the generated type name, and
`bindingInvalid`. Every hit was schema, generated bindings, the published
website, retired local `1.0` documents, or one stale ASCII diagram in this
service's own module doc. The only client is the admin SPA's install page,
which is a browser — the environment that cannot produce the signature at all.

**The lesson is not "the spec was wrong".** It is that *"the schema requires X
and the service omits X"* is a true sentence that says nothing about which
side is at fault, and reads as an accusation against the implementation. Both
histories needed checking before the note was written. That is now recorded in
the `KNOWN_DRIFT_COUNT` header, where the next person to read a drift note
will see it.

## Changes

- Route mounts and the admin SPA's install page retarget to `0.2` — four
  sites, no behaviour change, since the service already sent exactly what
  `0.2` describes.
- Both conformance entries promoted to `checked!`.
- Seven trust-task constants across four integration suites
  (`install_flow`, `install_claim`, `admin_bootstrap`,
  `emergency_bootstrap`) retarget to `0.2`. They failed on the first gate run
  — the header no longer matched the mount, which is the Trust-Task binding
  doing exactly its job.
- `routes/install.rs`'s module doc: the ASCII flow diagram still showed
  `did_binding_challenge` / `did_binding_signature` on the wire. Corrected,
  and the paragraph explaining the 2026-05 removal now records that the
  reasoning lived only in that comment for two months while the published
  task said otherwise.

## What is deliberately still absent

`0.2` states what the ceremony does *not* prove: the admin DID is **assigned
by** it, not **asserted by** the installer, and nothing demonstrates control
of a pre-existing identity.

Letting an operator claim admin under a DID they already hold is a genuinely
different proof — ownership of a **verification method present in that DID's
active DID document**, resolved live rather than taken from the request, and
signed outside the WebAuthn ceremony by the key that backs the DID. That
restores the distinction `0.1` was reaching for, because the passkey and the
DID key would then actually be different keys. It is named in the spec as a
future version rather than approximated here.

## The two that remain

Neither is a shape to fix; both need a `0.2` upstream because they replace
required members, and in both the service's shape looks like the stronger one:

1. **`auth/recognise`** — the payload is two loose credentials; this service
   takes one holder-signed VP embedding both, binding a nonce and this
   community's DID as `domain`. The VP carries a holder-binding proof two
   loose credentials cannot.
2. **`join-requests/submit`** — the response is `{requestId, status}` with
   `status` a `const: "pending"`; this service returns a four-valued verdict
   (allow / deny / refer / request_more) of which `pending` expresses one.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast`
- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `npm run lint` in `admin-ui`

Refs #1059

title: spec(vtc): recognise and submit 0.2 — a replay hole and a constant that hid three outcomes
body:
The last two VTC tasks whose published shape is weaker than what the reference
implementation actually does. Both replace a required member, so both are new
versions rather than in-place edits.

## `auth/recognise/0.2` — the payload was a replayable impersonation token

`0.1` took the two foreign credentials directly, as `{vec, vmc}`.

Both are bearer artifacts. Anyone who obtained the pair — from a relayed join,
an audit log, a backup, a compromised member device — held everything the
payload required, and the recognising community had no way to distinguish the
subject from someone holding a copy. There was no proof the caller controlled
the subject's key, no freshness, and no audience binding, so one captured pair
worked at **every** community that recognised the issuer, **indefinitely**.

`0.2` requires a holder-signed Verifiable Presentation embedding the same two
credentials, with `proofPurpose: authentication`, committing to the single-use
nonce from `vtc/auth/recognise/challenge` and naming the recognising
community's DID as `domain`.

Three properties, none redundant:

| | |
|---|---|
| holder signature | proves possession of the subject key |
| `nonce` | defeats replay |
| `domain` | stops a presentation minted for one community being spent at another |

Consumers MUST also refuse unless the presentation's holder is the
credentials' subject — otherwise one party is admitted on another's evidence.

An invalid-example pins that a `0.1`-shaped body is rejected, so the
replayable form cannot reach a `0.2` consumer.

The challenge half of this flow (`vtc/auth/recognise/challenge/0.1`) already
exists and is unchanged; `0.1` simply never required callers to use it.

## `join-requests/submit/0.2` — one constant for four outcomes

`0.1`'s response carried `status`, a `const: "pending"`. A submission has four
outcomes: admit outright, refuse outright, park for a human or quorum
decision, or ask the applicant for more evidence. A constant expresses one, so
the other three were reported as `pending` or not at all.

`0.2` returns a `verdict`. `pending` maps onto `refer`, which is what it
actually described: parked, waiting on the community.

The distinction that matters most is **`refer` versus `requestMore`**. Both
mean "not decided", and they place the next action with different parties —
`refer` waits on the community, `requestMore` waits on the applicant and names
what it needs. Collapsing them is what makes a join flow feel like a black
box: an applicant told "pending" cannot tell whether to wait or to act.

## `vtc/_shared/0.1/ceremony` — a new shared component

`Verdict`, `VerdictEffect`, `VerdictWith`. Shared rather than local to
`submit`, because the four outcomes are the same wherever a policy decides
something about an applicant, and the reference implementation already treats
this as one type across ceremony families.

`VerdictWith` is deliberately **one flat object** whose members are
effect-dependent by prose rather than by `if`/`then` per effect. That trades
schema strictness for a generated type that does not need a discriminated
union per family — the schema stays implementable, and the cost is stated in
the component's own description: consumers MUST branch on `effect`, never on
which members happen to be present.

## Versioning

Replacing a required member is breaking. Both specs are `status: draft`, and
SPEC §5.2 permits a breaking change to a draft artifact to be released as a
MINOR increment — hence `0.2` in both cases. The `0.1` pair moves to `retired`
with `supersededBy`, a permitted `draft → retired` transition (§5.3).

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 348 specs, 65 shared schemas, 533 example documents
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — no drift
- `npm run check-bindings` — 348 specs against 348 TS and 343 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — 33 suites, no failures

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.12 and `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.12.

The link checker earned its place here: it caught `../../challenge/0.1/` in the
new prose, where `challenge` is a sibling of the version folder rather than two
levels up.
