title: feat(vtc)!: distinguish half-edges from complete edges in the relationships graph
body:
Closes the remaining graph work on #1054. One of the two open items is built,
one is deliberately not, and the reasoning for the second is the part worth
reading.

## Built: half-edges vs complete edges

DTG Credentials defines a DTG edge as **two** VRCs, one in each direction.
`GET /v1/relationships/graph` returned one entry per stored VRC, so a mutual
relationship and a unilateral claim rendered identically — two members who had
each vouched for the other looked the same as one member asserting an edge the
other has never acknowledged.

That distinction is what the dropped subject-membership check was replaced
*with*. #1061 stopped requiring the subject to be a current member, on the DTG
rule that "community membership is not a precondition for issuing, holding, or
presenting a VRC", and on the reasoning that the subject's consent to an edge is
their publication of the reciprocal VRC. An operator who cannot see whether that
reciprocal VRC arrived cannot see the consent signal at all.

The response now groups by unordered pair (`build_graph`,
`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:817`). Each edge carries:

- `endpoints` — the two DIDs, sorted, so a pair has one identity whichever half
  was published first
- `halves` — every VRC published between them, oldest first, each with the row
  id that `DELETE /v1/relationships/{id}` takes
- `complete` — a VRC exists in **both** directions

Two cases that are easy to get wrong, both pinned by tests:

- **Several VRCs in one direction do not complete an edge.** Idempotency is
  keyed on the credential hash, not on direction
  (`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:322`), so a member can publish three
  A→B VRCs. `complete` checks for a VRC in each direction, not for two rows.
- **A self-issued VRC (`issuer == subject`) is never complete.** No counterparty
  can reciprocate, and the naive both-directions test matches the same row
  twice. Nothing on the publish path rejects a self-issued VRC, so this is
  reachable.

Admin UI (`vtc-service/admin-ui/src/plugins/relationshipsGraph.tsx`): complete
edges draw solid and double-headed, half-edges dashed and single-headed pointing
at the party who has not answered; the overview counts the two separately and a
selected node's edge list reads "mutual with" vs "not reciprocated".

**Breaking:** `edges[]` was `{id, issuerDid, subjectDid, createdAt}` per VRC and
is now `{endpoints, halves, complete}` per pair, with the old fields moved onto
`halves[]`. The only consumer is the in-repo admin UI, updated here.

## Not built: making the graph derived rather than stored

Item 3 of the proposal on #1054 was "make the graph derived rather than
stored… without persisting an M-DID adjacency list." I did not build it. Three
reasons, recorded in full in
`docs/05-design-notes/vrc-publish-proof-of-possession.md`.

**The motivation was removed by #1061, not deferred.** The concern was a durable
*membership-DID* adjacency list. Since #1061 the stored DIDs are whichever
identifier the member chose to publish under: under the pairwise form an R-DID,
which names nobody and correlates nothing beyond the one relationship it was
minted for; under the attributed form a membership DID the member has
deliberately asserted, which DTG Credentials permits directly. Neither is what
item 3 was written against.

**"Derived" has no source to derive from.** The relationships keyspace is the
only place a published VRC exists on the VTC side — `Relationship.vrc_jsonld`
holds the credential verbatim, and `issuer_did`/`subject_did` are projections of
fields inside it (`vtc-service/src/relationships/mod.rs:62-85`). Deriving the
graph from something else means not storing published VRCs at all, which deletes
`POST /v1/relationships` and both read endpoints with it. The change that *is*
available is narrower — drop the two projected DID columns and re-read them from
the stored credential on each scan — and it removes no information, because the
credential containing them is still the row.

**Nothing publishes.** I checked the claim rather than taking it: `POST
/v1/relationships` is the only production writer to the keyspace and it has no
caller. Not in this workspace (only `vtc-service/tests/relationships.rs`), not
in `vta-sdk` (no relationship protocol module at all), not in `vtc-client`, and
not in `openvtc`. OpenVTC mints VRCs through `DTGCredential::new_vrc` and
exchanges them peer-to-peer over DIDComm
(`openvtc/src/state_handler/inbox_actions.rs:745`,
`openvtc/src/state_handler/main_page/mod.rs:2096`), then retains them locally;
it speaks the VTC's join, ACL, credential-exchange and self-remove Trust Tasks
but never `relationships/publish`. So the graph is empty in every deployment
that exists.

None of that makes the question wrong — a community that gets real publish
traffic under the attributed form does accumulate a correlatable edge set, by
design and with the members' assertion, and one that gets pairwise traffic
accumulates a set correlatable only to an operator holding the audit trail,
which #1061 already recorded as an accepted residual. It makes it premature.
The point to revisit is when something publishes, and the decision then is
whether to keep the two DID columns or read them out of the credential — not
whether to hold the credentials.

## Uncertainty worth flagging

The half-edge/complete rule assumes the two directions are linkable by DID
equality: A's VRC names B's identifier as subject and B's names A's as issuer.
Under pairwise identifiers that holds only because each party publishes the R-DID
its counterparty already knows. If a future flow has a party rotate its R-DID
mid-relationship, the two halves stop pairing and a complete edge silently
becomes two half-edges. Nothing in the stack does that today and the R-DID
uniqueness check would reject the rotated DID's second counterparty anyway, but
it is the assumption the grouping rests on.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 30 test binaries, 0 failures
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt`
- `npm run lint` in `vtc-service/admin-ui` (tsc, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on)

New coverage: 6 unit tests on `build_graph` (minted through
`DTGCredential::new_vrc`, not hand-rolled JSON) and 2 integration tests on the
endpoint (`graph_separates_complete_edges_from_half_edges` pins the wire shape,
`graph_is_admin_only` the gate — the endpoint had no test before).

Refs #1054

title: Pairwise relationship identifiers vs. the relationships ACL policy
body:
Raised from OpenVTC/openvtc#241, which proposes defaulting relationship
communication to pairwise Relationship DIDs (R-DIDs) rather than the persona
DID. That issue originates in an external RAHP/DRARM assessment finding
(`OVTC-RAHP-04`) scoring persona-DID relationship communication as stable-
identifier correlation.

The client-side half of that change is straightforward. But it collides with a
VTC policy, and the protocol question belongs here.

## The collision

`vtc-service/policies/default/relationships.rego` is the whole policy:

```rego
default allow := false
allow if {
	input.action == "publish"
	input.issuer_member.is_current
	input.subject_member.is_current
}
```

Both parties must be current, ACL-listed, non-tombstoned community members
(`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:122-134`, `:349-356`). And the issuer
is pinned to the authenticated session DID:

`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:97-107`
```rust
let issuer_did = extract_did_field(vrc, "issuer")?;
let subject_did = extract_subject_id(vrc)?;
if auth.did != issuer_did {
    return Err(AppError::Forbidden(format!(
        "session DID ({}) does not match VRC issuer ({issuer_did}) — \
         VRCs are self-issued; the VTC never mints them on a member's behalf", auth.did)));
}
```

A pairwise R-DID has no ACL row, so a VRC issued under one is rejected — 422
"subject DID … is not a current community member", or 403
`RelationshipPolicyDenied`. **The only enforcement that exists on this path
forbids pairwise identifiers rather than requiring them.**

`GET /v1/relationships/graph` (`routes/relationships.rs:446`) then deliberately
exposes the full correlatable member-to-member edge set to admins.

This is not a bug report — the ACL check is doing what it was designed to do.
It is a design question that the client cannot resolve on its own.

## The question

Should relationship communication use pairwise identifiers, and if so, how does
that reconcile with a trust graph whose entries are required to be attributable
to current members?

Some shapes worth weighing:

1. **Separate the two.** Pairwise identifiers govern the *communication channel*;
   the published VRC stays persona-attributed. This is roughly what OpenVTC does
   today — the R-DID carries post-handshake messages, the VRC `issuer` is the
   persona DID. It bounds the exposure to the graph, but the graph is exactly
   where the correlation the assessment describes lives.
2. **Pairwise in the graph, with a membership proof.** Let a VRC be issued under
   an R-DID accompanied by evidence that the R-DID belongs to a current member,
   without naming which. Costs a proof mechanism the stack does not have.
3. **Accept persona attribution as intended.** The trust graph's value may
   depend on edges being attributable; if so, say that explicitly so clients
   stop treating pairwise as an unrealised goal.

## What is currently true, for the record

The pairwise concept is absent from this repo and from `vta-sdk`. `pairwise`,
`R-DID` and `P-DID` do not appear as concepts; the word `pairwise` occurs once,
in an unrelated comment at `vtc-service/src/config.rs:764`. There is no
relationship protocol module in `vta-sdk` — the wire surface is four Trust Tasks
(`relationships/{list,graph,publish,revoke}/0.1`, `vtc-service/src/routes/mod.rs:631-644`),
and `PublishBody` is a single `vrc` field (`routes/relationships.rs:57`).
`vta-sdk` 0.27.0 → 0.28.0 changes nothing here.

Related prior decision: TSP relationship formation (the RFI/RFA invite→accept
FSM, and TSP's nested/pairwise VID APIs) was evaluated and dropped in favour of
relationship-free routed send —
`docs/05-design-notes/tsp-outbound-send.md:79-85`. Neither `form_relationship`
nor any nested-VID API is called anywhere in the repo.

The one "default to pairwise" statement in the design docs is
`design-docs/trust-task-delegation-architecture.md:278-285`, and it is scoped to
SIOPv2 / proxy-login subject DIDs against relying parties — not to relationship
edges.

## Why it matters more here than the generic pattern

The stable identifier in question is a published, resolvable `did:webvh` that
frequently carries a verified agent name. Two counterparties do not need traffic
analysis to correlate a persona across contexts — they compare a string and then
resolve it to a named identity. The linkage is a lookup, not an inference.

title: Tests hand-roll DTG credentials instead of minting them through the catalog
body:
## Summary

Where a test builds credential JSON by hand, it encodes the *implementation's
belief* about the wire form rather than the catalog's definition of it. The
test and the bug then agree with each other and with nothing that exists, and
the suite stays green through arbitrary drift.

This is the systemic cause behind #1062 and behind the VRC type error corrected
in #1061 — not a defect in itself, which is why it is worth fixing as its own
piece of work.

## Detail

The confirmed instance: `tests/recognise.rs` built its VEC as

```rust
let vec = sign_vc(issuer_seed, "VerifiableEndorsementCredential", &subject_did).await;
```

while `issue_endorsement` mints `EndorsementCredential` through
`DTGCredential::new_vec`. The handler matched the same fictional string, so
every recognition test passed and cross-community recognition was broken
against every genuinely-issued VEC. Changing only the fixture to the real wire
form — handler untouched — produced

```
400 presentation has no VerifiableEndorsementCredential
```

Both are fixed. The pattern is not: `sign_vc`-style hand-rolled builders remain
in `credentials/exchange/tests.rs` and elsewhere, and nothing prevents the next
one.

## Why it matters

A test suite that mints through the same catalog as production cannot disagree
with production about the wire form. One that hand-rolls can, silently, and the
green suite is then evidence of nothing.

## Suggested fix

1. Make `dtg_credentials` constructors the sanctioned way to build a DTG
   credential in a test. A helper crate-side (`test_support`) that wraps
   `new_vmc` / `new_vec` / `new_vrc` / `new_vic` + signing would cover most
   call sites.
2. Hand-rolled credential JSON becomes a deliberate, commented exception —
   legitimate for malformed-input cases, which genuinely need shapes the
   catalog cannot produce.
3. Consider a census test over the test tree for literal `"*Credential"` type
   strings, in the spirit of the existing `catalog_wire_shape` guard.

Conformance audit finding **F4**.

title: No shared ingress validator: DTG credentials are accepted without checking the common structure
body:
## Summary

DTG Credentials §Common Structure is normative and applies to every credential
type: `@context` MUST include both the W3C v2 and DTG contexts, and `type` MUST
include `VerifiableCredential`, `DTGCredential`, and exactly one concrete
subtype.

The stack asserts this on **everything it mints** and on almost nothing it
**accepts**.

## Detail

Issuance is in good shape. `credentials/dtg.rs` builds every VTC-minted
credential through the `dtg-credentials` catalog, and `catalog_wire_shape`
pins each one's exact `@context` and `type` arrays, in order, with a comment
explaining why order matters in JSON-LD. That is the pattern a reference
implementation should have.

Ingress has no equivalent. Until #1061 the VRC publish path never read `type`
at all, so any signed JSON with an `issuer` and a `credentialSubject.id` became
an edge in the community trust graph. #1063 fixes the same class in the
recognition path. Neither is a general solution — each closed one boundary by
hand.

Remaining boundaries that accept a DTG credential without validating the
common structure:

- `routes/recognise.rs` — validates type *classification* after #1063 but not
  `@context` or the `DTGCredential` base type
- `ceremony/verify.rs` / `ceremony/facts.rs` — credentials enter the decision
  pipeline as facts
- the join path — VIC handling validates temporal and single-use properties
  thoroughly, but not the common structure

## Why it matters

A credential that does not carry the DTG context is not a DTG credential, and
an edge is only interpretable if it says what it is. More practically: the two
bugs found so far (#1062 and the VRC type in #1061) were both invisible
*because* nothing validated the field they were wrong about.

## Suggested fix

One shared validator — `@context` entries, `DTGCredential`, exactly one
concrete subtype, classified through `dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType` —
applied at every boundary that accepts a DTG credential. `check_vrc_shape` in
`routes/relationships.rs` (added in #1061) is the shape to generalise; it
should move out of that module rather than be copied.

Found in a conformance audit of the stack against DTG Credentials, prompted by
#1054. This is finding **F2**; the systemic reason it survived is F4.

title: test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too (#1072)
body:
test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too (#1072)

* test(vtc)!: check ingressed credentials against the catalog, and test validators against it too

Audit findings F2 and F4, together — because either alone reopens the trap. A
shared ingress validator whose tests hand-roll their input validates the
implementation against itself, which is the exact condition that let a handler
match `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` for its entire life while nothing has
ever issued that type.

**One place decides what a DTG credential is.** `credentials::ingress` checks
§Common Structure — both required `@context` entries, `VerifiableCredential` +
`DTGCredential`, exactly one concrete subtype — and classifies through
`dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType`, the same catalog the issuing side mints
from. `check_vrc_shape` becomes a call to it. The recognition path gains the
check it never had: it classified on `type` alone, so a document carrying the
right subtype tag and neither `@context` entry was routed as though it were a
VEC.

**The tests assert against catalog output, not literals.** A literal in a test
can agree with a literal in a validator while both disagree with what any
client sends. So the guards mint through `new_vrc` / `new_vmc` / `new_vec` and
require the validator to accept the result. Change the catalog's wire form and
they fail; change a validator away from the catalog and they fail; no literal
in the file can make them pass.

`test_support::dtg_json` is the sanctioned way for a test to obtain a DTG
credential. Hand-rolled JSON stays correct for malformed-input cases — the
catalog cannot produce a credential missing its own `@context`.

Each guard was mutation-tested rather than assumed:

- accepted subtype in `check_vrc_shape` Relationship → Membership: the
  round-trip test fails
- the legacy tag re-added to `classify`: the refusal test fails
- the DTG context dropped from the recognition fixture: the end-to-end holder
  test fails, with the same 400 that #1062 produced

A guard that cannot fail is worth nothing, and three of these now demonstrably
can.

Also pinned: `VerifiableRecognitionCredential` and the `Verifiable`-prefixed
membership and endorsement tags are refused by name. All three were invented
here, none is a DTG type, and each has already cost a bug.

BREAKING CHANGE: a credential presented to `/v1/auth/recognise` that does not
carry the DTG common structure is now skipped rather than routed to its slot.
Credentials minted through `dtg-credentials` — which is every credential this
stack issues — are unaffected.

Refs #1054, #1062, closes #1064, closes #1066

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc): drop a duplicated #[test] attribute

An edit inserted a test function between `#[test]` and the function it
belonged to, leaving the new test with two attributes. Clippy's
`duplicate-macro-attributes` catches it under `-D warnings`, which is what
CI runs.

Harmless in effect — the affected test ran twice and passed twice, and the
displaced attribute was replaced — but the doubled name in the test output was
a signal, and it was there to be read before CI found it.

title: fix(join)!: require the DTG common structure on an ingested invitation (#256)
body:
fix(join)!: require the DTG common structure on an ingested invitation (#256)

`validate_invitation_credential` is careful and well-documented — it checks the
W3C VC Data Model 2.0 mandatory properties and the VIC profile the receiving
VTC enforces. It checked neither half of DTG Credentials §Common Structure,
which is normative for every DTG credential:

- `@context` MUST include `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`
- `type` MUST include `DTGCredential`

That string appears nowhere else in this repo. It is never required and never
checked, because everything openvtc *mints* goes through `dtg-credentials`,
which supplies it — so the one place a credential arrives from outside was also
the one place nothing verified it was a DTG credential at all. A document with
the right subtype tag and neither common-structure element passed as a VIC.

The fixtures agreed, which is why nothing noticed. `complete_vic` and
`pasteable_vic` both called themselves complete while carrying only the W3C
half, and the validator checked only the same half — so the test encoded the
implementation's belief about the wire form rather than the specification's
definition of it. Both now use the form `new_vic` actually emits, which is what
makes the new checks a regression test rather than a restatement: revert the
validator and nothing fails; revert the fixtures and the validator catches them.

Real VICs are unaffected. The VTC mints them through `DTGCredential::new_vic`
and its wire-shape guard pins both contexts and all three type entries, so a
credential any community actually issued already satisfies this.

The three constants are named in `openvtc-core` rather than spelled inline.
`dtg-credentials` builds all of them into what it mints but exports none of
them; removing the duplication needs a public constant upstream, requested in
OpenVTC/dtg-credentials#10.

BREAKING CHANGE: a pasted invitation lacking the DTG context or the
`DTGCredential` type is now refused at ingest with a message naming what is
missing, rather than accepted and submitted.

Refs OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1064

title: Audit events record credential type names that nothing issues
body:
## Summary

Emitted audit envelopes carry `credential_type: "VerifiableMembershipCredential"`
and `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"`. Neither is a DTG credential type, and
nothing in the stack mints either.

## Detail

- `vti-common/src/audit/event.rs:901-902` documents the field as the "wire-form
  credential type", naming both.
- `vti-common/src/audit/event.rs:1593,1612` write them.
- `vtc-service/src/routes/endorsements.rs:226` sets
  `credential_type: "VerifiableEndorsementCredential"`.

What is actually issued is `MembershipCredential` and `EndorsementCredential`
— pinned by `catalog_wire_shape` in `credentials/dtg.rs`, and by
`DTGCredentialType`'s `Display`.

## Why it matters

No protocol behaviour depends on these strings, so the impact is low. But the
audit trail is the record intended to be authoritative after the fact, and it
currently names credential types that do not exist — which is misleading in
precisely the artifact an operator reaches for when reconstructing what
happened.

It is also the same root cause as #1062: a `Verifiable`-prefixed literal that
was never a wire tag, surviving because nothing compared it to what the catalog
emits.

## Suggested fix

Record `DTGCredentialType`'s `Display` value rather than a literal. Since these
strings are persisted, decide explicitly whether to migrate existing rows or
leave historical entries as-is and note the changeover — the field is inside
the envelope's chained content, so rewriting rows is not free.

Conformance audit finding **F10**.

title: refactor!: delete the Verifiable-prefixed credential tags that were never DTG types (#1071)
body:
refactor!: delete the Verifiable-prefixed credential tags that were never DTG types (#1071)

`VerifiableMembershipCredential` and `VerifiableEndorsementCredential` are not
DTG credential types and never were. The specification defines seven concrete
subtypes; neither is among them, and nothing in this stack has ever issued
either. They survived as a name, a pair of literals and a compatibility shim,
and between them they broke cross-community recognition for every real
presentation (#1062).

Four places, one cause.

**The SDK constant.** `VERIFIABLE_MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` held the value
`"MembershipCredential"`, with a doc comment explaining that the prefix in the
name was historical and the tag did not have it. A constant whose name
disagrees with its value is an invitation, and it was taken: someone reading
the name hand-rolled `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` into the recognition
path, where it matched nothing. Renamed to `MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE`, and
`ENDORSEMENT_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` added beside it so the VEC tag has a home rather
than being a literal at the point of use.

**The compatibility shim.** #1063 added `LEGACY_TYPE_TAGS`, accepting both
prefixed tags from peers predating the catalog adoption. Nothing is published,
so no such peer exists — and a reference implementation that accepts a type the
specification does not define reintroduces exactly the drift the function it
sits in was written to prevent. Removed; the test that pinned the behaviour now
pins its refusal.

**The audit trail.** Emitted envelopes recorded `credential_type:
"VerifiableMembershipCredential"` / `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` — tags
no credential ever carried, in the one record meant to be authoritative after
the fact. They now record what was issued.

**The policy input.** `issuer_member` / `subject_member` were carried alongside
`issuer` / `subject` for operator policies written against the pre-#1061 shape.
There are no deployed operator policies to preserve, and two spellings of one
concept is how the concept drifts. The duplicates are gone and the surviving
fields carry `is_current`.

Docs: the `relationships` rows in the MVP spec described the old input shape and
the old default-policy rule. The retired `publish/1.0` trust-task doc called a
VRC a "Verifiable Recognition Credential" — wrong in every version, so corrected
in place rather than left as a retired-doc excuse.

Deliberately untouched: `subject_member` in `removal.rego` and the ceremony
documents is an unrelated input shape that happens to share a name.

BREAKING CHANGE: `vta_sdk::protocols::members::VERIFIABLE_MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE`
is renamed to `MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` (value unchanged). The
`relationships.rego` input drops `issuer_member` / `subject_member`; the shipped
default policy is updated, and an operator policy reading the old names now
denies rather than silently passing. Recognition no longer accepts the
`Verifiable`-prefixed tags.

Refs #1054, #1062, closes #1070

title: feat(relationships)!: issue the VRC under the relationship DID, not the persona (#255)
body:
feat(relationships)!: issue the VRC under the relationship DID, not the persona (#255)

The last half of #241, and the half that mattered most.

Relationship communication has defaulted to a pairwise R-DID since #254, but
the credential it produces did not. `prepare_accept_vrc_request` minted the VRC
with `issuer = persona_did`, signed with the persona key. The subject was
already the peer's R-DID, so only the issuer half was persona-attributed — and
that was enough: the pairwise channel led straight back to the persona.

It is the worst place to leak it. The handshake DIDs are observed once, by the
mediator, at establishment. The VRC is the durable artifact both parties retain
and may publish to a community trust graph, where it correlates every
relationship a persona holds for as long as anyone keeps a copy. #241 said the
same: "The handshake persona DID is observed once; a published VRC correlates
indefinitely."

This could not be fixed here before now. The VTC pinned a published VRC's
issuer to the authenticated session DID, so a VRC issued under a relationship
DID was rejected outright — the only enforcement that existed forbade pairwise
identifiers rather than requiring them. Lifted in
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1061, which separates membership (proven
by the session) from the identifier the credential carries.

Both ends move together, so this is breaking on the wire:

- **Issuance** signs as whichever identity the relationship uses, keyed on
  `is_persona_did` — the same discriminator `listener_id_for_did` routes sends
  on. A relationship established without a dedicated R-DID still signs with the
  persona key, unchanged.
- **`vet_vrc_issued` gate 2** now requires the issuer to be the sender's DID in
  *this* relationship rather than their persona DID. That is strictly tighter
  as well as more private: gate 1 already matched the authenticated DIDComm
  sender against the same field, so the credential is pinned to the channel it
  arrived on instead of to a persona that could have issued it anywhere.
  Relationships with no R-DID are unaffected — `remote_did` equals
  `remote_p_did` there, and a test pins that.

The `#key-1` verification-method convention that `generate_did_peer_from_secrets`
imposes was already load-bearing in two places and spelled out longhand in
both. It is now named — `relationship_signing_vm_id` — with the secret lookup
beside it in `openvtc-core`, so the TUI crate does not reach into the secrets
resolver directly.

Docs: the note deferring "full pairwise operation, including the VRC issuer
field" to upstream work is replaced by what actually happens, including why the
issuer field mattered more than the handshake routing does. The example
credential showed a `did:webvh` issuer; it now shows the `did:peer` one it
would really carry.

What #241 leaves open after this is the handshake routing itself, which is
intrinsic — the mediator must route request/accept/finalise before a pairwise
channel exists — and worth closing as accepted rather than outstanding.

BREAKING CHANGE: a VRC issued by a peer running an older build carries their
persona DID and is now refused, and one issued by this build is refused by
older peers. Nothing is published yet, so no compatibility window is provided.

Refs #241, OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054

title: Cross-community recognition matches a VEC type string nothing issues
body:
## Summary

`POST /v1/auth/recognise` routes a presented credential to its VEC slot by
matching the literal string `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"`
(`vtc-service/src/routes/recognise.rs:305-311`). No VEC this stack produces
carries that type. A real, catalog-minted VEC falls through to `continue`, the
`vec_cred` slot stays `None`, and recognition fails.

## Detail

The VTC mints VECs through the DTG catalog — `issue_endorsement` calls
`DTGCredential::new_vec` (`vtc-service/src/credentials/dtg.rs:148-157`) — and
the wire-shape guard asserts the resulting `type` array exactly:

```
["VerifiableCredential", "DTGCredential", "EndorsementCredential"]
```

(`dtg.rs`, `catalog_wire_shape::endorsement_credential_wire_shape`)

There is no `VerifiableEndorsementCredential` in that array, in
`dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType`, or in the DTG Credentials specification,
which requires `type` to include `"EndorsementCredential"`.

The VMC branch immediately below gets this right, because it uses the shared
constant `VERIFIABLE_MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` — whose *value* is
`"MembershipCredential"`. A comment in `tests/recognise.rs` already warns about
exactly this trap:

> The VMC's wire tag is `MembershipCredential` — NOT
> `VerifiableMembershipCredential`. The `VERIFIABLE_` prefix lives in the
> constant's *name* only (it's historical) [...] Use the constant, not a literal.

The VEC branch uses a literal, and hit the trap the comment describes.

## Why it is green

`tests/recognise.rs:365` hand-rolls the presented VEC with the same fictional
type the handler matches:

```rust
let vec = sign_vc(issuer_seed, "VerifiableEndorsementCredential", &subject_did).await;
```

So the test mints the bug and the handler matches the bug, and they agree. The
suite validates the implementation against itself rather than against the
credential the VTC actually issues. Nothing in the recognition path is
exercised against a catalog-minted VEC.

## Suggested fix

1. Match on the catalog, not on a string — classify with
   `dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType::try_from(&types)` and select
   `Endorsement` / `Membership`, so issuer and verifier cannot drift apart.
2. Build the VEC in `tests/recognise.rs` with `DTGCredential::new_vec` rather
   than `sign_vc(.., "VerifiableEndorsementCredential", ..)`, so the test would
   have failed.
3. Audit the remaining `"Verifiable*Credential"` literals — `audit/event.rs`
   records `credential_type: "VerifiableMembershipCredential"` /
   `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"` in emitted events, which is at best
   misleading in an audit trail.

## Severity

Cross-community recognition is the path by which a member of one VTC obtains a
session at another. If this analysis is right it does not work against any
genuinely issued VEC, and no test would notice.

Worth confirming with an end-to-end check that mints through `issue_endorsement`
and presents the result, before assuming the analysis over the green suite.

Found while making the VRC publish path conformant in #1061, which fixes the
same class of problem for `RelationshipCredential`.

title: fix(vtc): route a presented VEC by the type the catalog actually mints (#1063)
body:
fix(vtc): route a presented VEC by the type the catalog actually mints (#1063)

Cross-community recognition rejected every genuinely-issued VEC.

`extract_vec_vmc` routed a presented credential to its VEC slot by matching
the literal `"VerifiableEndorsementCredential"`. Nothing mints that.
`issue_endorsement` builds through `DTGCredential::new_vec`, and the catalog
wire-shape guard pins the result as `["VerifiableCredential", "DTGCredential",
"EndorsementCredential"]` — no `Verifiable` prefix, because the prefix belongs
to the concept and never to the wire tag. So a real VEC fell through to
`continue`, the slot stayed empty, and the request died at

    400 presentation has no VerifiableEndorsementCredential

naming a credential type that does not exist in DTG Credentials.

The VMC branch beside it was always correct, because it read the shared
`VERIFIABLE_MEMBERSHIP_CREDENTIAL_TYPE` constant — whose *value* is
`"MembershipCredential"`. A comment in `tests/recognise.rs` already warned
about precisely this trap and said to use the constant rather than a literal.
The VEC branch used a literal.

Classification now goes through `dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType`, so the
routing side and the minting side share one definition of the wire form and
cannot drift apart again. Pre-catalog peers are still accepted: recognition is
cross-community, and a VTC predating `cb06fb31` hand-rolled the prefixed tags,
so those route with a warning — here and nowhere else.

The suite was green throughout because the test hand-rolled its VEC with the
same fictional type the handler matched. Test and bug agreed, and neither
agreed with what the VTC issues. `sign_vc` now emits the DTG wire form, which
is what makes this a regression test rather than a restatement: revert the
handler and `matching_holder_clears_the_binding_gate` fails.

Three unit tests pin the classification directly — catalog form, legacy form,
and types the gate must ignore.

Found while auditing the stack against DTG Credentials for #1054.

Closes #1062

title: feat(vtc)!: let a member publish a relationship edge without naming themselves in it (#1061)
body:
feat(vtc)!: let a member publish a relationship edge without naming themselves in it (#1061)

* feat(vtc)!: let a member publish a relationship edge without naming themselves in it

Publishing a VRC required the credential's `issuer` to equal the caller's
session DID. That one line is why a member's membership DID ends up inside
the durable, publishable credential — and the community graph built from
those credentials is a correlatable member-to-member edge set. DTG
Credentials asks for the opposite: R-DIDs are RECOMMENDED, unique per
counterparty "even within the same community", and M-DID edges are a
bootstrapping allowance to migrate away from.

The pin was conflating two properties. The first — the VRC was made by the
party it names as issuer — is provided by the data-integrity proof and is
untouched here. The second — the party publishing it is the party that
issued it — is what the pin actually provided, and it is worth keeping:
issuance and publication are different disclosures, and appearing in the
community graph should be the issuer's disclosure to make, not that of
whoever happens to hold a copy.

So the pin is replaced rather than removed. The session proves community
membership; a publish authorization signed by the issuing key proves control
of it. Neither requires them to be the same string.

The authorization binds to `{type, vrc-hash, aud, sessionId, issuedAt}`, each
field covering a distinct replay: signatures made over other objects, other
credentials, other communities, other members' sessions, and unbounded reuse
within a live session. It is verified and dropped — never stored, logged or
audited, because it carries `sessionId` and persisting that would rebuild the
exact membership-to-relationship linkage pairwise identifiers exist to
remove. Two tests assert that directly, on the stored row and on the audit
store, since it is the kind of property a later debug log undoes silently.

The subject-must-be-a-member check is dropped on the pairwise path. It is not
merely unanswerable once the subject is an R-DID; DTG Credentials is explicit
that "community membership is not a precondition for issuing, holding, or
presenting a VRC". The subject's consent to the edge is their publication of
the reciprocal VRC — the two-VRC edge model — not this community's assertion
that they exist.

BREAKING CHANGE: the `relationships.rego` policy input gains
`authenticated_member`, `issuer.pop_verified` and `subject`. `issuer_member`
and `subject_member` are still supplied, and for a pairwise VRC both report
`is_current: false`, so an operator policy written against the old shape
denies the publish rather than being silently loosened. The shipped default
policy allows both forms; the deprecated one — `issuer` equal to the session
DID, no authorization — is accepted for one release.

Refs #1054, trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#21

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc)!: publish the credential the spec defines, and check that it is one

There is no such thing as a recognition credential. DTG Credentials defines
seven concrete subtypes and `RelationshipCredential` is the one a VRC carries;
`VerifiableRecognitionCredential` was never among them.

It survived here because the publish path never inspected `type` at all. The
string appeared only in this repo's fixtures, doc comments and an architecture
table — describing a credential nothing produces. openvtc has always minted
VRCs through `DTGCredential::new_vrc`, which emits the correct
`["VerifiableCredential", "DTGCredential", "RelationshipCredential"]`, and the
VTC accepted those only because it accepted anything.

So the tests added in the previous commit were exercising a wire form no client
sends. They now use the real one, and the gap they were papering over is
closed: `check_vrc_shape` rejects a credential that does not carry both
required `@context` entries, the `DTGCredential` base type, and exactly the
`RelationshipCredential` subtype. Classification goes through
`dtg_credentials::DTGCredentialType` — the same catalog `new_vrc` mints from —
so issuer and verifier share one definition of the wire form rather than
string-matching independently.

The VTC does not mint VRCs; they are self-issued. But it decides what becomes
an edge in the community's trust graph, and an edge is only interpretable if it
says what it is.

Four tests cover the shape gate, including a regression guard naming the
invented type directly, so it cannot drift back in unnoticed.

The recognition *protocol* — cross-community session minting from a foreign
VEC + VMC pair — is a different concept and is untouched.

BREAKING CHANGE: `POST /v1/relationships` now rejects a VRC that is not in the
DTG Credentials wire form. Clients minting through `DTGCredential::new_vrc`
are unaffected.

Refs #1054

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vtc)!: hold a relationship DID to what it claims, and let a community say what it expects

Two identifier forms, both permanent and supported. Neither is a migration
state, and the previous commit was wrong to call one deprecated.

**Attributed** — the VRC is issued under the member's own membership DID. The
edge names them and the graph is correlatable on purpose. A public
open-source community wants exactly this, and DTG Credentials permits it
directly: "the member may also assert the M-DID in any VRC where the member
wishes to assert a VTC relationship." Telling such a community its normal
operation is legacy, as the deprecation warning did, was a misreading of the
specification's bootstrapping language.

**Pairwise** — the VRC is issued under a relationship DID scoped to one
counterparty, with a publish authorization proving control of it.

The member chooses per relationship. The community *declares* which it expects
in the profile (`relationshipIdentifierDefault`, defaulting to `pairwise` to
match the specification's recommendation), so a client can read the expectation
before minting. It is a declaration, not a gate: both forms are accepted, and a
community that wants to require one enforces it in `relationships.rego`, which
now receives `identifier_form` on every publish.

An identifier presented as pairwise must actually be pairwise. DTG Credentials
requires "a new, unique R-DID for every single entity they connect with, even
within the same community", and publish now enforces it — unconditionally,
because it is type integrity rather than a privacy policy a community can
switch off. A verifier reading a pairwise edge is entitled to conclude the
identifier says nothing beyond that one relationship; a reused R-DID breaks
that inference for every reader of the graph, not just for whoever reused it.
The community is also the only party who can see the violation, since each
counterparty sees only its own edge.

Nothing is lost by holding the type to its meaning: a member who wants to be
recognised across relationships uses the attributed form. The rule does not
apply there, because a membership DID is not claiming to be pairwise.

The admin-config round-trip tests caught a real break rather than a shape nit:
adding a required field to CommunityProfile made every config export taken
before it unreadable. The field is `serde(default)` and the comment says why.

BREAKING CHANGE: `relationships.rego` input gains `identifier_form`. The
shipped default policy accepts both forms; an operator policy written against
the old shape still denies pairwise publishes rather than being silently
loosened. `CommunityProfile` gains `relationshipIdentifierDefault`, absent from
older exports and defaulted on read.

Refs #1054, trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#21

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc): attribute a published edge to the member, not to the identifier that issued it

The audit trail recorded the VRC's issuer as the actor. Under the pairwise
form that is a relationship DID, which names nobody — so the trail could not
answer "which member published this edge" for anyone, at any access level,
ever. Not redacted; never captured.

The actor is now the authenticated member.

This is a deliberate, narrow exception to this branch's own rule that the
membership-to-relationship linkage must not be persisted, so the reasoning for
drawing it here and nowhere else:

What #1054 set out to remove is *public, permanent, unavoidable* correlation —
a membership DID welded into a credential anyone can retain and republish. The
audit store is none of those. `AuditEnvelope` HMACs the actor under a rotating
key, with the hash covered by the tamper-evidence chain; it keeps the plaintext
in a field deliberately excluded from that chain digest so RTBF can null it
without breaking verification; and the surface is admin-gated. It is the store
purpose-built to hold privileged records.

Giving it up would also buy little. `VrcPublishedData` carries `vrc_id`,
`vrc_id` resolves to the row, and the row holds the relationship DIDs — so any
trail that both references the edge and names the member creates the mapping
transitively. There is no variant that attributes without linking.

And moderation needs the reverse lookup. "This edge is abusive, who made it?"
is the question an operator actually has; attributing to a hash alone answers
only the forward one.

The residual is real and stated in the code and the design note: an operator
with audit access can map every pairwise edge to its member. That is the cost,
it is accepted, and it is why the linkage stops at the audit store — the
`info!` on the publish path still carries the relationship DID and not the
member, because logs have neither the redaction machinery nor the access
controls that make this trade defensible.

The decision is not VRC-specific. It answers "when a member acts under a
pairwise identifier, what does the audit trail record?", and should hold for
every pairwise-capable operation added later.

Refs #1054

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: Add the delegation credential (VDC) to the catalog
body:
## Summary

`DTGCredentialType` carries six live subtypes — Membership, Relationship,
Invitation, Persona, Endorsement, Witness — and correctly deprecates `RCard`
per Working Draft 01. It has no `Delegation`.

DTG Credentials defines the VDC as a DTG **edge** credential, so nothing
downstream can be conformant until the catalog carries it.

## Detail

Required shape per the specification:

- `type` MUST include `"DelegationCredential"`
- `issuer`: the delegator — an R-DID or M-DID for a person, device or agent; a
  C-DID where a community delegates to a VTA or other service; a P-DID where
  the delegation is made under a persona
- `validUntil`: **REQUIRED**, unlike the base structure — "an appointment with
  no expiry cannot be reasoned about by a verifier that cannot reach the
  delegator"
- `credentialStatus`: **REQUIRED** — revocation is how a delegator withdraws an
  appointment already made, so it must be checkable without contacting them
- `credentialSubject.id`: the delegate
- `credentialSubject.delegation.scope`: array, MUST contain at least one entry.
  "A VDC MUST NOT express an unbounded appointment by omitting or emptying
  `scope`."

Two of those are unusual enough to be worth encoding in the constructor rather
than left to callers: `validUntil` and `credentialStatus` are optional on every
other type and mandatory here, and an empty `scope` is a specification
violation rather than a permissive default. A `new_vdc` that takes them as
non-optional parameters, and rejects an empty scope, makes the invariant
unforgeable by construction.

## Why it matters beyond adding a variant

The specification is explicit that the VDC differs **in kind**, not only in
payload: the other types *attest* that something is true about the graph, while
a VDC establishes *representation*. Verifying one requires scope containment,
chain resolution, invocation binding and timely revocation — none of which the
other types need.

That is worth flagging here because a catalog variant is necessary but nowhere
near sufficient: a consumer that treats a `DelegationCredential` like any other
DTG credential will accept a party as standing in for another without having
bounded what it may then do. The catalog should make the credential
constructible; it cannot make it safely verifiable on its own.

## Sequencing

The VDC arrived in the specification recently (`d7130a6`), and
trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#19 is the open draft adding it. Worth landing the
catalog variant behind that settling rather than ahead of it.

## Smaller, unrelated

`DTGCredentialType` derives no `PartialEq`, so consumers assert by pattern
(`matches!`) in tests rather than by equality. Trivial to add and it improves
every downstream test — happy to send that as a separate PR whenever.

Found in a conformance audit of the VTI stack against DTG Credentials
(OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1054). Finding **F6**.

title: Witness credentials are reasoned about but never built or verified
body:
## Summary

The ceremony engine treats `WitnessCredential` as a policy fact — with
trusted-issuer, validity and holder-binding predicates — but no VWC is ever
constructed or verified anywhere in the stack. `DTGCredential::new_vwc` and
`digest_multibase` are never called.

## Detail

`WitnessCredential` occurs in `ceremony/verify.rs`, `ceremony/facts.rs`,
`ceremony/evaluate.rs`, `routes/ceremonies.rs` and `policy/default.rs` — in
every case as a `credential_type` string in a fact the policy reasons over, not
as a credential the code builds or checks.

The exacting part is therefore entirely untested here. Per DTG Credentials the
VWC's `credentialSubject.digest` MUST be:

- the SHA-256 hash of the witnessed VRC,
- canonicalised with JCS (RFC 8785),
- encoded as a Multibase-encoded Multihash,
- `sha2-256` (header `0x12`, length `0x20`), base58btc (`z` prefix).

And Security Considerations 4 requires a verifier relying on that binding to
have the referenced VRC in hand, recompute the hash, and compare **decoded
digest bytes rather than encoded strings**.

`dtg-credentials` implements all of this correctly (`DTGCredential::digest`,
`digest_multibase`), including the recent multibase change. Nothing calls it.

## Why it matters

A ceremony can currently reach a decision on the *assertion* that a witness
credential was present, without any code path that could have established it
was valid or that it witnessed the edge in question. Security Considerations 4
is explicit that without recomputing the digest against the referenced VRC, a
VWC "should not be treated as evidence of which edge was witnessed".

## Suggested fix

1. Build VWCs through `new_vwc` on whatever path is meant to issue them.
2. On receipt, recompute the digest against the referenced VRC and compare
   decoded bytes.
3. `taskContext` is REQUIRED on the VWC specifically — see #1065, which is a
   prerequisite rather than a parallel task.

Conformance audit finding **F8**.

title: Trust Task Context Binding is not implemented
body:
## Summary

`taskContext` does not appear anywhere in `vtc-service` or `vta-sdk` — zero
occurrences. DTG Credentials marks it REQUIRED for the VWC and defines Trust
Task Context Binding as the mechanism preventing a credential from escaping the
exchange that produced it.

## Detail

From the specification:

- §Trust Task Context Binding: "For credential types where this specification
  marks `taskContext` as REQUIRED (currently only the VWC), issuers MUST
  include it."
- Security Considerations 5, **context collapse**: "A credential presented
  outside the trust task exchange in which it was issued may be misinterpreted
  as evidence of a completed ceremony. The requirements of Trust Task Context
  Binding exist to prevent this class of attack and must be enforced by
  verifiers."

This stack has a full ceremony engine (`ceremony/{facts,verify,evaluate}.rs`)
that evaluates credentials as facts and decides on them — and no binding
between a credential and the exchange it came from.

## Why it matters

The named attack is exactly the one the ceremony pipeline is exposed to: a
credential that is cryptographically valid, correctly typed, and issued during
some *other* exchange, presented as evidence that *this* ceremony reached its
terminal state.

## Suggested fix

1. Carry `taskContext.threadId` through issuance for the credential types the
   specification requires it on.
2. Require it on receipt where required, and reject its absence rather than
   defaulting.
3. Make ceremony evidence assert the thread it belongs to, so a credential from
   another exchange cannot satisfy a fact in this one.

Worth scoping against the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols specification —
some of the surface may be settled there first, and
trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#11 tracks the normative dependency on that
unpublished model.

Conformance audit finding **F3**.

title: No removal notice reaches a member the VTC removes
body:
Surfaced while scoping the client half of OpenVTC/openvtc#240. The client has a
`Removed` membership state with no way to ever enter it, because the VTC never
tells a member they were removed.

## Problem

There is no outbound message on any removal path. `AppState::send_to_member`
(`vtc-service/src/server.rs:241`) is the single outbound funnel, and its only
caller is `vtc-service/src/credentials/delivery.rs:176`. Every delivery call site
is a credential push on an *approve* / *present* / *renew* path:

- `vtc-service/src/messaging.rs:1339`
- `vtc-service/src/join/orchestrate.rs:303`
- `vtc-service/src/ceremony/orchestrate.rs:112`
- `vtc-service/src/routes/join_requests/present.rs:269`
- `vtc-service/src/routes/join_requests/decide.rs:161`
- `vtc-service/src/routes/members/request_vmc.rs:89`

None is on a removal path.

What exists and is **not** a removal notice:

- `spec/vtc/members/removed/0.1` — an *admin query* listing tombstoned members
  (`vtc-service/src/routes/mod.rs:568` → `routes/members/read.rs:198-220`).
- `MEMBER_SELF_REMOVE_TYPE` / `MEMBER_SELF_REMOVE_RECEIPT_TYPE`
  (`vta-sdk/src/protocols/join_requests.rs:324,330`) — the member-initiated
  leave and its receipt, i.e. a reply to the member's own request.
- `spec/vtc/members/admin-remove/0.1` — admin-facing. `admin_remove`
  (`vtc-service/src/routes/members/remove.rs:127-149`) accepts an optional
  `reason` (capped 1024, `remove.rs:69`) and returns `RemoveResponse` **to the
  admin**. The reason never leaves the audit log.

The only thing a removed member can observe is a side effect: the revocation bit
on their VMC flips (`vtc-service/src/ceremony/execute.rs:468-492`, `flip_revocation`
at `:497`). They must discover their own removal by polling a status list, and
even then learn nothing about why.

## Why it matters

Removal is the most consequential thing a community can do to a member, and it
is the one decision delivered with the least information — currently zero. The
operator sees their access stop working. Any client-side "you were removed, here
is why" UI is unreachable until this exists: in OpenVTC,
`CommunityRecord::remove()` has no production caller at all, precisely because
nothing on the wire triggers it.

## Proposed change

Send the removed member a notice on both admin removal paths, carrying:

- a typed disposition/code,
- the operator `reason` already accepted at `remove.rs:69`,
- the decision timestamp,
- the deciding authority.

On that last point — `reject_pending` knows `admin.0.did` (`decide.rs:242`) and
writes it to audit as the actor, but it never reaches any wire response. Same
shape here.

## Related

The response document is unsigned (`proof: None` in
`trust-tasks-rs/src/document.rs:387-407`), and `issuer` is echoed from the
request's `recipient` field, which the *applicant* set. So a removal notice as
things stand would not be independently verifiable — a removed member could not
prove to a third party who removed them, when, or on what grounds. Worth deciding
whether a removal notice should carry a proof; it is the case where forwardable
evidence matters most.

## Acceptance

- Admin removal and purge each emit a notice to the affected member.
- The notice carries code, reason, decision timestamp and deciding authority.
- A member with no live socket receives it on reconnect (or can recover it from
  a poll).

title: feat(vtc): tell a member when the community removes them (#1060)
body:
feat(vtc): tell a member when the community removes them (#1060)

Removal was the most consequential thing a community does to a member and the
one it delivered with the least information — none. There was no outbound
message on any removal path. The only signal a removed member could observe was
a side effect: the revocation bit on their membership credential flipping. They
inferred their own removal from a status list and learned nothing about why.

`vtc/members/removal-notice/0.1` (published upstream as
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#256) now goes out from both admin paths,
carrying the deciding administrator, the moment the decision took effect, the
resolved disposition, and the operator's reason.

**Signed, because the recipient is not the audience.** Authcrypt already proves
the sender to the member. But this is the one member-facing message whose value
lies in showing it to somebody else — an appeal, a dispute, another community
weighing a rejected applicant. Forwarded, an unsigned notice is an assertion
anyone could have written. So it is a Trust Task document with a Data Integrity
proof, packed in the trust-task envelope — note `TRUST_TASK_ENVELOPE_TYPE`, not
the task URI, which is a mistake this workspace has made before and which a
conformant peer rejects silently.

**Thirty days, because there is no second route.** `resolve_auth_role` refuses
any DID without an ACL row and removal hard-deletes it, so a removed member
cannot authenticate at all: every authenticated route, including any poll that
might have served the notice, closes at the moment the removal lands. The act
this reports is the act that ends their ability to ask about it. `send_to_member`
already had a durable outbox, so this needed a deadline parameter rather than
new machinery — `send_to_member_by`, with the six existing callers keeping the
24h default.

A member offline beyond the window still never learns. No window fixes that; the
honest fix is a retrieval path not gated on an ACL row, which is a larger design
than this. Stated in the spec and in the constant's doc comment rather than left
for someone to discover.

**Never for a self-leave.** `remove_inner` serves both the admin path and the
DIDComm self-leave. A member who chose to leave already has their receipt, and
telling them they were "removed" is a different and worse thing to be told.

**Best-effort.** The notice never fails the removal. That has already happened
and is durable; refusing the operator's request because the notice could not be
*queued* would leave the member removed and the operator believing they were
not. Failures log loudly — and log "queued", not "sent", because a DIDComm `Ok`
means the mediator accepted the frame and nothing more (R1.1).

Seven tests. Four unit: payload shape, a blank reason omitted rather than sent
as an empty string, the two codes distinguishable, and the payload validated
against the *published* schema — the check that catches the implementation
drifting from the spec it claims to implement.

Three end-to-end over a real mediator, because only a peer holding the document
demonstrates the feature: an admin removal arrives signed with its reason and
deciding admin, a purge says it was a purge, and a self-leave sends nothing. Two
of them first failed on `no active removal policy`, which was the paths
differing exactly as specified — a purge deliberately skips the removal policy,
which is why that one passed before the fixture seeded any.

Closes #1053

title: Persist and surface decision evidence for rejected or removed community membership
body:
Surfaced by an external RAHP/DRARM assessment of the Cypress release
(sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#18, finding `OVTC-RAHP-03`). This issue
covers the **client half** only; the governance half (appeal, review,
restoration) belongs in VTC/VTI and is tracked separately.

## Problem

When a VTC rejects a join request or removes an active member, the decision
evidence reaches us on the wire and we throw it away.

VTC returns a typed reject code plus a reason
(`vtc-service/src/messaging.rs:974` in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure`). All
four inbound paths in `openvtc-core/src/messaging.rs` have that code and reason
in hand:

- `:308` — `status: "rejected"` on a join-status reply
- `:392` — `VerdictEffect::Deny`, which even logs `code` and `reason`
- `:473` — `FORBIDDEN` problem-report (invitation not accepted)
- `:564` — join-denial `trust-task-error`, which logs `code` and `detail`

Each one then calls `record.reject()`, and
`CommunityRecord::reject()` / `remove()` take **no arguments**
(`openvtc-core/src/config/account.rs:441-454`). They set a status and clear
`acknowledged`. Nothing else is persisted.

The net effect for the operator: a community flips to `Rejected` or `Removed`,
the actions-required badge lights up, they press a key to acknowledge it — and
the *why* exists only in a `tracing` line they will never see. There is no
record of who decided, on what basis, or when. Acknowledging an outcome you
cannot inspect is not meaningful acknowledgement.

`Expired` has the same shape but is client-generated, so it is less severe —
still worth carrying the timeout basis for consistency.

## Proposed change

1. Give `reject()` and `remove()` a decision-evidence argument and persist it on
   `CommunityRecord`:
   - deciding authority (the VTC DID that sent the decision)
   - decision code (typed) and human-readable reason
   - decision timestamp (theirs if present, ours as received otherwise)
   - the inbound path it arrived on, so the evidence is reconstructable
2. Surface it wherever the terminal state is shown — the communities list detail
   view and the actions-required notice — not only in the acknowledge prompt.
3. Keep it stable across the config round-trip (serde) so history survives a
   restart; inactive records are already retained for re-join
   (`docs/design/multi-community-support.md` R-S-1), and the evidence should be
   retained with them.
4. Where no reason is supplied by the VTC, say so explicitly ("no reason given")
   rather than rendering an empty field — absence of a reason is itself
   information the operator should see.

## Out of scope

Appeal/review endpoints, policy-version context, and correction/restoration
semantics after an overturned decision. Those need the governing layer to define
them first; this issue makes OpenVTC ready to surface them.

## Acceptance

- A rejected join and a removal each persist and display authority, code, reason
  and timestamp.
- A decision arriving with no reason renders explicitly as such.
- Round-trip test: evidence survives save/load.
- No decision evidence is lost between the four inbound paths — a test per path.

title: Join status poll strips the rejection code and reason
body:
Surfaced while scoping the client half of OpenVTC/openvtc#240 (persist and
surface decision evidence for a rejected join). The VTC has the evidence and
drops it on the poll path.

## Problem

`project_status` projects `needs` / `presentationDefinition` **only** for
`Deferred`. A `Rejected` request is projected as bare
`{requestId, status: "rejected"}` — no code, no reason.

`vtc-service/src/routes/join_requests/status.rs:131-155`

The evidence exists. Both rejection paths store it:

- **Auto-deny at submit** — `vtc-service/src/join/orchestrate.rs:391-394` sets
  `status = Rejected` *and* `policy_decision = Some(verdict)`, where the verdict
  is a typed `ceremony::verdict::Deny { code, reason }`.
- **Admin reject** — `vtc-service/src/routes/join_requests/decide.rs:225-267`
  takes an operator `reason` (capped 1024, `decide.rs:35`) and writes it to
  `AuditEvent::JoinRequestRejected`.

So on the auto-deny path the reason is already persisted on the row and simply
isn't projected; on the admin path it reaches only the audit log.

## Why it matters

The correlated `VerdictResponse` (`vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:272-282`)
is the *only* place a `{code, reason}` ever reaches an applicant. That makes the
reason a one-shot delivery: if the applicant's socket was down, the reply was
missed, or the rejection came from an admin after the fact, the reason is
unrecoverable. The poll is the natural recovery path and it is the one path that
deliberately strips it.

Concretely, an admin-rejected applicant **can never learn why** — `reject_pending`
emits no message to them (§ separate issue for removal), and the poll returns
`status` alone.

## Proposed change

Project the decision onto the status response for `Rejected`, the same way
`needs`/`presentationDefinition` are projected for `Deferred`:

- `code` and `reason` from the stored `policy_decision` on the auto-deny path.
- The operator `reason` on the admin path (with a stable code — `admin-reject`
  or similar — since there is no policy verdict to source one from; cf. the
  `policy_decision: None` comment at `vti-common/src/audit/event.rs:806-816`).
- A decision timestamp. `issuedAt` on the response document is the time the
  *document* was produced, not the time the decision was made — for an admin
  reject those diverge arbitrarily.

This needs a field on `JoinRequestStatusResponseBody`
(`vta-sdk/src/protocols/join_requests.rs:178-189`), which is additive and
`skip_serializing_if`-able, so it should not be a breaking change.

## Note on the deny constructor

`VerdictResponse` has `allow` (`join_requests.rs:282`) and `refer` (`:304`)
constructors but no `deny` — the deny is hand-assembled in
`trust_tasks/mod.rs:272-282`. Worth adding one alongside this so the two
producers cannot drift.

## Acceptance

- A poll of an auto-denied request returns the policy code and reason.
- A poll of an admin-rejected request returns the operator's reason.
- A decision timestamp distinct from the document's `issuedAt`.
- Round-trip test per path.

title: fix(vtc)!: tell a rejected applicant why, on the one path built to recover it (#1058)
body:
fix(vtc)!: tell a rejected applicant why, on the one path built to recover it (#1058)

`project_status` projected `needs` / `presentationDefinition` for a
`Deferred` request and bare `{requestId, status}` for a `Rejected` one.
The evidence existed on both rejection paths and neither reached the
applicant through the poll.

The correlated `VerdictResponse` was the only place a `{code, reason}`
ever reached an applicant, which makes it a one-shot delivery: a socket
that was down, a reply that was lost, or a rejection an admin took hours
later, and the reason was unrecoverable. The poll is the natural recovery
path and it was the one path that deliberately stripped it. An
admin-rejected applicant could never learn why at all — `reject_pending`
emits no message to them, and the operator's reason reached only the
audit log, which no applicant can read.

Both paths now write one `JoinRequest::decision` field — code, optional
reason, and the decision's own timestamp — and the poll projects it. One
field rather than two, because the whole failure was two producers of the
same fact drifting apart. It is deliberately *not* `policy_decision`: an
operator's decision is not a policy verdict, and recording it as one
would make the audit trail lie about where the refusal came from. The
admin path carries `ADMIN_REJECT_CODE` ("admin-reject"), which is what
lets a client tell "the rules refused you, satisfy them and re-apply"
from "a human refused you, re-applying changes nothing".

`decidedAt` is separate from the response document's `issuedAt` because
`issuedAt` is when *this document* was produced. For an admin reject the
two diverge by however long the applicant takes to poll. The test proves
the distinction the only way it can be proved: poll twice, and `issuedAt`
moves while `decidedAt` names the same moment.

Rows rejected before this existed are not abandoned. An auto-deny always
wrote the serialized `Deny` verdict, so `decision_for_applicant` falls
back to it — recovering the code and reason, and reporting `decided_at:
None` rather than back-filling a timestamp that would tell the applicant
they were rejected the instant they polled. A legacy *admin* reject has
nothing to recover and answers exactly as it did before.

Also adds `VerdictResponse::deny`, which the issue asked for alongside:
the deny shape had `allow` and `refer` constructors but was hand-assembled
at its one call site, and this change gave it a second producer.

BREAKING CHANGE: `JoinRequestStatusResponseBody` gains three public
fields, so an exhaustive struct literal outside `vta-sdk` no longer
compiles (`constructible_struct_adds_field`, confirmed by
cargo-semver-checks). The wire form is additive — every field is
`skip_serializing_if`-able and defaulted — so deserializing clients are
unaffected. `#[non_exhaustive]` is not the fix here: `vtc-service`
produces this body from another crate and would lose the ability to
construct it at all.

Closes #1052

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: spec(vtc): tell a member when a community removes them
body:
Adds `vtc/members/removal-notice/0.1`. Step 1 of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1053 — the implementation cannot land first, since the VTC's URI census requires every `trusttasks.org/spec/…` constant in its source to resolve in the published registry.

## The gap

Removal is the most consequential thing a community does to a member and, so far, the one it delivers with the least information — **none**. There is no outbound message on any removal path. A removed member's only observable signal is a side effect: the revocation bit on their membership credential flips. They infer their own removal from a status list, and learn nothing about why.

The notice says who removed them, when the decision took effect, and the reason given.

## Deliberately not a receipt

`vtc/members/self-remove-receipt` is the adjacent task and the contrast drives the design. A receipt answers a request the member made, correlated to it, and the member is already waiting. **This answers nothing** — the member did not ask, is not waiting, and may well be offline.

That asymmetry is why `decidedBy` and `reason` are carried here and not there. A departing member already knows why they left.

## `proof` is REQUIRED, not RECOMMENDED

This is the one member-facing message whose value depends on being shown to somebody else: an appeal, a dispute, another community assessing a rejected applicant.

Authenticated transport establishes the sender **to the recipient** and stops there. A member forwarding an unsigned notice forwards an assertion anyone could have written — so an unsigned notice evidences nothing at exactly the moment it is needed.

## `decidedBy` names a person

More disclosure than a community strictly has to make, and communities where removal is contentious may find it uncomfortable. It is required because the alternative — *"the community removed you"* — is unanswerable and unappealable. A member cannot contest a decision whose maker is unnamed.

## A delivery property, not a transport

This task has a problem no other member-facing task has: **the act it reports is the act that ends the member's ability to ask about it.** Removal withdraws access, so a consumer cannot fall back on polling — the endpoint that would answer is the endpoint that now refuses them. (Verified concretely in the reference implementation: `resolve_auth_role` returns `Forbidden("DID not in ACL")`, and removal hard-deletes the ACL row.)

So the spec states the property a transport must have rather than naming one: durable retrying delivery over a window measured in weeks, on a channel that survives the removal. A conforming notice that cannot arrive is not a conforming implementation.

It also notes the uncomfortable half honestly: nothing here can compel a community to send. What the spec can do is make the notice verifiable when it *is* sent, so its presence is meaningful and its absence is a visible choice rather than a technical limitation.

## Shape

`## Request` with no `## Response` — the fire-and-forget form from CONTRIBUTING-SPECS, and the payload schema carries no `$defs.Response`.

Worth noting this is also what earns the two examples their generated round-trip tests. Under an `## Examples` heading the codegen does not harvest them (`extract_examples` scans `## Request` / `## Response` only), which is why the adjacent `self-remove-receipt` spec has none. Framing it correctly took the suite 450 → 452.

## Verification

- `npm run build` — 344 specs validated, 533 example documents (both new ones included, now that #255 validates framework 0.4)
- `npm run check-bindings` — 344 specs against 344 TS and 339 Rust modules, all agree
- `cargo test --workspace` — 33 suites, 0 failed

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.3 → 0.11.4, `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.3 → 0.12.4 (additive, patch).

*Unrelated and left alone: `npm install` wants to sync `package-lock.json`'s `engines.node` from `>=20` to `>=24` to match `package.json`. Real but not mine — excluded to keep this diff to the spec.*

title: build: validate example documents against every framework version on disk
body:
Fixes #254.

`checkExampleDocuments()` compiled envelope validators from a hard-coded
`['0.1', '0.2', '0.3']`. A spec declaring `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`
resolved to no validator, and its example documents were skipped by a silent
`continue` — indistinguishable in the build output from a clean pass.

## What changed

Both of the hardenings the issue proposed, because they close different things:

1. **Derive the version list from disk** (`specs/_framework/*/trust-task.schema.json`)
   rather than hand-listing it. A new framework version is covered the moment its
   envelope schema lands. This is what stops the recurrence at 0.5.
2. **`warn()` when a document's target resolves to no validator**, counted per
   target. Deriving the list closes this instance; the warning is what would have
   *caught* it, and it still catches the next way a target can name a version with
   no schema — a typo in front matter, or a schema not yet written.

## Verification

On `100471d` (the commit the issue reports against):

```
before:   validated 476 example documents against the framework envelope schema
after:    validated 531 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

The build **passes** with the check enabled — no `fails the framework 0.4
envelope schema` errors, no unvalidated-target warnings, and the only remaining
warnings are the pre-existing `$defs.Response` ones. Every document that was
being skipped happens to be valid, which is exactly what makes turning this on
cheap now and expensive once 0.5 has a backlog behind it.

The warning path was exercised directly by pointing `trust-task-control/0.1` at a
nonexistent `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.9"`:

```
  warn: 3 example document(s) target framework 0.9, for which no envelope schema
  compiled — add specs/_framework/0.9/trust-task.schema.json, or correct the
  targetFrameworkVersion that names it. These documents were NOT validated
  validated 498 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

531 → 498 with the 3 documents named rather than silently dropped. Working tree
restored afterwards; that edit is not in this branch.

## One correction to the issue's numbers

The issue says 22 specs / 55 documents. On `main` today it is **16 specs** — the
55-document delta includes the six unmerged `vta/app-state` specs from #252/#253.
The 476 → 531 figure reproduces exactly either way, since those specs are what the
issue author had in tree when measuring.

## Scope

Build script only — no spec, schema, or generated-library changes, so no binding
regeneration or version bumps are implicated. Nothing else hard-codes the framework
version list (`build-ts-bindings.mjs` references `_framework` only in comments and
path conventions).

title: checkExampleDocuments() silently skips every framework-0.4 example (55 documents unvalidated)
body:
`checkExampleDocuments()` in `scripts/build-registry.mjs` compiles envelope validators for framework `0.1`–`0.3` only. A spec declaring `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"` therefore resolves to **no validator**, and its example documents are skipped without a warning.

## Where

`scripts/build-registry.mjs:558`

```js
for (const version of ['0.1', '0.2', '0.3']) {
```

The skip itself is a silent `continue` further down:

```js
const target = targetByTypePrefix.get(bare) ?? '0.2';
const validate = validators.get(target);
if (!validate) continue;          // <- 0.4 lands here, no warning
```

`specs/_framework/0.4/trust-task.schema.json` exists, so there is a schema to compile — the version is simply absent from the list.

## Scale

**22 specs** currently declare `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.4"`, contributing **55 example documents** that are never checked.

## Reproduction

On `100471d` (current `main`):

```
$ npm run build
  validated 476 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

Add `'0.4'` to the list on line 558 and re-run:

```
$ npm run build
  validated 531 example documents against the framework envelope schema
```

476 → 531. The 55-document delta is the gap.

## The fix appears safe to land as-is

With `'0.4'` added the build still **passes** — no `fails the framework 0.4 envelope schema` errors, and no new warnings beyond the pre-existing `$defs.Response` ones. So every currently-unvalidated document happens to be valid, and enabling the check does not require fixing a backlog first.

That is worth stating because it is the thing that makes this cheap now and expensive later: the longer 0.4 stays unchecked, the more likely it is that turning it on surfaces a real failure in someone else's spec, and then the fix and the cleanup arrive together.

## Why it matters beyond the count

The function's own docstring makes the case:

> an example document is the thing implementers copy: a wrong one is a bug that propagates, and nothing checked them before.

That reasoning applies to 0.4 examples exactly as much as to 0.1–0.3 — and 0.4 is where new specs are being written, so the unvalidated set is the *growing* one.

## Suggested hardening

Beyond adding `'0.4'`, the failure mode is worth closing permanently: the list is hand-maintained and will drift again at 0.5. Two options —

1. Derive the versions from `specs/_framework/*/trust-task.schema.json` on disk rather than hard-coding them, so a new framework version is covered the moment its envelope schema lands.
2. Failing that, `warn()` when a document's target resolves to no validator, so the skip is at least visible. Today it is indistinguishable from "validated fine".

Option 1 is what stops this recurring; option 2 is what would have caught it.

## Context

Found while adding `vta/app-state/*` (#252, #253), which targets 0.4 — I validated those six specs' documents out of band against `_framework/0.4/trust-task.schema.json` (56 documents, 30 payloads, 0 failures) precisely because the build would not. Filing rather than fixing inline, since turning the check on newly validates 16 other specs and that is not mine to land inside an unrelated spec PR.
