title: chore(deps)!: move to trust-tasks-rs 0.11, and fix the wire drift it exposed
body:
Started as "did the sibling release fix the duplicate `trust-tasks-rs`?" — yes.
But the upgrade turns on schema validation for 22 tasks that previously had
none, and **three of them were sending non-conforming payloads**.

## The graph

`trust-tasks-https` / `-didcomm` / `-proof` / `-tsp` / `-capability-client` /
`-didcomm-v1` now all require `^0.11`, and `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.19.9 /
`-mediator` 0.18.20 followed. Until every one agreed, bumping the direct
dependency put **two** `trust-tasks-rs` nodes in the graph and the types crossed:

```
error[E0308]: expected `MediatorAcl`, found a different `MediatorAcl`
note: there are multiple different versions of crate `trust_tasks_rs`
```

Refreshing the lock to the versions that agree collapses it to one node.

## Three live defects, all the same class as #919

They were shipping before this PR. Nothing failed only because neither end had a
schema to check against.

1. **`CreateDidWebvhRequest` serialized snake_case.** Canonical wire is camelCase
   (R3.1) and the schema is `additionalProperties: false`. It worked solely
   through `CreateDidWebvhBody`'s back-compat aliases — which is exactly what made
   it invisible.
2. **`update_context` sent `null`** for unset members, where the schema types them
   as optional *strings*. Now built from `UpdateContextBody`, which skips `None`.
3. **`WebvhPathMode` emitted `auto_assign`** where the schema pins `autoAssign`
   with a `const` per `oneOf` branch.

**Number 3 is the one worth your attention.** The drift was in a *discriminant
value*, not a member name — so it slipped past every review and every convention
that watches member casing. And it was only reachable after fixing #1: the payload
had to get past the field-name check before the value check could fail. One drift
was hiding another.

Aliases keep the retired spellings accepted, so a peer built against the old shape
still parses; only what we **emit** moves. A round-trip test pins both directions,
and the REST test that posts the old spelling is annotated as the back-compat
coverage it now is — please don't let anyone "modernise" it.

## Four census guards, all shrinking

Every debt list in the workspace fired, each in the good direction:

| Guard | Change |
|---|---|
| manifest debt (`UNPUBLISHED_CANONICAL_OK`) | 36 → 14 |
| conformance witnesses | +22, each schema-validated with the mandatory non-vacuity check |
| `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` | −22 |
| producer-payload `UNPUBLISHED` | −2 |

I **de-rotted one test rather than re-pinning it**. `an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default`
hard-coded `webvh/dids/create` as its unspecced example — which this PR publishes,
so it failed for the best possible reason. It now derives one from the debt list at
runtime, so it follows the debt down instead of breaking every time a spec lands,
and returns early with a note to delete itself when the list empties.

## Follow-up I'd propose rather than bolt on

The 22 new witnesses use hand-written `json!`, which proves *the schema accepts a
shape*. Where a typed body exists (`CreateDidWebvhBody`, `UpdateContextBody`, …),
`to_v(typed)` is strictly stronger — it asserts **our types** conform, which is
what caught all three defects here. That's a second audit pass and will likely
surface more drift, so it deserves its own PR.

## BREAKING CHANGE

`WebvhPathMode` serializes as `wellKnown` / `autoAssign` instead of `well_known` /
`auto_assign`. Deserialization accepts both, so this breaks only a consumer that
string-matches on what we emit. Title carries `!`; expect the advisory semver job
to report it.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- [x] `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- [x] `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` — **4514 passed, 0 failed** across 145 binaries
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: fix(sdk/service): take trust-tasks-rs 0.11, and fix the four defects it exposes
body:
## What this is

Moving to `trust-tasks-rs 0.11` brings the `vta/contexts/*` and `vta/webvh/*`
schemas into `schema_index`. **Everything else in this PR follows from that one
fact** — four separate guards refuse to let a task be dispatched against a
schema the registry now serves without being checked against it.

It also unblocks the `vta/services/*` handlers, which is what I set out to do;
those are a follow-up PR.

## Four real defects, none previously reachable by any test

Client-side `validate_payload` only runs for tasks whose schema resolves. Under
0.9 these four resolved to nothing, so the payloads went out unchecked. Each
would have been rejected by a conforming agent as `malformedRequest`:

| Defect | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `create_did_webvh` sent `context_id`, `server_id`, `pre_rotation_count`, … | schema names `contextId` and forbids additional properties — **every** create over a task transport was malformed |
| `update_context` omitted `contextPolicy` entirely | a caller setting a policy had it silently accepted and never sent; **it failed by doing nothing** |
| `update_context` emitted `null` for unset members | bypassed `skip_serializing_if` via a hand-written `json!`; same shape as #919 |
| `WebvhPathMode` emitted `{"mode":"auto_assign"}` | schema's `oneOf` spells `autoAssign` |

The last one is worth separating from an ordinary casing slip: it's a
**discriminator value**. A `oneOf` keyed on `mode` matches *no branch*, so the
whole payload is malformed rather than oddly-spelled. It now emits camelCase
and accepts the old spelling via `alias`; its unit test was pinning the wrong
wire and now pins the right one plus the intake path.

Both `update_context` and `create_did_webvh` now build from their typed request
structs, so the wire comes from the same declaration the schema is generated
against and can't drift by hand again.

## 22 conformance witnesses

These families were dispatched against unpublished URIs, so the sweep skipped
them and they sat in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`. They move out of that list and
into the witness table — which is what the list is *for*: it shrinks
monotonically as specs land.

**Written as raw JSON, not through the producer types, deliberately.** Two of
those producer types were wrong when the schemas arrived, so a witness built
from them would have encoded the defect and passed green. The schema is the
authority here, not the code that feeds it.

## The debt lists shrink

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| vtc-service unpublished bound URIs | 36 | **14** |
| `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` (contexts/webvh) | 22 | **0** |
| `producer_payload_conformance` UNPUBLISHED | 4 | **2** |

36 → 14 is the largest single fall that manifest count has taken. Its comment
already carried the history of the number moving, including a URI that went up
and back down in a day with the note *"That is the whole mechanism working, not
an exception to it."* I extended it rather than just editing the digit.

`an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default` needed a new fixture for the same
reason: it named `webvh/dids/create` as its example of an unspecced task, and
that task is now validatable, so its fail-closed half had stopped proving
anything.

## One witness I got wrong, caught by the round-trip check

I wrote `aclEntriesRemoved` / `aclEntriesUpdated` as counts. They're arrays of
ids. `every_witnessed_task_round_trips_through_its_generated_types` caught it —
exactly the hand-written-witness error class it exists for.

## Dependency chain behind this

This needed four upstream releases, each blocked on the last:
affinidi-tdk-rs#717 (`affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.9`, so `acl_setup`'s
`MediatorAcl` stops being a duplicated type) → trust-tasks #250 (the six
sibling crates, whose manifests required 0.11 while crates.io still served
tarballs built on 0.9).

## Test

```
cargo test --workspace --features session,tsp   4523 passing, 0 failures
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   clean
```

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **New/changed wire types: camelCase, schema registered, all consumers
      updated (R3.\*)** — the substance of this PR; four wire defects corrected
      against their published schemas, with `alias` on the discriminator so a
      producer mid-migration still parses
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

body:
fix(sdk/service): take trust-tasks-rs 0.11, and fix the four defects it exposes (#1015)

* build(deps): move to trust-tasks-rs 0.11 and affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.19.9

trust-tasks-rs 0.11 carries the vta/services/* families this branch implements.
The move needed affinidi-messaging-sdk to go first — acl_setup hands a
MediatorAcl to TrustTasks::account_update, so two semver-incompatible copies of
trust-tasks-rs made that a type error rather than a link. That landed as
affinidi-tdk-rs#717 and published as 0.19.9.

vta-sdk builds clean on this. The workspace does NOT yet: vtc-service still
hits a duplicated TrustTask<Value> because the trust-tasks sibling crates
(trust-tasks-didcomm, -https, -proof, -tsp, -capability-client, -didcomm-v1)
changed their requirement to 0.11 without moving their own versions, so
crates.io still serves tarballs built against 0.9. dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf's
release/siblings-on-0.11 fixes that; this branch waits on it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(sdk): two payload defects the 0.11 schema index made visible

Taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 brings the vta/contexts and vta/webvh schemas into
`schema_index`, which turns on client-side validate_payload for tasks that had
no resolvable schema under 0.9. Two real defects surfaced immediately — both
would have been rejected by a conforming agent as malformedRequest, and neither
was reachable by any test before now.

**create_did_webvh sent snake_case.** `CreateDidWebvhRequest` predates the
schema published in trust-tasks #240 and carried `context_id`, `server_id`,
`pre_rotation_count`, `add_mediator_service`, `set_primary`. The schema names
`contextId` and friends and forbids additional properties, so every create over
a task transport was malformed:

    Additional properties are not allowed ('add_mediator_service', 'context_id',
    'pre_rotation_count', 'server_id', 'set_primary' were unexpected);
    "contextId" is a required property

**update_context dropped the policy and sent nulls.** Its payload was a
hand-written `json!` naming four members. It omitted `contextPolicy` entirely,
so a caller setting a policy had it silently accepted and never sent — the
worse of the two bugs, because it fails by doing nothing. And it read
`req.name`/`req.did`/`req.description` directly, bypassing their
`skip_serializing_if` and emitting `null` for each unset one, which the agent
refuses: an absent optional must be ABSENT, not null. That is the same shape as
#919.

Both now build from the typed request struct, so the wire comes from the same
declaration the schema is generated against and cannot drift from it by hand.

client_rest 86 passing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(service): witness the 22 families 0.11 made checkable, and the defects they found

Taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 brings the `vta/contexts/*` and `vta/webvh/*`
schemas into `schema_index`. Everything here follows from that one fact, and
none of it is optional: four separate guards refuse to let a task be dispatched
against a schema the registry now serves without being checked against it.

**22 conformance witnesses.** These families were dispatched against
unpublished URIs, so `schema_for` could not resolve them and the sweep skipped
them entirely — they sat in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` instead. They now move
out of that debt list and into the witness table, which is what the list is
for: it shrinks monotonically as specs land.

The witnesses are written as raw JSON rather than through the producer types,
deliberately. Two of those producer types were WRONG when the schemas arrived,
so a witness built from them would have encoded the defect and passed green.
The schema is the authority here, not the code that feeds it.

**Two more producer defects, on top of the two already fixed.**

`WebvhPathMode` emitted `{"mode":"auto_assign"}` where the schema's `oneOf`
spells `autoAssign`. Worth separating from an ordinary casing slip: this is a
discriminator VALUE, and a `oneOf` keyed on `mode` matches no branch at all, so
the whole payload is malformed rather than oddly-spelled. It now emits
camelCase and accepts the old spelling on intake, and its unit test — which was
pinning the wrong wire — pins the new one and covers the alias.

The `preview-delete` witness first claimed `aclEntriesRemoved` and
`aclEntriesUpdated` were counts. They are arrays of ids. The round-trip check
caught it, which is exactly the class of hand-written-witness error it exists
for.

**The debt lists shrink.** 22 URIs off `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`, two off
`producer_payload_conformance`'s UNPUBLISHED census, and vtc-service's
unpublished-URI count falls 36 → 14 — the largest single fall that number has
taken. `an_unspecced_task_proceeds_by_default` needed a new fixture for the
same reason: it named `webvh/dids/create` as its example of an unspecced task,
and that task is now validatable, so the fail-closed half of it had stopped
proving anything.

Workspace: 4523 passing, clippy clean with --all-targets.
Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: retrigger the PR-title check after retitling

`commit lint` reads `github.event.pull_request.title`, but this workflow's
`on: pull_request` has no `types:`, so it defaults to opened/synchronize/
reopened — an edit does not retrigger it. Re-running the job does not help
either: a rerun replays the original event payload, so it would still read the
old title. Only a push produces a fresh payload.

The title was `fix(sdk,service): ...`; the scope charset is [a-z0-9._/-], so
the comma was rejected. It is now `fix(sdk/service): ...`.

Empty on purpose, and it disappears on squash-merge — which is the merge mode
this check exists to serve, since the PR title becomes the squash subject.

body:
release: publish the six siblings that now require trust-tasks-rs 0.11 (#250)

#245 and #246 moved the sibling crates' `trust-tasks-rs` requirement to 0.11
without moving their own versions. `cargo publish` skips a version already on
crates.io, so none of them republished: main requires 0.11 while the registry
still serves tarballs built against 0.9.

That is not cosmetic. A consumer taking trust-tasks-rs 0.11 together with any of
these crates gets two semver-incompatible copies of the same types, and the
build fails on a duplicated `TrustTask<Value>` — which is how this was found,
from vtc-service:

    error[E0308]: expected `TrustTask<Value>`, found a different `TrustTask<Value>`

Minor bumps: these crates carry `trust_tasks_rs` types in their public APIs, so
a semver-incompatible move of that dependency is breaking for their consumers.

  trust-tasks-didcomm            0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-https              0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-proof              0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-tsp                0.9.0 -> 0.10.0
  trust-tasks-capability-client  0.8.0 -> 0.9.0
  trust-tasks-didcomm-v1         0.8.0 -> 0.9.0

The guard added in #245 should have caught this and did not. It watched
`trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` only, so a change that alters what a crate publishes
without touching its source — which is exactly what a dependency-requirement
bump is — was invisible to it. It now checks every publishable workspace member
against any change under its directory, which is the shape the TDK's equivalent
guard has had all along.

Workspace builds clean.

title: spec(vta): specify retiring an orphaned webvh slot
body:
Specifies `vta/webvh/servers/retire-orphan/0.1` — the remedy for the one
divergence `vta/webvh/servers/reconcile` can name but nothing could repair.

## Why the gap exists

`reconcile` reports two divergences and repairs neither, deliberately, because
they want opposite remedies. The `agentOnly` side has one: retry the publish, or
delete the local record. The `hostOnly` side — an **orphan**, a slot the host
serves for an agent that has no record of it — has none, and the reason is
structural rather than incidental.

Every delete addresses a DID *through its local record*: the record is what says
which server to talk to and which keys to sign with. An orphan is defined by that
record's absence, so the lookup fails before a request ever leaves the agent. Nor
can the producer remove it directly — the agent holds the server credentials, not
the producer.

So a slot that both parties can see, and neither can remove, accumulates.

## The one property everything else rests on

**The agent decides whether the slot is orphaned. The producer does not get to
claim it.**

A conforming agent re-derives orphanhood at the moment of the request, by the
same comparison `reconcile` performs, and refuses if it holds any record for the
slot. A live DID has a record, and the record is what makes the refusal
automatic — so a producer cannot use this to remove a live DID by mislabelling
it.

That inversion is what makes an undo-less operation safe to expose at all.
Without it the task is "delete anything on the host, unaudited by the agent's own
state" wearing a narrower name. If you review one thing, review whether §
*The precondition is checked, not asserted* actually closes that.

## Three refusals, two of them uncertainty

`notOrphaned`, `listingUnavailable`, `didMismatch`. The middle one is worth
noting: an agent that *cannot* confirm orphanhood refuses rather than proceeding
on the producer's word. That is uncertainty, not contradiction — and the spec
argues the asymmetry explicitly, because the alternative to a false refusal is a
retry and the alternative to a false removal is nothing.

## It forbids automation, and says why

A conforming agent MUST NOT retire on a schedule or a sweep. The signal a sweeper
would act on is an **absence**, and absences are produced by bugs as readily as by
orphaning — a read that fails open, a record written under the wrong server id, a
migration half-applied. Each presents to a sweeper as an orphan, and the response
is to make a published identifier stop resolving, silently and irreversibly.

The population is finite anyway: agents holding an idempotency key across retries
stop producing the create-retried kind, and agents that confirm the remote leg
before dropping a local record stop producing the delete-failed kind. Automating
cleanup of a set that stops growing trades a permanent risk for a temporary
saving.

## `expectedDid`

The optimistic-concurrency guard. A reconcile response is a comparison at an
instant, and a slot may be published to between the report and the request.
Naming the DID the producer saw turns a stale report into a refusal rather than a
surprise. Optional, because a slot reserved but never published to has no DID and
is exactly as orphaned.

## Housekeeping

Per the bump-and-republish rule:

- Rust bindings regenerated (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`)
- TS bindings regenerated (`npm run build-ts-bindings`)
- `trust-tasks-rs` 0.11.0 → **0.11.1**, changelog entry added, `Cargo.lock` refreshed
- `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.12.0 → **0.12.1**

Additive on both sides — a new generated module, no existing type touched — so a
patch bump on each.

No new category, no reserved slug, no new binding, so none of the three
hand-maintained lists needs updating.

## Verification

- [x] `npm run build` — 337 specs validated
- [x] `npm run check-bindings` — 337 specs against 337 TS and 332 Rust modules, all agree
- [x] `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` — 426 + 5 + 7 + 16 + 3 passed
- [x] DCO signed

## Downstream

This unblocks the VTA-side implementation of the same operation
(`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1009`), which cannot bind the URI until
the registry serves it — a workspace guard there asserts exactly that.

title: docs: define who owns retry, and what a lost reply costs
body:
Fifth of six PRs closing #1009 (the count grew by one — see "What's left"). Docs
only, no code.

#1009 item 4 asked for a **defined retry owner per failure domain** so the
delivery layer, the SDK and application code cannot multiply attempts
independently. The mechanism landed in #1010–#1012; this writes the contract
down, which is the part that has to survive the next person to touch it.

## The rule

Three layers can independently decide to send a request again. Left
uncoordinated they multiply — three application attempts over three transport
attempts is nine executions of an operation the server dedups at neither.

| Layer | Retries? | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| Messaging delivery | yes — durable outbox + backoff | *delivery* of a message |
| `vta-sdk` client | yes — `VtaClient::idempotent` | *one logical operation* |
| Application code | **no** | nothing |

The point worth stating plainly, and the reason this is a rule rather than a
preference: **a hand-rolled application retry loop is worse than nothing.** It
re-invokes a client method, which builds a fresh document, so it cannot hold a
key stable — converting "one operation, retried" into "two operations", which is
the exact failure the key exists to prevent. The note carries the before/after.

## What else is recorded

Decisions a reader would otherwise have to reverse-engineer from the code:

- why `RetrySafe` is deliberately **not** called "idempotent" (half its members
  aren't — a second `auth/challenge` mints a second challenge; they're grouped
  because a repeat does no *harm*, which is the only question a retry layer asks)
- why some responses are never replayed, and what would break if they were
- why conflict is reported ahead of in-flight
- why a failed task releases its claim rather than recording it
- how the 24h retention window is sized, and why every keyed Trust Task uses
  `NonDestructive` even when it destroys something
- the two dedup layers (`replay.rs` vs `idempotency.rs`) and why both stay

## Two limits stated rather than left implicit

Both are judgement calls I'd rather have on the record than discovered later:

1. **The retry hint rides the rejection *document*, not an HTTP `Retry-After`
   header.** DIDComm and TSP drop HTTP status entirely, so a header serves one
   transport of three; the document is the transport-agnostic answer. Adding the
   header *as well* is a reasonable follow-up for HTTP intermediaries — it is not
   a correctness gap, and threading headers through `TrustTaskOutcome` for it
   would be disproportionate.

2. **No outbound client in this repo retries HTTP at all.** I checked
   `webvh_client` and the foreign-fetch path: single attempt, no loop. So DRARM
   `RLA-029` (Retry-After non-compliance) has **nothing to remediate here today**
   — which is worth saying explicitly rather than quietly closing the item. Rule 3
   in the note is what keeps it true for the next client that does retry.

## Placement

Indexed in `docs/README.md`, and the ownership rule is promoted into the
workspace `CLAUDE.md` beside R2.1 — the cross-service networking section is where
someone lands before adding a service call, so that is where the rule needs to be.

## What's left on #1009

Item 6, the reconciliation path for `did:webvh` entries already orphaned by a
retried auto-assign, is the last piece. It needs its own design pass (enumerate
against the host, decide what "orphan" means when the local record is the only
reference, and whether retirement is automatic or operator-confirmed), so it gets
its own PR rather than being appended here.

Refs #1009.

## Pre-merge

- [x] Docs only — no code, no `version =` edits, no changelog file
- [x] Factual claims verified against the source, not assumed (the "no outbound
      retry" claim in particular)

title: test(vta): prove the lost-reply contract by counting effects, not statuses
body:
Fourth of five PRs closing #1009. Tests only — no production code. Independent of
#1012 (these drive raw documents against the router, so they test the *wire
contract* #1011 established rather than the SDK's key-carrying, which #1012
unit-tests).

## Why this needs an integration test

#1011's unit tests cover the store's state machine. Nothing yet proved the
property the feature exists for: that a retry of a lost reply produces **one**
durable effect rather than two.

That property needs testing precisely because **its failure mode is silence**.
Asserting the retry returned `200` proves nothing — two successful creates also
return `200` twice. So every test here submits the same document twice and then
**counts what actually exists on the server**.

## The control is the most important test here

`no_key_still_creates_two`. Without it, every other assertion in this file would
still pass if idempotency silently did nothing and `keys/create` happened to be
naturally convergent. It also doubles as the backwards-compatibility guarantee:
an unkeyed resubmission still creates a second key, exactly as before.

If you review one thing, review whether that control actually holds the rest of
the file honest.

## Fresh envelope ids, deliberately

Every document carries a new `id`. That is what a real retry looks like, and it
is the reason the `(actor, envelope-id)` replay cache cannot catch this case. A
test that reused the envelope id would be exercising the *other* dedup layer and
passing for the wrong reason.

## The nine cases

| Test | Property |
|---|---|
| `no_key_still_creates_two` | control + backwards compatibility |
| `a_retry_under_the_same_key_converges_to_one_effect` | the contract — and asserts the **original `keyId`** comes back, not just a 200 |
| `distinct_keys_still_create_distinct_effects` | a key must not collapse genuinely separate work |
| `the_same_key_with_a_different_payload_is_refused` | and creates nothing |
| `the_same_key_on_a_different_task_is_refused` | a key is scoped to one operation |
| `one_callers_key_does_not_block_another` | per-principal scoping — no collision, no probing |
| `a_key_on_a_retry_safe_task_is_ignored_not_rejected` | reads cost no record |
| `an_unusable_key_falls_back_to_unkeyed_behaviour` | a blank key must not break a caller |
| `a_failed_task_does_not_hold_its_key` | the retry after a failure actually runs |

The last one is the one I'd most like a second opinion on: it induces failure via
a bad `contextId`, which fails inside the handler rather than at the schema gate,
so the claim is genuinely taken and then released. If there is a cleaner way to
provoke a post-claim failure in this harness, I'd rather use it.

Refs #1009.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all`
- [x] `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets` — clean (CI lints test targets since #1008)
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-service --test idempotency_trust_task` — 9 passed
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: site(bindings): list one card per binding, the latest version
body:
## What

`/bindings` counted and listed every published *version* rather than every binding: **7 cards for 5 bindings**, with `didcomm` and `didcomm-v1` each appearing twice. The hub now collapses to one card per slug — the latest version — reusing the existing `latestPerSlug()` helper that the registry and shared-schema hubs already use. The heading count derives from the same array, so it stays in sync on its own.

Shown after this change: `tsp/0.1`, `https/0.1`, `didcomm/0.2`, `didcomm-v1/0.2`, `push/0.1`.

## Two things that came with it

**A version switcher on the binding detail page.** The hub was the only navigation to `didcomm/0.1` and `didcomm-v1/0.1`; collapsing it without this would have left them reachable only by typing the URL. It mirrors the shared-schema page's switcher — `Versions · **v0.2** · v0.1`.

**Versionless `/binding/<slug>` now resolves to the latest.** Both resolutions used `find()`, which picks whichever entry is listed first — so `/binding/didcomm-v1` served **0.1**. Fixed in the route builder (`index.html`) and in `BindingSpecPage`, which is the path a direct page load actually takes. The strict-lookup behaviour for an unknown or missing slug is unchanged.

## Not changed

`website/assets/bindings.js` — every version stays registered, published and routable. `checkBindingRegistry()` still sees all seven on-disk bindings, so `npm run build` passes.

## Verified

`npm run build` clean; checked against a local `npm run serve` build in the browser — 5 cards, no console errors, `/binding/didcomm-v1` renders 0.2, and the switcher navigates to 0.1 correctly.

title: refactor(loop): lift action handling out of main_loop, and test it
body:
`main_loop` was ~1,600 lines, 900 of them a single `match` over `Action`, with no seam a test could reach.

That is why every fix in this release was verified by reading the code, by a live debug log, or by a unit test on some piece extracted from the loop — and why a change whose entire purpose was compile-time exhaustiveness (#236) still shipped broken across feature sets, because nothing exercised it.

## Why this is a lift and not a rewrite

The R14 sweep is what made it possible. The arms are now uniformly *resolve owned inputs → claim a domain → spawn → apply on the outcome*, so they need a fixed set of resources and no longer interleave network work with loop-local state.

`ActionCtx` is that set: eleven **borrowed** fields, no ownership moved. The single-mutator invariant is untouched — everything is still mutated from the loop thread, and a borrowed context cannot escape it.

Three arms stay in the loop because they are not about acting on state: `Exit` and `UXError` signal the terminator and break with the loop's own outcome type, and `StartJoin` drives the join flow's own action loop using the receiver this one selects on. They remain listed in the handler's match, so **#236's guarantee moves across intact**.

## Two things the move surfaced

* **`ping_sent_at` is loop state, not `State`.** A stopwatch for a manual trust-ping, read by the inbound arm. It becomes a context field rather than being smuggled into the UI model to make the move easier.
* **`Settings` can end the process** — a confirmed profile wipe — which a handler cannot do. So `handle_action` returns `Handled::{Continue, ExitUserInt}` and the loop honours it.

Five helpers that took `&self` and never touched it become free functions. That is what let the arms move at all, and it is worth noticing they were free functions wearing a method signature the whole time.

## The tests are the point

Nine, none of which could be written yesterday:

* opening the agent-name manager **dispatches** — the exact property #235's three silently-dropped surfaces violated;
* doing it with no persona selected explains itself instead of doing nothing;
* doing it with no VTA session says so;
* a second verb while one is in flight is refused **out loud**;
* a VIC refresh without a session does not leave the panel claiming a query is running, and with one it dispatches;
* navigation still routes through the shared reducer;
* an ordinary action reports `Continue`;
* a claimed domain really does have a job behind it — asserted by *receiving its outcome*, not by trusting the claim.

The harness needs no network: `TDK` builds offline (`with_load_environment(false)`, already proven by `join_flow`'s tests) and `VtaClient::new` is synchronous, so a client pointed at a dead address asserts the dispatch exactly as well as a live one.

## Scope

No behaviour change. `mod.rs` 4,380 → 3,630 lines; `runtime_actions.rs` is 1,036 including its tests.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` **and** `--no-default-features` — 333 + 334 + integration.

## Follow-ups this opens

* **Point the degraded loop at the same handler.** Divergence stops being something the compiler merely *checks* (#236) and becomes structurally impossible. This PR deliberately does not do it — the two loops still differ in what they can service, and collapsing that is a behavioural decision, not a move.
* **The inbound-DIDComm arm** (192 lines) is the next-largest and the one worth testing for message routing.

title: feat(sdk)!: hold one idempotency key across every attempt of an operation
body:
Third of five PRs closing #1009, and the one that makes the rest actually
engage. Independent of #1011 — SDK-only, branched from main — but inert until
#1011 lands, since nothing server-side reads the key yet.

## The problem this solves

#1011 makes the VTA dedup keyed Trust Tasks on an `idempotencyKey`. That only
helps if the **retry carries the same key as the attempt it is retrying**, and a
hand-rolled retry loop structurally cannot do that: it re-invokes a client method
that builds a fresh document each time.

Minting the key *inside* the client method has the identical failure the envelope
id already has — attempt two gets a new one, the VTA sees an unrelated request,
and the second durable effect happens anyway. This is exactly why OpenVTC's
`vta_retry` cannot be fixed in OpenVTC.

So the key has to be scoped **outside** the call.

```rust
let key = client.idempotent(|| client.create_key(req.clone())).await?;
```

`idempotent` mints one key, holds it in a task-local for the closure's duration,
and retries transient faults inside that scope. Every dispatch the closure makes
carries the same key; envelope ids still differ per attempt, which is the point.

A task-local rather than a parameter because it has to reach all twenty-odd typed
methods without changing twenty signatures, and because it is genuinely ambient —
it belongs to the operation, not the call. Same pattern as `WIRE_VERSION` in
`vta-service`.

## Where the key is attached

Only when the task is one a second execution would actually harm
(`retry_safety`). A read or a convergent mutation gets nothing — attaching a key
there costs the VTA a dedup record and buys nothing. Pinned by
`a_retry_safe_task_carries_no_key_even_in_scope`.

Top-level beside `id`, where the VTA reads it from `TrustTask::extra` and a
Data-Integrity proof covers it, so a relayer cannot rewrite it to split one
operation into two.

I pulled the document construction out of `dispatch_trust_task` into
`build_task_document` purely so this decision is testable without standing up a
transport.

## One retry owner (remediation item 4)

Retry layers compose badly. The messaging delivery layer already retries a
durable outbox with backoff underneath this, so an application loop on top
multiplies attempts against a server that dedups at neither.

`idempotent` is the application-layer owner: 3 attempts, exponential backoff, and
it honours the server's `retryAfter` **capped at 30s** — an unbounded wait on a
server-chosen value is a stall the server can trigger at will. A stale hint
(already in the past) retries promptly rather than treating it as a reason to
wait.

Callers should use this *instead of* their own loop, not around one. The OpenVTC
side of that migration is a follow-up in the other repo.

## BREAKING CHANGE — `VtaError::Unavailable`

Flagged by cargo-semver-checks (advisory `continue-on-error` job, so a 0.x break
is *known* rather than shipped as a patch). Title carries `!`.

Typed rather than folded into `Protocol(String)` because it is the one wire
rejection meaning **"ask again"** rather than "this failed" — #1011's idempotency
layer returns it while a first attempt on the same key is still running, and a
retry loop reading it as terminal gives up on exactly the answer it was told to
wait for.

Worth knowing *why* it needed a variant at all: `unavailable` maps to HTTP 503,
and `VtaError::Server` (already retryable) would have covered it — except the
REST leg parses the error document **before** the status (R3.7), so the code
collapsed to a string and the 503 never surfaced. The DIDComm leg drops status
entirely.

## Scope

No behaviour changes for existing callers. `idempotent` is opt-in; a call made
outside it builds a byte-identical document to today. Nothing in this repo calls
it yet.

Refs #1009.

      warnings under `--features client` are pre-existing on main; verified by
      stashing)
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-sdk --features client` — 368 + 19 + 86 + 3 + 2 passed

title: feat(sdk)!: hold one idempotency key across every attempt of an operation (#1012)
body:
feat(sdk)!: hold one idempotency key across every attempt of an operation (#1012)

The VTA deduplicates keyed Trust Tasks on an `idempotencyKey` (#1011).
That only helps if the retry carries the *same* key as the attempt it is
retrying — and a hand-rolled retry loop structurally cannot do that,
because it re-invokes a client method that builds a fresh document each
time. Minting the key inside the method has the identical problem the
envelope id already has: attempt two gets a new one, the VTA sees an
unrelated request, and the second durable effect happens anyway.

So the key has to be scoped *outside* the call. `VtaClient::idempotent`
mints one, holds it in a task-local for the duration of a closure, and
retries transient faults inside that scope:

    let key = client.idempotent(|| client.create_key(req.clone())).await?;

Every dispatch the closure makes carries the same key. A task-local
rather than a parameter because it has to reach all twenty-odd typed
methods without changing twenty signatures, and because it is genuinely
ambient — it belongs to the operation, not the call.

The key is attached only when the task is one a second execution would
actually harm (`retry_safety`); attaching it to a read would cost the
VTA a dedup record and buy nothing. It goes top-level beside `id`, where
the VTA reads it from `TrustTask::extra` and a Data-Integrity proof
covers it — so a relayer cannot rewrite it to split one operation
into two.

## One retry owner

Retry layers compose badly. The messaging delivery layer already retries
a durable outbox with backoff underneath this, so an application loop on
top multiplies attempts against a server that dedups at neither. This is
the application-layer owner: bounded at 3 attempts, backed off, and
honouring the server's `retryAfter` up to a 30s cap — an unbounded wait
on a server-chosen value is a stall the server can trigger at will.

Callers should use it *instead of* their own loop, not around one.

## BREAKING CHANGE

`VtaError` gains an `Unavailable { retry_after }` variant (exhaustive
enum), reported by cargo-semver-checks so the release moves the
compatibility field rather than shipping it as a patch.

It is typed rather than folded into `Protocol(String)` because it is the
one wire rejection meaning "ask again" rather than "this failed" — the
idempotency layer returns it while a first attempt on the same key is
still running. A retry loop reading it as terminal gives up on precisely

title: feat(vta)!: dedup keyed Trust Tasks on an idempotency key
body:
Second of five PRs closing #1009. Rebased onto main now that #1010 (the
classification) has merged, so this diff is its own work only.

## Breaking change, deliberately — `semver checks` is reporting it correctly

Two API breaks in `vti-common`, both flagged by cargo-semver-checks (an advisory
`continue-on-error` job, by design, so a 0.x break is *known* rather than shipped
as a patch):

- `Principal` gains a `Did` variant — exhaustive enum.
- `CacheEntry` gains a `state` field — exhaustively constructible struct.

**No stored-record break.** `state` is `#[serde(default)]`, so a record written
before it existed reads back as `Completed`; the module's 13 pre-existing tests
pass unchanged. The only source break is an exhaustive `match` on `Principal` or a
struct literal for `CacheEntry`, and nothing outside `vti-common` did either — the
module had no consumers. Title carries `!` so release-plz moves the compatibility
field.

## The headline: I did not write a new store

`vti_common::idempotency` **already exists** — a persistent
`(principal, key) → response` cache with class-based TTLs, request-hash conflict
detection and an Axum middleware, written for the VTC's `Idempotency-Key` header
and never wired to a consumer. I started building a parallel implementation
before finding it. This PR extends that one instead and makes the VTA its first
consumer, so the VTC's HTTP path inherits the additions when it wires up.

The 13 existing tests pass unchanged; the middleware needed a one-field
construction fix and nothing else.

## What the shared store was missing

**1. `Principal::Did`.** `AuthToken` scopes the cache to the bearer credential,
and its own doc comment notes that "token rotation resets the cache namespace
(conservatively)". For a *retry* that is not conservative, it is wrong — a retry
straddling a token refresh starts a fresh namespace and re-runs the operation,
which is precisely what the cache exists to prevent. It is also the only identity
DIDComm and TSP have; without a DID variant, every Trust-Task caller on those
transports collapses to `Anonymous` and shares one namespace.

**2. An in-flight claim.** `get` then `put` leaves a real window: two concurrent
attempts both read `None`, both run, both produce the effect. `claim()` closes it
with `insert_if_absent`, so exactly one wins. The loser gets `Unavailable` with a
retry hint rather than "duplicate" — at that instant nobody knows the outcome, and
saying "duplicate" would assert something untrue.

A claim orphaned by a crash goes stale after a grace window (10 min, past the
longest handler timeout of 60s) so a retry can reclaim it instead of being blocked
forever.

One ordering detail worth checking in review: **conflict is reported ahead of
in-flight**. A mismatched body under a live claim gets `Conflict`, not "try
again" — telling that caller to retry would loop it forever on a request that can
never be accepted.

**3. `CompletedNotRetained`.** This is the part I'd most like scrutinised.

Result-caching idempotency wants to replay the stored response. For
`seeds/export-mnemonic`, `backup/complete-export` and `provision/integration`
that means persisting a mnemonic / a sealed bundle / the whole VTA under a
passphrase, a second time, indefinitely, in a keyspace that exists for retry
bookkeeping. The workspace already has a standing invariant that the mnemonic
plaintext is never cached anywhere; a naive result cache would violate it.

So those record completion **without** the body. The duplicate effect is still
prevented — which is the actual goal — and the retry receives an error saying the
result is not replayable, naming the read operation that can fetch it. An empty
body would have been silently misread as a real response, hence the explicit
state rather than a `None`-shaped absence.

Oversized responses (>64 KiB) take the same path, so one large listing task can't
let a caller size a dedup record with whatever it asked for.

## Wire format

A top-level `idempotencyKey` member. It lands in `TrustTask::extra`
(`#[serde(flatten)]`), so **no change to the upstream `trust-tasks-rs` document
type is needed** — and because a DI proof covers every member except `proof`, the
key is signed. A relayer cannot rewrite it to split one operation into two.

The request hash binds the **type URI as well as the payload**, so one key cannot
carry a `keys/create` answer to a `dids/create` retry.

## Blast radius

Deliberately small:

- No `idempotencyKey` → none of this runs. Dispatch is byte-identical to today.
- Only tasks the classification marks `Keyed`/`KeyedSecret` are recorded.
- A store error **logs and dispatches unguarded**. Failing closed would turn a
  storage blip into an outage of every keyed operation, to prevent a duplicate
  that only matters when a reply is *also* lost. Deliberate; argue if you disagree.
- A failed task **releases** its claim rather than recording it — caching failures
  would make one transient error sticky for 24h.

The claim sits after payload validation (a malformed request must not consume a
key) and before the policy gate (a denial releases through the same path every
other failure takes).

## Also

- New `IDEMPOTENCY` keyspace, in `EXCLUDED_FROM_BACKUP` — short-lived retry state,
  and scoped to the VTA that served the original request, so restoring it
  elsewhere would claim to have already performed operations that instance never
  did. Census test passes.
- `idempotency_sweeper`, alongside acl/consent/vault. Not audited, unlike those —
  they remove a *grant* (a security event); this removes retry bookkeeping, and a
  row per expiry would bury the audit log. Unreadable rows are deleted rather than
  skipped: a row that cannot decode can never be served, and leaving it in place
  permanently blocks its key.

## Not in this PR

Nothing sends a key yet — the SDK change is PR 3, and until it lands this is
inert in production. Retry-ownership and the orphan reconciliation sweeper are
PRs 4 and 5.

Refs #1009.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all`
- [x] `cargo clippy` on all four touched crates, `--all-targets` — clean
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — 831 passed
- [x] `cargo test -p vti-common` — 408 passed (13 pre-existing idempotency tests unchanged, 10 new)
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-sweepers -p vta-keyspaces` — passed
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: feat(vta)!: dedup keyed Trust Tasks on an idempotency key (#1011)
body:
feat(vta)!: dedup keyed Trust Tasks on an idempotency key (#1011)

A client that retries a timed-out request is doing the right thing. The
dangerous case is the one where the VTA processed it and only the reply
was lost, because the retry then produces a second durable effect —
`webvh/dids/create` being the sharp example, where auto-assigned paths
mean the retry mints a *different* DID and the first stays published
with nobody holding a reference to it.

The existing `trust_tasks::replay` layer cannot catch that. It keys on
`(actor, envelope-id)` and every SDK path mints a fresh `urn:uuid:` per
attempt, so a genuine retry sails past it. Its own module docs name this
work as the deliberate follow-up.

## Built on the store that was already here

`vti_common::idempotency` already implements a persistent
`(principal, key) -> response` cache with class-based TTLs and
same-key-different-body conflict detection, written for the VTC's
`Idempotency-Key` header and never wired to a consumer. Rather than add
a second implementation to the same workspace, this extends that one and
makes the VTA its first consumer. The VTC's HTTP path gets the additions
for free when it wires up.

## BREAKING CHANGE

Two additive-but-breaking API changes in `vti-common`, both reported by
cargo-semver-checks so the release moves the compatibility field rather
than shipping them as a patch:

- `Principal` gains a `Did` variant (exhaustive enum).
- `CacheEntry` gains a `state` field (exhaustively constructible struct).

Neither changes stored-record compatibility: `state` is
`#[serde(default)]`, so a record written before it existed reads back as
`Completed`, and the module's 13 pre-existing tests pass unchanged. The
only source break is an exhaustive match on `Principal` or a struct
literal for `CacheEntry`, and nothing outside `vti-common` did either —
the module had no consumers.

## What the shared store was missing

- **`Principal::Did`.** `AuthToken` scopes the cache to the bearer
  credential, so token rotation mid-retry silently starts a fresh
  namespace and re-runs the operation — the exact failure the cache
  prevents. It is also the *only* identity DIDComm and TSP have, so
  without this a Trust-Task caller on either transport collapses to
  `Anonymous` and shares a namespace with every other caller.

- **`EntryState` + `claim`/`complete`/`release`.** `get` then `put`
  leaves a window where two concurrent attempts both read `None` and
  both run. Claiming before dispatch closes it: the write is
  `insert_if_absent`, so one attempt wins and the other is answered
  `Unavailable` with a retry hint — not "duplicate", because at that
  instant nobody knows the outcome. A claim orphaned by a crash goes
  stale after a grace window so the retry can reclaim it.

- **`CompletedNotRetained`.** Some responses carry a mnemonic, a sealed
  bundle, or the whole VTA under a passphrase. Caching those to serve a
  retry would persist the secret again, indefinitely, in a keyspace that
  exists for something else. Those tasks record the *fact* of completion
  without the body: the duplicate effect is still prevented, and the
  retry gets an error saying the result is not replayable rather than an
  empty body it would misread as one. The same path takes oversized
  responses, so one large listing cannot let a caller size a dedup
  record with whatever it asked for.

## Wire

A top-level `idempotencyKey` member, landing in `TrustTask::extra`
(`#[serde(flatten)]`), so the upstream document type needs no change.
Because a Data-Integrity proof covers every member but `proof`, the key
is **signed** — a relayer cannot alter it to split one operation into
two. The request hash binds the type URI as well as the payload, so one
key cannot carry a `keys/create` answer to a `dids/create` retry.

## Blast radius

A request with no `idempotencyKey` takes none of these paths, and only
tasks `vta_sdk::retry_safety` marks as needing a key are recorded at
all. A store error logs and dispatches unguarded rather than failing
closed: idempotency is an improvement on the status quo, not a
precondition for it, and a storage blip should not take out every keyed
operation to prevent a duplicate that only matters when a reply is also
lost. A failed task releases its claim rather than recording it, so one
transient error does not become a sticky one.

Refs #1009

title: perf(r14): move the last two network actions off the loop
body:
Closes the R14 sweep. Contains the progress mechanism, then the credential request, then the persona mint — in that order, because each needed the one before.

## 1. A way for a running job to report progress

`DispatchOutcome::Progress` is the **only** outcome that does not finish its domain: the job that sent it is still running, and finishing would let a second start alongside it. It carries a typed `ProgressUpdate`, not a bare string, so a new consumer cannot silently borrow another's display surface.

Both loops already have a dispatch arm, so both get this for free — no second channel, no new `select!` arm.

Without it, the persona overlay would have gone from a step-by-step account of a slow operation to a spinner that says nothing for half a dozen round-trips. That is how a working mint comes to look like a hang, which is the exact confusion this whole R14 sweep started from.

## 2. The credential request

**I was wrong when I called this a restructure.** Only one of twelve `CredentialAction` variants touches the network; the other eleven are state or config. It is one arm: the loop resolves the relationship's two DIDs, builds the message and picks the listener; the job sends.

The satisfying consequence is that `credential_actions::dispatch` loses its TDK and messaging parameters and stops being `async` — which is the clearest possible statement of what that module now is.

## 3. The persona mint

`mint_standalone_persona` no longer takes `Config`: its two reads become `MintInputs`, and it returns a `MintedPersona` (the `SetupState` and DID) instead of persisting.

**The persist deliberately stays on the loop.** `mint_persona_into` is shared with the join flow and is not worth restructuring for this, because everything it does is local — key info, an `ATMProfile`, `profile_add(.., false)` (registration explicitly *without* a socket), and secrets-resolver inserts. My earlier claim that this batch would have to touch the join path was wrong, and reading it properly is what made this tractable.

That persist is `async` and mutates `Config`, which the shared applier cannot do — so `AfterApply` generalises the return added in #243 to `Nothing | Deregister | PersistPersona`. Both loops settle it through one helper, because **a first persona is minted in State A** and must be persisted exactly as one minted at runtime.

### The ordering that matters

The overlay is marked Done *after* the persist, not when the VTA finishes minting. A persona shown as created but absent from the config would be a claim the next launch contradicts. When the persist fails, the message says the DID was **minted but not saved** — it exists at the VTA, and a retry would mint a second.

`DispatchOutcome::Persona` is boxed: a `MintedPersona` carries a whole `SetupState` (~2 KB) against ~136 bytes for the next largest variant, and unboxed, every dispatch of every domain would pay for it. Clippy caught that.

## Tests

Progress renders a step without freeing its domain, and is dropped for a closed overlay; a sent VRC request creates the tracking task while a failed one creates none; a successful mint defers completion to the persist and shows no DID before it; a failed mint is terminal.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` **and** `--no-default-features`.

## R14 after this

Five batches: agent names (#237), VIC vault (#239), capabilities (#242), community sends (#243), and this. Every network action a keypress can start now runs off the state-handler loop.

What still awaits on it is local by nature: settings, openpgp-card token operations, listener teardown for withdraw/delete-community, the in-memory secrets reads before a signature, and the already-migrated prepare steps. `StartJoin` remains deliberately modal, with the join flow owning its own loop.

title: spec(vta): two gaps in services that only writing the handlers revealed
body:
## How these were found

#243 specified the family from the REST routes' request and response types.
Wiring the actual VTA handlers against it found **two operations the schema
cannot express**. Both came out of implementation, which is what implementation
is for — neither was visible from reading the routes.

## 1. Rollback can legitimately write nothing

The operation returns a `kind` — `disabled` / `enabled` / `updated` / `noOp` —
and on `noOp`, where the previous state already equals the current one, **no log
entry is published**. The shared `ServiceMutationResult` requires
`logEntryVersionId`, so the spec had no way to say that.

It is a **success**: the requested state holds. Calling it a failure would be
wrong, and calling it an ordinary success would name a log entry that doesn't
exist.

Rollback therefore gets its own `RollbackResult` — `kind` required,
`logEntryVersionId` optional — rather than relaxing the shared type. `enable`,
`update` and `disable` genuinely always produce an entry, and weakening their
contract to accommodate rollback would throw that guarantee away.

## 2. Disable takes a drain window, and can't always honour it

`drainTtlSecs` was missing entirely. The omission matters less than the rule
that came with it:

> `0` = immediate teardown (REST only; over DIDComm transport, minimum 1h is
> enforced)

**`0` is not always obeyed.** The agent enforces a floor when the request
arrived *through the mediator being torn down*, because cutting it mid-request
discards the reply to the very task asking for it.

A spec omitting that invites a caller to send `0`, read no `drainUntil`, and
conclude the mediator is gone. The field is now specified along with the
constraint, and the prose says plainly: the caller proposes the window, the
agent decides it — read `drainUntil` to learn what actually happened.

## Legitimacy of changing a published 1.0

Both specs are `status: draft`, whose stated contract is that the schema **MAY
change without notice**. This is that. Nothing implements them yet — the VTI
handlers are the work that surfaced this — so no consumer is broken.

## Verification

```
336 specs validated; 336 TypeScript and 331 Rust modules — all agree
trust-tasks-rs   424 passing
workspace        557 passing
trust-tasks-ts    50 passing
```

Both generated trees changed, so both packages are bumped — **ts 0.11.0 →
0.12.0**, **rs 0.10.0 → 0.11.0** with the sibling requirements carried. The
guards from #244 and #245 would have caught it had I forgotten, which is the
first time they've been exercised on a real change.

title: feat(sdk): classify what a lost reply costs every Trust Task
body:
First of five PRs closing #1009. This one adds no behaviour — it adds the
*fact table* the rest of the work reads.

## Why

A client that retries a timed-out request is doing the right thing: the dominant
transport fault is a request that never arrived. The dangerous case is the other
one — the VTA processed it and only the reply was lost — and whether that is
harmful depends entirely on the operation.

Callers cannot currently tell those apart, so they guess. OpenVTC's `vta_retry`
guesses conservatively for everything and documents the residual risk in a
comment; that comment is what the RAHP assessment found.

## What

`vta_sdk::retry_safety` — a `RetrySafety` classification over all 148 URIs in
`ALL_URIS`, with a census test that fails if a task joins the catalog
unclassified. Same discipline that pins `REST_ROUTED_URIS`.

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ReadOnly` | No durable effect. |
| `RetrySafe` | Mutating, but a repeat is harmless — converges, or leaves an inert self-expiring duplicate. |
| `Keyed` | Non-convergent: a repeat leaves a second durable artefact that matters. |
| `KeyedSecret` | As `Keyed`, but the response carries secrets, so it is never cached. |

**`RetrySafe` is deliberately not called "idempotent".** Half its members are not
idempotent — a second `auth/challenge` mints a second challenge. They are grouped
because the only question a retry layer asks is "does a repeat do harm", and for
both members the answer is no.

**`KeyedSecret` is the class worth reviewing.** Result-caching idempotency wants
to replay the stored response; for `seeds/export-mnemonic`,
`backup/complete-export` and `provision/integration` that means persisting the
secret again, indefinitely, to serve a retry. The effect still gets deduped —
only the replay is refused. This is also why the mnemonic-export guard's
"don't cache the plaintext anywhere" invariant survives contact with this work.

## Judgement calls

Where convergence is not obvious from the contract, the entry is `Keyed`. The
asymmetry is nearly free: over-classifying costs one dedup record;
under-classifying loses the protection in exactly the rare case the table exists
for. `device/register` is the clearest example — it is addressed by a
caller-supplied device identity, which looks convergent, but it also mints
credentials and the contract does not say whether those are re-minted.

Two entries are worth a second opinion from anyone who knows the flows better:

- **`auth/refresh/0.1` → `Keyed`.** Token rotation consumes the old token as it
  issues the new one, so a lost reply leaves the caller holding a spent token and
  no replacement. That is a lockout, not an orphan.
- **`did/rollback` → `Keyed`.** Read as a *relative* step, so applying it twice
  rewinds twice. If it is absolute (roll back *to* a named version), it is
  `RetrySafe` and I have it wrong.

## Scope

Nothing consumes this yet, and classification gates nothing on its own — it
changes how a *keyed* request is handled, and no client sends a key today. The
VTA-side dedup store and the client-side key are the next two PRs.

Refs #1009.

## Pre-merge

- [x] `cargo fmt --all`
- [x] `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk --all-targets` — clean
- [x] `cargo test -p vta-sdk` — 289 passed
- [x] No `version =` edits, no changelog file

title: release(rs): trust-tasks-rs 0.10.0, and guard it like the TS package
body:
## I fixed half of this in #244

#244 added a version-bump guard so regenerated bindings can't merge without a
release. **It only covered `trust-tasks-ts`.** The Rust crate has exactly the
same problem, and #243's families were stranded on *both* sides — I closed one
half and said the recurrence was handled.

`trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/vta/services/` has been on main since #243 while the
crate stayed at **0.9.0**, which is what crates.io already holds. `cargo
publish` refuses a version already published, so the eight `vta/services/*`
families can't be depended on from `verifiable-trust-infrastructure` — which is
precisely where the handlers implementing them have to be written.

## What's here

- **0.9.0 → 0.10.0**, plus the `^0.9` requirement carried to the six sibling
  crates that declare it (`tsp`, `didcomm`, `didcomm-v1`, `capability-client`,
  `proof`, `https`). Without that the workspace won't resolve.
- **`rust.yml` gets the mirror of ts.yml's `version-bump`**, with the same
  keying: the generated tree is committed, so *"did the published content
  change"* is answerable exactly. If `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` differs from the
  PR's base and `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml` doesn't, the PR fails.

A change that regenerates nothing — a dependency bump, a Rust-only fix, a prose
edit — is exempt with no override needed, which is what stops the check becoming
something people route around.

## Verified by replay, not by reasoning

```
#243's merge      specs CHANGED; version 0.9.0 → 0.9.0  ⇒ FAILS, correctly
h2 advisory fix   specs unchanged                        ⇒ exempt
```

My first attempt at this replay used the wrong base (`main~1` is #244, which
touched no Rust) and reported "unchanged". The numbers above are against #243's
actual merge commit.

## Test

`cargo test --workspace` — **557 passing, 0 failures**.

Note the second commit: I pushed the bump before reading the build output, which
had already told me the workspace wouldn't resolve. Left as its own commit
rather than squashed, since the failure is the reason the sibling-crate change
belongs here at all.

title: perf(r14): send community leave and VMC issuance off the loop
body:
Fourth R14 batch: the two verbs addressed at a community — leaving it (`members/self-remove`) and issuing it the reciprocal membership credential (`members/vmc`).

## Why these matter more than their size suggests

Both send to a peer that may be exactly the thing that has gone wrong. **An unreachable community is a likely reason to leave one**, and that is precisely when `send_message_with_retry` retries longest — so the arm most likely to hang was the one for getting out.

## The design question this batch forced

Leaving needs more than the shared apply path: a successful leave also tears down that community's messaging session, and the session manager belongs to the runtime loop — while `apply_outcome` is shared with the degraded loop, which has no sessions at all.

Threading the session manager into a shared signature that one of its two callers cannot satisfy would have been the wrong shape. Instead `apply_outcome` now **returns** the community still owed a teardown:

```rust
pub(crate) type PendingDeregistration = Option<(String, PersonaId)>;
```

The runtime loop performs it; the degraded loop ignores it, and says why. The teardown itself is local — removing a listener — not a network call.

## Preserved behaviour worth stating

The record moves **on the send, not on a receipt**. The community's acknowledgement is advisory, and a member who has announced a departure should not still be shown as a member if the community never answers. That was the inline behaviour and it is unchanged.

`issue_member_vmc_for` stays in `message_dispatch`: a second caller answers a VTC's `request-vmc` from the inbound path, which does not run on this loop. I deleted it first and the compiler caught the other caller — only the loop arm stopped using it.

## Tests

A successful leave asks for a session teardown and marks the config dirty; a failed leave keeps the session (the membership is still live, and the session is what would carry a retry); issuing a credential touches neither session nor record; a failed issue reports why.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` **and** `--no-default-features`.

## R14 status after this

Done: agent names (#237), VIC vault (#239), capabilities (#242), community sends (this).

What is left is no longer a queue of similar ports:

* **`Action::Credential`** delegates to `credential_actions::dispatch`, a sub-dispatcher that mutates config and state and uses the messaging service — it needs restructuring into prepare/job/apply the way `inbox_actions` already is, not a lift.
* **create-persona** still needs its own design: `mint_persona_into` interleaves config mutation with network work, is shared with the join flow, and streams progress into the overlay.
* **`WithdrawJoin`, `DeleteCommunity`** have no network send at all — their only awaits are local listener teardown.
* **`StartJoin`** is deliberately modal; the join flow owns its own loop.
* The `Settings` and openpgp-card awaits are local.

title: release(ts): 0.11.0, and make the missing bump fail rather than advise
body:
## What happened, again

#243 added the eight `vta/services/*` families. They're in
`trust-tasks-ts/src` on main and **absent from npm**, because the publish
workflow skips a version already published and the version didn't move —
exactly how #240's families were stranded until #242 bumped to 0.10.0.

Twice in two consecutive spec PRs is a process that doesn't work. This bumps to
**0.11.0** and adds the check that would have caught both.

## Why it's worse than "not released yet"

`0.10.0` on npm and `0.10.0` on main are **different trees**. A consumer
installing the package to use a family that is merged, documented and live on
the website gets a module-not-found, with the version number giving no hint
that it's stale.

A version that hasn't been published yet is a normal state. One version number
meaning two different things is not.

## The guard keys on the bindings, not on `specs/**`

`trust-tasks-ts/src` is committed, so *"did the published content change"* is
answerable exactly:

- generated bindings differ from the PR's base **and** the version didn't move → **fail**
- bindings unchanged → **exempt**, no override needed

That exemption is what stops it becoming noise people learn to bypass: a prose
fix, a ceremony change or a Rust-only PR regenerates nothing and is silently
fine.

## Verified against real history, not by reasoning

Replayed the guard over actual commits:

```
#243's merge          bindings CHANGED; version 0.10.0 → 0.10.0  ⇒ FAILS, correctly
#242 (the 0.10.0 bump)  bindings unchanged                        ⇒ exempt
h2 advisory fix         bindings unchanged                        ⇒ exempt
sideEffects: false      bindings unchanged                        ⇒ exempt
didcomm-v1 binding 0.2  bindings unchanged                        ⇒ exempt
```

## Note

`bindings-drift` already told authors to bump, in its own failure text — the
convention was documented and unenforced. This makes it enforced.

## Verification

```
336 specifications checked against 336 TypeScript and 331 Rust modules — all agree
YAML parses; 5 jobs
```

title: spec(vta): specify the services family — the transports an agent advertises
body:
## Why

The 20 `/services/*` REST routes were the **last block with no Trust Task twin
at all**, which is why they were excluded when the rest of the agent's REST
surface was marked superseded (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1007) —
there was nothing to point them at. This is that missing half.

## Eight families, parameterised by service

The 20 routes are four transports — `didcomm`, `rest`, `tsp`, `webauthn` —
crossed with enable/disable/update/rollback, plus list, get and two drain
operations.

Seventeen near-identical families would have been the mechanical reading. Eight
parameterised ones say the same thing, and mean a **fifth transport needs a
config variant rather than four new specs**. The existing wire already agrees:
`ServiceState` in `vta_sdk::protocol::services` is a tagged union on `kind`.

| Family | Covers |
|---|---|
| `vta/services/list` | `GET /services` |
| `vta/services/get` | `GET /services/{kind}` |
| `vta/services/enable` | 4 routes |
| `vta/services/update` | 4 routes |
| `vta/services/disable` | 4 routes |
| `vta/services/rollback` | 4 routes |
| `vta/services/drain/list` | `GET /services/didcomm/drain` |
| `vta/services/drain/cancel` | `POST /services/didcomm/drain` |

`service` is the discriminator; `config` carries kind-specific settings. **The
two MUST agree** — a `rest` payload carrying `mediatorDid` is malformed, not a
request with a harmlessly ignored field. Treating it as ignorable is how an
operator comes to believe they configured something they did not.

## Drain is two families, not one

The shape this started from had a single `drain`. It can't be: `GET` lists what
is draining, `POST` **cancels** a drain. A read and a destructive mutation
cannot share a task — they differ in side-effect level, in proof requirement,
and in what a consumer may do with the answer.

`drain/cancel` is `destructive`, not `mutating`: it discards messages still in
flight, which is precisely what the drain window existed to prevent.

## Three things the prose is deliberate about

Each is a way to be *confidently* wrong:

- **A drain is not a finished disable.** While `drainUntil` is in the future the
  old mediator still accepts delivery. Reporting "disabled" then is wrong in the
  direction that loses messages — and decommissioning on the strength of it
  loses them for certain.
- **`serverless: true` means nobody else can see the change yet.** The log entry
  is written locally but unpublished. Reporting success without surfacing this
  tells an operator a change is live when no verifier can observe it.
- **Rollback writes a *new* entry.** The log is append-only, so a rollback is a
  forward step restoring an earlier state, never an erasure — an audit sees both
  the mistake and the correction.

## A schema bug the round-trip tests caught

`force` is didcomm-only but I gave it `"default": false`, so the generated type
materialised it into **every** config — including `rest`, where the same schema
says it doesn't apply. The `update` example then failed its own round-trip.

The example wasn't wrong; the schema was. The default is gone, and the prose
states the reading instead: absent means the handshake runs. Same class of
finding as #240, and exactly what those tests are for.

## Verification

```
Validated 336 specs (was 328), indexed 63 shared schemas
336 specifications checked against 336 TypeScript and 331 Rust modules — all agree
trust-tasks-rs   424 passing (was 408 — the 16 new round-trip tests)
trust-tasks-ts    50 passing, tsc --noEmit clean
```

## Follow-on, not in this PR

With these specified, `vta-service` can grow the handlers and the 20 routes can
join the superseded set that #1007 measures. That's a VTI change and wants its
own review.

title: perf(r14): send capability documents off the state-handler loop
body:
Third R14 batch: opening the capabilities view, refreshing it, and committing a toggle.

## Why these looked cheap and were not

The awaits here are a **send**, not a round trip — the community's answer arrives later on the inbound channel and is matched by thread id. That is what made them easy to leave inline.

But `send_message_with_retry` retries against an unreachable peer, and **it is the same loop that drains the inbound channel**. So a retrying send blocked reception of the very reply the view was waiting for, on top of every other keystroke and event. The worse the peer, the longer both halves stall.

## What stays on the loop, deliberately

* Resolving the persona's DID, messaging profile and mediator — that reads `Config`.
* Reading the signing key for a toggle. It *is* an `await`, but on the TDK secrets resolver: an in-memory store populated at startup, not I/O. Doing it here is what lets the job own a `Secret` instead of borrowing `Config`.

## Correctness once the UI stays live

The outcome is dropped if the view has closed or moved to another community. The operator can navigate while a send retries, and arming a thread id on the wrong community would match a reply that answers a question nobody asked there.

The failure asymmetry from the inline code is preserved: a failed **query** fails the view (there is nothing to show), while a failed **toggle** keeps the list and says so in the status line (the list is still valid; only the write did not go out).

`message_dispatch::capabilities_list_for` and `capability_toggle_for` are gone — their config reads became the loop-side resolver and their sends became the job.

## Tests

A sent query arms the view; a failed query fails it; a failed toggle keeps the list; an outcome for another community is dropped; an outcome with no view is dropped.

Worth recording: the first draft of those tests **failed**, because `PersonaId::default()` mints a fresh v4 UUID on every call — so they compared two different personas and the guard correctly discarded the outcome. The tests now pin one id, which doubles as a demonstration that the guard does its job.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` **and** `--no-default-features`.

## R14 status

Done: agent names (#237), VIC vault (#239), capabilities (this).
Left: credential exchange, VMC issuance, community self-removal — and create-persona, which still needs its own design because `mint_persona_into` interleaves config mutation with network work and is shared with the join flow.

title: perf(r14): send capability documents off the state-handler loop (#242)
body:
perf(r14): send capability documents off the state-handler loop (#242)

Third R14 batch: opening the capabilities view, refreshing it, and
committing a toggle.

These awaits were a *send*, not a round trip — the community's answer
arrives later on the inbound channel and is matched by thread id. That
made them look cheap. They are not: `send_message_with_retry` retries
against an unreachable peer, and it is the same loop that drains the
inbound channel. So a retrying send blocked reception of the very reply
the view was waiting for, on top of every other keystroke and event.

What stays on the loop is deliberate. Resolving the persona's DID,
messaging profile and mediator reads `Config`. Reading the signing key
for a toggle is an `await`, but on the TDK secrets resolver — an
in-memory store populated at startup, not I/O — and doing it here is what
lets the job own a `Secret` instead of borrowing `Config`.

The outcome is dropped if the view has closed or moved to another
community. The UI stays live while a send retries, so the operator can do
exactly that, and arming a thread id on the wrong community would match a
reply that answers a question nobody asked there.

A failed *query* fails the view, because there is nothing to show. A
failed *toggle* keeps the list and says so in the status line: the list
is still valid, only the write did not go out. That asymmetry was in the
inline code and is preserved.

`message_dispatch::capabilities_list_for` and `capability_toggle_for` are
gone; their config reads are the loop-side resolver and their sends are
the job.

Tests: a sent query arms the view; a failed query fails it; a failed
toggle keeps the list; an outcome for another community is dropped; an
outcome with no view is dropped. The first draft of those tests failed —
`PersonaId::default()` mints a fresh v4 UUID per call, so they compared
two different personas and the guard correctly discarded the outcome. The
tests now pin one id, which is also a demonstration that the guard works.

title: docs(messaging): correct the stale bounded-channel comment on the DIDComm event channel
body:
The comment above the DIDComm event channel in `state_handler/mod.rs` still
described the pre-#224 behaviour — bounded, with overflow surfacing as
`try_send` warnings and the message left in the mailbox for `pickup_stored` to
collect on the next connect. It sat directly above `mpsc::unbounded_channel()`.

#224 removed that bound precisely because the drop was not deferral. The
delivery layer acks before the event reaches this channel, and an ack is a
delete at the mediator, so an overflow destroyed membership credentials and
join verdicts outright — #221 is what that looked like from the outside.

This points the comment at the ADR on `DIDCOMM_EVENT_CHANNEL_CAPACITY`, which
carries the full reasoning (including why backpressure was never on offer).

Comment-only; no behaviour change.

Found by an external RAHP/DRARM assessment of the Cypress release
(sankarshanmukhopadhyay/rahp-toolkit#18). The stale comment was the strongest
evidence behind that assessment's "unbounded queue growth" finding, which the
ADR already answers — so the comment was actively costing us review time.
