title: perf(r14): run the VIC vault mutations off the state-handler loop
body:
Second R14 batch. Stacks alongside #237 (agent names) — independent files apart from `background_dispatch.rs` and the two loops' arms, so whichever lands second may want a trivial rebase.

## Problem

Import, archive, unarchive, restore, soft-delete and purge each ran their vault round-trip inline on the state-handler thread, and each was followed by a listing re-read. One keypress parked inbound DIDComm, listener lifecycle, the save scheduler and the keyboard for **two** round-trips.

## The split is at the validation boundary, not the action boundary

Parsing a pasted credential and checking it really is an invitation is local and instant — and it is what decides whether the operator stays on the input field to fix it. That stays on the loop. Only the store is carried into the job.

A bad paste therefore cannot reach a `Failed` phase at all: the distinction the inline code drew between *"fix your paste"* and *"the vault refused it"* is now preserved by construction rather than by matching on an error string.

## Ordering

Mutations share the `Vic` domain with the listing, which is what makes this safe: a mutation and a refresh cannot overlap and leave a list reflecting neither.

The follow-up refresh is **requested** by the outcome rather than started by it, through the `vic_refresh_queued` flag that the dispatch arm already re-issues when the domain frees — the same path a refresh rejected by the busy-guard takes. A *failed* mutation asks for one too: that is precisely when the panel is most misleading.

## Also

The six per-verb wrappers are gone. `VicJob` calls the vault directly and the verb is data, which is what let the six near-identical `run_vic_lifecycle` arms collapse. `list_vics` stays — the refresh still needs it.

## Tests

A mutation requests a refresh; a failed one requests it too and puts the reason in the log; an import moves the overlay to a terminal phase either way; a lifecycle verb leaves the import overlay alone.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` (no warnings); `cargo test --workspace` **and** `--no-default-features`.

## On create-persona, which I did not do

It was next by user-visible pain, and it needs its own design rather than this shape. `mint_standalone_persona` takes `&mut Config` and its tail — `Config::mint_persona_into` — interleaves config mutation with network work, including `atm.profile_add`. Splitting it means changing a path the join flow shares, and it also streams progress into the overlay, which needs a channel this mechanism does not have yet. Worth doing, worth scoping separately.

Remaining after this: capabilities, credential exchange, VMC issuance, community self-removal, and create-persona.

title: ci: lint test targets too, and fix the one warning that hid there
body:
## The gap

`cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` lints only lib and bin targets.
Anything under `tests/` is never checked, so dead code accumulates there unseen.

Concretely: a dead `wiremock::matchers::path_regex` import left behind by
#1000 sat on main until I happened to run `--all-targets` by hand while working
on #1007. Nothing would have caught it. Closing the gap is what stops the next
one lasting as long.

## What it surfaces

Exactly one further warning, in `backup_export_via_didcomm` — a call to the
`#[deprecated]` `backup_export`.

That call is **deliberate**: the `backup/*` pair is twinless (#861), the legacy
inline path is precisely what the test covers, and it has to keep working for
as long as it ships. So the fix is `#[allow(deprecated)]` scoped to that single
test with the reason recorded — silencing the lint globally, or deleting the
test, would each throw the warning away for the callers it's actually aimed at.

## Also

The `vta-service` rest-only feature-combo step gets `--all-targets` too, so it
matches the tsp-without-didcomm step beside it, which already had it. I checked
that combination is clean under the flag before changing the workflow rather
than after.

## Verification

```
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings   → clean
cargo clippy -p vta-service --no-default-features --features rest --all-targets -- -D warnings   → clean
```

Note the workspace was already only *two* warnings from clean under this flag —
this is a cheap change that permanently closes a class of blind spot rather
than one instance of it.

title: release(ts): @openvtc/trust-tasks 0.10.0
body:
## Why this is needed now

#240 added 22 task families — `vta/contexts/*` and the `vta/webvh/*` DID
lifecycle — and #239 marked the package side-effect free. **Neither has reached
a consumer.** The publish workflow skips any version already on npm, and the
version was never bumped, so the run triggered by #240 merging did nothing.

That leaves the worse of the two failure modes. `0.9.0` on npm and `0.9.0` on
main are now **different trees**:

| | `vta/webvh/dids/*` | `vta/webvh/agent-name/*` |
|---|---|---|
| main (`trust-tasks-ts/src`) | create, delete, get, list, register-with-server, rotate-keys, update | check, disable, enable, list, remove, set |
| npm `0.9.0` (installed) | `update` only | absent |

So anyone installing the package to use a family from #240 gets a
module-not-found for a spec that is merged, documented and published on the
website — with the version number giving no hint that it's stale. "Not yet
released" is a normal state; "same version, different contents" is not.

Found while implementing those families in `@openvtc/pnm-core`, which is
blocked on this.

## Minor, not patch

22 new families is additive surface and nothing existing changed shape.

## Verified before bumping

```
node scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs   → Generated 386 TS modules
npm run check-bindings               → 328 specifications checked against
                                       328 TypeScript and 323 Rust modules
                                       — all agree
```

## Worth a follow-up

Merging a spec doesn't bump the package version, so this can silently recur —
the next spec PR will land in `src` and stay unpublished exactly the same way.
Options are a release-please style automation on `specs/**`, or a CI check that
fails when `specs/**` changes without a `trust-tasks-ts/package.json` version
change. Happy to raise whichever you prefer.

title: perf(r14): run the agent-name verbs off the state-handler loop
body:
First R14 batch, and the worst offender of the 32 inline `.await` calls left in the runtime loop's action arms.

## Problem

Each agent-name Trust Task carries a **60-second timeout**, and every mutation is *two* of them — the change, then the authoritative re-read of the registry. Awaiting that inline parked the one thread that services everything: inbound DIDComm, listener lifecycle, the save scheduler, and every keystroke including `q`. Up to two minutes, for one keypress.

It was easy to under-read. The overlay's `Working` phase locks its own input, so from inside the overlay the pause looks like the overlay waiting on a network call. It was the whole application stopping — the same defect as the Tab lag (#230) and the startup freeze (#233), which were the two instances that happened to get reported.

## Fix

`agent_name_actions` follows the shape `inbox_actions` and `relationship_actions` already use: the loop resolves what the job needs and hands over owned values, the job does I/O only, and every mutation lands back on the loop in `AgentNameOutcome::apply`.

The four runners and the four helpers they shared are gone. What remains on the loop is resolving *which* persona and *which* name — pure state.

## Two things the outcome has to get right

Now that the UI stays live while a job runs, results can arrive into a changed world:

* **An outcome for a persona the overlay is no longer showing must not write its registry into the overlay.** The operator can close it, or open another persona's, mid-flight. One persona's names appearing under another's heading is exactly the class of confusion #231 and #234 were about.
* **The cached display name applies anyway.** It is a fact about the DID, established by a round-trip that completed, and it does not stop being true because a panel closed.

A rejected claim carries `names: None` — the registry did not change, so the list is left exactly as it was rather than re-read or blanked.

## Unchanged on purpose

Input locking: `Loading`/`Working` still swallow keys, so a mutation cannot be double-fired. Whether Esc should now back out of an overlay whose job is still running is a UX question this PR does not answer — the application being responsive is what makes it askable at all. Worth deciding separately.

## Tests

A listing populates the overlay and caches the served name; a failed read-back marks the list stale rather than rendering empty as "no names"; an outcome for another persona leaves the overlay alone; the cached name still applies with the overlay closed; a rejected claim leaves the existing rows untouched.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` **and** `--no-default-features` (the configuration that caught #236) — all green.

## Remaining R14 batches

Roughly 24 inline awaits left, in rough order of user-visible pain: create-persona (mint), the VIC lifecycle and import, capabilities, credential exchange, VMC issuance and community self-removal. Each is a separate PR of this shape.

title: harden(loops): make both action matches exhaustive, so divergence cannot recur
body:
## The risk this closes

OpenVTC services actions in **two** loops — `main_loop`, and `run_degraded_loop` for an account with no community — and each matched a hand-written list of `Action` variants ending in a silent `_ => {}`.

The lists could drift apart, and did. The agent-name verbs, `DeleteDid` and the entire settings surface were all missing from the second one (#235). Every one presented identically — a key that did nothing — and each was found only when a user reported it. #235 audited them back into agreement, but nothing stopped the next omission.

## The fix

Both matches now cover every variant, with **no catch-all**. Adding an `Action` fails to compile until someone decides what *each* loop does with it, and rustc names the loop and suggests the arm.

Verified by adding a probe variant to the enum:

```
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `Action::ProbeVariantForHardeningCheck` not covered
```

Exactly **two** such errors — one per loop — then reverted.

## Why the arms are grouped the way they are

The grouping is the documentation. Each listed-for-exhaustiveness arm says why it is there:

* **Serviced by `handle_nav_action` in the guard arm above.** Needed because Rust's exhaustiveness checker cannot see through a guarded arm — `_ if handle_nav_action(…)` does not count toward coverage — so every nav action must still be named.
* **Owned by the join-flow and setup-wizard sub-loops**, which run their own action loops and never delegate.
* **Genuinely needs a community** and the messaging runtime that comes with it. This is the only reachable-and-inert group, and it now says so on screen instead of doing nothing.

The groups were derived by partitioning all 98 variants against what each loop, `handle_nav_action`, and the sub-loops actually match — not by hand.

## Scope

No behaviour change beyond that one message. Every arm that did work still does.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` — all green.

Authority, delegation, approval, or revocation semantics

title: feat(service): signal every superseded REST route, from one layer
body:
## Why

`crate::deprecation` already sets the policy — removal is gated on
`deprecated_route_requests_total` reaching zero, explicitly **not** on a guessed
calendar date, which is why it emits no `Sunset`. But the signal reached only
**4 routes** out of the ~56 a Trust Task supersedes. A metric covering a twelfth
of the surface can't justify deleting anything.

This makes the metric trustworthy enough to act on.

## The mapping is recovered, not guessed

Before #1000 deleted them, each `build_rest` closure in the SDK paired a
Trust-Task constant with the exact REST route it fell back to. Reading them
back out of git yields **60 route→task pairs with zero ambiguity** — the
mapping the client itself used, rather than one inferred from matching names.

Two entries look wrong at a glance and are not. Both are documented at their
SDK call sites:

| Route | Successor | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /webvh/dids/{scid}/log` | `dids/get/1.0` | the dedicated get-log task folded into it behind `includeLog` |
| `PATCH /webvh/servers/{id}` | `servers/register/1.0` | #850 folded add + update into one task |

## One layer, not 56 handler edits

The per-handler form threads a `HeaderMap` back through the return type. These
handlers have **39 distinct return shapes** — `Result<Json<T>>`,
`Result<(StatusCode, Json<T>)>`, `Result<StatusCode>`, and so on.

A handler with several `Ok(...)` arms only has to miss one for its route to
fall silent — and **a silent route reads exactly like an unused one**. Since
the entire purpose is deleting routes on the strength of a zero reading, a
signal that can be half-applied is worse than no signal at all. Matching on
`MatchedPath` in one place cannot be half-applied.

The four existing per-handler calls are removed with it, so there's one
mechanism rather than two that double-count the same request.

## Only a successful response counts

A 404, or a request rejected before it reached the handler, says nothing about
a client depending on the route. Counting those would hold the metric off zero
forever and the route could never be retired — defeating the point of gating on
it.

## 56 routes are deliberately *not* marked

`/services/*` (21) has no Trust-Task twin at all and needs specs authored
first. `/auth` (8), `/bootstrap`, `/attestation` (7), `passkey_vms` (4), backup
blob streaming, the import wrapping key, `/metrics` and `/.well-known` are
genuinely REST and aren't going anywhere. The table comment records this so the
next reader doesn't have to re-derive it.

## Tests

Three, holding the property that actually matters — that the signal is really
attached, since a silent middleware would look identical to "nobody calls this":

- `superseded_route_advertises_its_trust_task_successor` — right task URI, RFC
  8288 `rel="successor-version"`
- `a_route_with_no_trust_task_twin_is_not_marked` — `/auth/challenge` stays
  unmarked
- `an_unauthenticated_rejection_is_not_counted_as_usage`

`cargo test --workspace --features session,tsp` — **4472 passing, 0 failures**.

## One drive-by, and a gap worth a follow-up

Removes a dead `path_regex` import in `client_rest.rs` left behind by #1000.

It's worth knowing **why that survived**: CI runs `cargo clippy --workspace --
-D warnings`, which does **not** lint test targets. Adding `--all-targets`
would have caught it. The workspace is two warnings away from being clean under
that flag — this import, and a deliberate `#[deprecated]` call in
`vti-e2e-tests` that would want an `#[allow(deprecated)]`. Happy to raise that
separately if you want it.

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*) — none; response headers only
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] **Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.\*)** — the substance of
      this PR: the counter must mean "a client used this route", so rejections
      don't count
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

`Action` fails to compile until someone decides what *each* loop does
with it; rustc names the loop and suggests the arm. Verified by adding a
probe variant to the enum: exactly two E0004 errors, one per loop, under
both the default and `--no-default-features` builds.

The `openpgp-card` variants are split into their own `#[cfg]`-gated arms.
They do not exist in a default build, so one flat list compiles under a
single feature set and breaks the other — which is what CI caught on the
first attempt, where every `Test` job failed on the `--no-default-features`
half it runs alongside the default one.

The remaining arms are grouped by why they are listed, because the
grouping is the documentation: serviced by `handle_nav_action` in the
guard arm above (which the exhaustiveness checker cannot see through,
since guarded arms do not count toward coverage); owned by the join-flow
and setup-wizard sub-loops, which run their own action loops; or
genuinely needing a community and the messaging runtime that comes with
it. Only the last group is reachable and inert, and it says so on screen.

No behaviour change beyond that message. The groups were derived by
partitioning all 98 variants against what each loop, `handle_nav_action`
and the sub-loops actually match, not by hand.

Gate: cargo fmt --all; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings;
cargo test --workspace AND cargo test --workspace --no-default-features.

title: feat(service): signal every superseded REST route, from one layer (#1007)
body:
feat(service): signal every superseded REST route, from one layer (#1007)

`crate::deprecation` gates route removal on `deprecated_route_requests_total`
reaching zero rather than on a calendar date — that policy was already written
down, but the signal reached only 4 routes out of the ~56 a Trust Task
supersedes. A metric that covers a twelfth of the surface cannot justify
deleting anything.

**The mapping is recovered, not guessed.** Before #1000 deleted them, each
`build_rest` closure in the SDK paired a Trust-Task constant with the exact
REST route it fell back to. Reading them out of git gives 60 route→task pairs
the client itself used, with no ambiguity. Two look wrong at a glance and are
not: `GET /webvh/dids/{scid}/log` points at `dids/get`, because the dedicated
get-log task folded into it behind `includeLog`; `PATCH /webvh/servers/{id}`
points at `servers/register`, because #850 folded add and update into one task.
Both are documented at their call sites in the SDK.

**One layer, not 56 handler edits.** The per-handler form threads a `HeaderMap`
back through the return type, and these handlers have 39 distinct return
shapes — `Result<Json<T>>`, `Result<(StatusCode, Json<T>)>`,
`Result<StatusCode>`, and so on. A handler with several `Ok(...)` arms only has
to miss one for its route to fall silent, and a silent route reads exactly like
an unused one. Since the whole purpose is deleting routes on the strength of a
zero, a signal that can be half-applied is worse than no signal. Matching on
`MatchedPath` in one place cannot be half-applied. The four existing
per-handler calls are removed with it, so there is one mechanism rather than
two that double-count.

**Only a successful response counts.** A 404, or a request rejected before it
reached the handler, says nothing about a client depending on the route.
Counting those would hold the metric off zero forever and the route could never
be retired.

**56 routes are deliberately not marked.** `/services/*` (21) has no Trust-Task
twin at all and needs specs first; `/auth`, `/bootstrap`, `/attestation`,
backup blob streaming, the import wrapping key, `/metrics` and `/.well-known`
are genuinely REST. The table comment says so, so the next reader does not have
to re-derive it.

Three tests hold the property that matters: the successor link carries the
right task URI and the RFC 8288 relation, a route with no twin is not marked,
and an unauthorised rejection is not counted as usage.

Also removes a dead `path_regex` import in `client_rest.rs` — left behind by
#1000, and invisible to CI because `cargo clippy --workspace` does not lint
test targets without `--all-targets`.

title: fix(state-a): service agent names, identity removal and settings before a community exists
body:
## Problem

An account with no community runs a second, smaller event loop (`run_degraded_loop`). It routes pure navigation through the shared `handle_nav_action` and then matches a **hand-written list** of everything else — with a silent `_ => {}` at the end.

Three separate surfaces had never been added to that list, and all three failed the same way: the key did nothing, and nothing said why.

* **`g` on a freshly minted persona.** State A is where an account's *first* persona is created, so it is the first place anyone wants to name one. The four agent-name verbs existed only in the runtime loop. The overlay's pure-state actions (input, select, close, remove-confirm) already went through `handle_nav_action`, so the only half missing was the half that talks to the VTA.
* **`y` on the remove-identity confirm.** `DeleteDid` was commented as "intentionally inert" here, but nothing about it is — and `prepare_delete_context_did`, which is what *clears* the confirm prompt, never ran. The prompt stayed on screen with nothing behind it, which reads as a hang.
* **The entire settings surface.** `settings_actions::dispatch` takes the config, the state and the save scheduler — no messaging, no VTA session — so every settings action is serviceable in State A. All of them were dropped, so a new account could not change its own protection, logging or mediator.

The diagnosis came from an activity log that showed `Created persona DID …` and then, on `g`, **not even** the "No persona selected" line the open path logs when it finds no persona. That absence is what proved the action was dropped before reaching any handler.

Restarting made agent names work, which is why this survived: an account that already holds a persona starts in the full runtime loop instead.

## Fix

The three surfaces are wired to the join context that is already here for `CreatePersonaSubmit` — it holds both the config the mutating verbs persist into and the admin VTA session they dispatch through. The session is cloned rather than borrowed, because those verbs need `&mut ctx.config` at the same time and a `VtaClient` clone is cheap and shares the underlying connection.

`ReconnectMediator` is the one settings outcome this loop cannot honour — there is no persona listener to rebuild yet — so it says the setting takes effect when messaging starts, which is true: the dispatch has already persisted it.

**The catch-all now speaks.** It swallowed all three of these, and in every case the symptom was a dead key: indistinguishable from a broken keyboard, and impossible to tell from an action that is legitimately unavailable.

## The audit

Rather than wait for the next report, every `Action` variant was checked against both loops:

| | |
|---|---|
| 98 | `Action` variants total |
| 39 | pure nav — shared by both loops via `handle_nav_action` |
| 23 | serviced by the join-flow and setup-wizard sub-loops |
| 16 | still runtime-only — **all genuinely need a community** |

The 16 are the inbox, relationships, credential exchange and the community verbs (leave / archive / withdraw / switch / capabilities / VMC). There is nothing for them to act on in State A, and they now say so instead of doing nothing.

## Not covered by a test

Neither loop is factored into a test-callable unit, so the divergence between their action coverage — the actual structural fault — is still only caught by reading both, or by the audit script above. The catch-all's message is the runtime backstop.

## Gate

`cargo fmt --all`; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`; `cargo test --workspace` — all green.

title: ci: guard the release workflows too, minus the cancellation
body:
## Why now

#1002 hardened `ci.yml` and deliberately left the release workflows alone, on
the grounds that they needed someone looking at the release path rather than a
blanket sweep. Having looked, one of them has the same bug — in a worse place.

## `publish.yml` carries the unhardened apt step, twice

```yaml
run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libdbus-1-dev pkg-config
```

That is the exact step that hung for up to an hour on **five separate CI runs**
this morning, and here it sits in front of publishing crates. The failure mode
isn't a slow build — it's a release that never happens, with nothing saying
why.

It now uses the same block `ci.yml` proved on main: check what's missing with
`dpkg -s`, install from the index the runner image already ships (`pkg-config`
is present on ubuntu-24.04), and fall back to a bounded, retried `apt-get
update` only if the package genuinely isn't there. On CI that took the step
from a 20–60 minute hang to **5 seconds**.

## Timeouts on all three jobs

From observed durations, not guesses:

| Job | Observed | Ceiling |
|---|---|---|
| Release-plz PR | 9m | 30 |
| iOS xcframework | 27m | 60 |
| Release-plz release | (no-op on last run) | 60 |

The release job gets the most headroom **on purpose**. A ceiling that fires
part-way through publishing a workspace of crates leaves a partial release —
worse than the hang it guards against. It is set to catch a wedged job and
nothing tighter.

## No `concurrency` group, deliberately

This is why the release workflows warranted their own PR rather than riding
#1002. `cancel-in-progress` on a workflow that publishes crates or ships an
xcframework could kill it mid-flight and leave a partial release. These want
**bounding, not cancellation** — so they get timeouts and the apt fix, and no
concurrency group.

## Verification

- Both files parse as YAML; every job carries `timeout-minutes`
- The apt block is copied from `ci.yml` rather than re-written, and passes
  `bash -n`
- Neither file gained a concurrency group (asserted, not assumed)

title: fix(sdk): build these two task payloads from their typed bodies
body:
## What

`get_key_secret` and `list_dids_webvh` were the last two `rpc_tt` call sites
building their payload as a hand-written `serde_json::json!` literal, so they
emitted `key_id`, `context_id` and `server_id` — snake_case, against a
SPEC §4.10 contract that says lowerCamelCase.

Both now build the typed body (`GetKeySecretBody`, `ListDidsWebvhBody`).

## Why the earlier casing fold missed them

#1000's fold rewrote **structs** via `rename_all`. A `json!` literal has no
struct to fold, so it kept whatever spelling was typed — this was called out as
the "known gap" in that PR and this closes it.

Nothing was broken: both structs carry `#[serde(alias = "…")]` for the old
spelling, so the VTA accepted what the SDK sent. But the SDK was emitting a
non-canonical spelling of its own published contract, and a consumer generated
from the schemas would not have recognised it.

Building from the typed body means the wire spelling now comes from the same
struct the schema is generated from, so the two cannot drift again — which is
the actual fix, rather than correcting three strings.

## A second, smaller win

`list_dids_webvh`'s literal emitted `"context_id": null` for an absent filter.
`ListDidsWebvhBody` carries `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"`, so the
key is now omitted entirely.

## Verification

`list_dids_webvh_filters_by_context` asserted the old spelling and now asserts
`contextId` / `serverId` — the test is the proof the **emitted wire** changed,
not merely the source.

A sweep confirms none are left:

```
snake_case keys left in rpc_tt payloads: none
```

- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` — 0 errors
- `cargo test --workspace --features session,tsp` — **4469 passing, 0 failures**

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **New/changed wire types: camelCase, schema registered, consumers updated
      (R3.\*)** — this is the whole PR; the receiving structs already accepted
      both spellings, so no consumer needs a lockstep change
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

title: fix(wire)!: emit canonical lowerCamelCase on Trust Task payloads, accept snake_case
body:
## What

53 wire structs across `vta-sdk/src/protocols/**` (plus `webvh.rs`,
`contexts.rs`, `context_policy.rs`, `did_templates/mod.rs`) emitted snake_case
on Trust Task payloads. SPEC §4.10 makes lowerCamelCase the wire contract, so
every consumer generated from the published schemas disagreed with what this
agent actually sends.

The fold is Postel's: `rename_all = "camelCase"` changes what is **emitted**, a
per-field `alias` keeps the old spelling accepted on **intake**. 126 fields
carry an alias, so a producer written against the previous wire keeps working
while it migrates.

## Why it was invisible

Nothing round-trips both sides. A hand-transcribed TS type has nothing to
disagree with, and the Rust side never reads its own output — so the drift only
surfaces when someone writes a client from the spec and it doesn't work.
Specifying the families upstream (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#240) is the
other half of this fix.

## Three exclusions that are not oversights

- **Config (`setup/from_toml.rs`)** — TOML, where snake_case is idiomatic. Not
  a wire.
- **Persisted stores and the backup format** (`backup_management/types.rs`,
  `drain_store.rs`) — read back from disk. Re-casing these would fail to read
  data already written, which is a worse bug than the one being fixed.
  `WebvhDidRecord` is both wire and persisted: it *is* folded, and existing
  snake_case records still read because of the aliases.
- **`protocols/credential_exchange.rs`** — OID4VCI/OID4VP structures
  (`vp_token`, `credential_offer`, `dcql_query`). §4.10 requires externally
  owned names to be carried verbatim. A first pass re-cased `vp_token` and the
  conformance harness caught it, which is exactly what that test is for.

## Deliberately out of scope

REST request/response bodies (`routes/`, `client/types.rs`, `protocol/`) are a
further 54 structs with the same problem. Unlike task payloads, no published
schema pins their casing and they have no aliases to fall back on, so changing
what they emit breaks readers silently.

The follow-up PR takes a different route: it removes the bespoke REST bodies
from the picture entirely by carrying Trust Tasks over the HTTPS binding, which
makes their casing moot rather than needing a second fold.

## Known gap

The fold rewrites **structs**. A payload built as an inline `serde_json::json!`
literal has no struct to fold, so it keeps whatever spelling was typed —
`list_dids_webvh` and `get_key_secret` still emit `context_id` / `server_id` /
`key_id`. Nothing breaks (the receiving structs carry aliases), but the SDK is
emitting a non-canonical spelling of its own contract. Building the typed body
instead of a literal is the durable fix and is not in this PR.

## Test

13 integration assertions read the old spelling and now read the new one.
Full suite green: 823 lib, 119 `api_integration`, 90 conformance, plus the rest.

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()` (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **New/changed wire types: camelCase, schema registered, all consumers
      (incl. JS) updated (R3.\*)** — this is the whole PR; the JS side lands in
      the plugin's casing commit and the schemas in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#240
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers — see the exclusions and known gap

- **`protocols/credential_exchange.rs`** carries OID4VCI and OID4VP structures

Thirteen integration assertions read the old spelling and now read the new one.
Full suite green: 823 lib, 119 api_integration, 90 conformance, plus the rest.

* style: wrap the serde attributes the casing fold widened

Adding a per-field `alias` pushed several `#[serde(...)]` attributes past the
line width, so rustfmt wants them broken across lines. No semantic change —
`cargo fmt --all` output, nothing hand-edited.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(sdk): carry Trust Tasks over the HTTPS binding on REST too (#1001)

* fix(sdk): carry Trust Tasks over the HTTPS binding on REST too

`rpc_tt` forked on the transport: DIDComm and TSP dispatched a Trust Task,
while REST built a bespoke per-operation request from a `build_rest` closure
and parsed a bespoke response. REST was therefore the one transport whose wire
did not match the published schemas — the same operation had two shapes
depending on how you reached it, and only one of them was specified.

`dispatch_trust_task` already spoke the HTTPS binding, so the fork was not
buying anything. Both `rpc_tt` and `rpc_tt_void` now dispatch the task on every
transport and all three arms are identical.

Checked before making the change:

- **Path.** The service serves `/api/trust-tasks` (routes/mod.rs:398), the SDK
  posts it and the plugin defaults to it, so nothing moves. Worth recording
  that the binding spec says `POST /trust-tasks` — everything agrees with
  everything except the spec, which is a conformance item, not a break.
- **Coverage.** All 52 tasks referenced by `rpc_tt` call sites are dispatched
  by the service. Nothing was routed to a task the VTA does not implement.

Two error-path defects fell out of it, both now fixed here:

The REST arm decided on the status before reading the body, so a refused task —
which answers with a `trust-task-error` document carrying a machine-readable
`code` and a human `message` — was reported as `unknown error: {raw json}`.
That also swallowed `ConsentRequired`, turning a question the caller could have
answered into a dead end. The body is parsed first now, per R3.7.

And `dispatch_trust_task` handed the whole error body to `VtaError::from_http`,
where the bespoke routes had truncated it at 256 characters. A server-controlled
page of text reaching logs and CLI output is a regression this fold would have
introduced everywhere at once; the truncation is restored on the shared path.

Tests move with the wire. Query-string assertions become task-payload
assertions, which is strictly more precise — the payload is what the VTA acts
on, and `list_acl` proves the point by naming the filter `scope` in the payload
and `context` in the query it replaced. Operations with no task twin keep their
routes and get `mount_rest_json`/`mount_rest_status`: backup blob streaming,
the import wrapping key, and the deprecated legacy-`rpc` DID verbs.

Full workspace: 144 suites, 4469 tests, 0 failures.

* style: rustfmt the binding test helpers

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(sdk): delete the REST closures the binding made dead

`cargo clippy -- -D warnings` in CI turns this into an error rather than a
warning, so the cleanup the previous commit deferred is not actually optional:

    error: unused variable: `build_rest`                          (rpc_tt)
    error: unused variable: `build_rest`                          (rpc_tt_void)
    error: associated function `handle_delete_response` is never used

Once `rpc_tt` and `rpc_tt_void` dispatch the Trust Task on every transport,
their `build_rest` closure has no caller. 60 of them go, along with the
parameter itself, and then the cascade the compiler exposes behind them:

- `encode_path_segment` and the bespoke REST request types
  (`UpdateContextDidRequest`, `RenameKeyRequest`, …) — imported only to build
  those requests.
- `handle_delete_response` — it existed for `rpc_tt_void`'s DELETE route. The
  binding answers with a task response document, which
  `extract_trust_task_payload` already decodes.
- `enc` in `audit.rs` — it percent-encoded query parameters because an RFC 3339
  timestamp ends in a `+00:00` offset that a query-string decoder reads as a
  space, so an unencoded bound arrived as an unparseable datetime. The payload
  is JSON now; that hazard cannot occur, and the helper goes with the class of
  bug it existed to prevent.

The legacy `rpc` helper keeps its `build_rest` — `update_did_webvh` and
`rotate_did_webvh_keys` still ride it, and both remain deprecated in favour of
their canonical `*_by_did` twins.

This is SDK-side only. The service still serves every bespoke route, so a
client built before the binding fold keeps working; retiring those routes
needs a deprecation window sized against what is deployed, and is not this
commit's business.

`cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` clean, and so is the rest-only
feature combination that failed alongside it.

title: ci: bound every job, and stop superseded PR runs racing the new one
body:
Two gaps that surfaced together on #1000, where CI sat for an hour and reported
nothing.

## No job had a timeout

All five long jobs were stuck on the **same step** for sixty minutes:

```
in_progress  Install system dependencies     ← 60 min
pending      Run dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
pending      Run actions/cache@v5
pending      Run cargo test --workspace
```

That step is `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libdbus-1-dev
pkg-config`. They never reached the Rust toolchain, let alone the tests — an
apt hang on GitHub's runners.

With no `timeout-minutes`, that hangs indefinitely, and an indefinite hang is
indistinguishable from a slow build until someone reads the step list by hand.
I only found it because I went looking; the PR just looked slow.

Ceilings are ~2× each job's observed p100, taken from real runs rather than
guessed:

| Job | Observed | Ceiling |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile build | 22m | 45 |
| Feature combos | 20m | 45 |
| semver checks | 17–22m | 45 |
| Test | 13m | 30 |
| Clippy | 4m | 20 |
| MSRV / Enclave build / Check | 3m | 20 |
| Format, cargo-deny, lockfile self-pins, commit lint | <1m | 10 |

The headroom is deliberate. These exist to bound a **hang**, not to enforce a
performance budget — a job that fails because a runner had a slow day is worse
than no limit at all.

## No `concurrency` group

Pushing a fixup to an open PR left the superseded run executing and racing the
new one for the same runner pool. #1000 had two full runs live simultaneously,
and the older one was still churning through jobs the newer one had already
finished.

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
```

**Cancellation is scoped to pull requests on purpose.** A push to `main` or
`nightly` gates releases and is the record of what that commit did, so those
runs are left to finish even when another lands on top. Only PR runs — where a
superseded result tells you nothing worth waiting for — get cancelled. This is
slightly more conservative than the unconditional `cancel-in-progress: true`
the browser-plugin repo uses.

## Scope

`ci.yml` only.

- `docker.yml` and `join-didcomm-soak.yml` already carry timeouts.
- **`publish.yml` and `release-mobile-ios.yml` have neither, and are
  deliberately untouched.** `cancel-in-progress` on a workflow that publishes
  crates could kill a publish part-way through — a worse failure than the one
  being fixed here. They want their own change, made by someone looking at the
  release path properly.

## Test

YAML parses; 12 jobs, all now carrying `timeout-minutes`, verified
programmatically rather than by eye:

```
YAML parses; 12 jobs
concurrency: {'group': 'ci-${{ github.ref }}',
              'cancel-in-progress': "${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}"}
no timeout: []
```

The concurrency behaviour proves itself on this PR: pushing again should cancel
the previous run rather than leave it racing.

body:

for sixty minutes, never reaching the Rust toolchain, let alone the tests. With
no `timeout-minutes` a hung apt mirror hangs the job indefinitely, and an
indefinite hang is indistinguishable from a slow build until someone reads the
step list by hand. Every job now has a ceiling of roughly twice its observed
p100, taken from real runs:

    Mobile build 22m → 45    Feature combos 20m → 45    semver checks 22m → 45
    Test         13m → 30
    Clippy        4m → 20    MSRV            3m → 20    Enclave build 3m → 20
    Check         3m → 20
    Format, cargo-deny, lockfile self-pins, commit lint (<1m) → 10

The headroom is deliberate. These bound a hang; they are not there to enforce a
performance budget, and a job that fails because a runner had a slow day is
worse than no limit at all.

**No `concurrency` group.** Pushing a fixup to an open PR left the superseded
run executing and racing the new one for the same runner pool — #1000 had two
full runs live at once, and the older one was still churning through jobs the
newer one had already finished.

Cancellation is scoped to pull requests. A push to main or nightly gates
releases and is the record of what that commit did, so those runs finish even
when another lands on top; only the PR runs, where a superseded result tells
you nothing, get cancelled.

Scope is ci.yml. `docker.yml` and `join-didcomm-soak.yml` already carry
timeouts. `publish.yml` and `release-mobile-ios.yml` have neither, and are
deliberately untouched: `cancel-in-progress` on a workflow that publishes
crates could kill a publish part-way through, which is a worse failure than the
one being fixed here. They want their own change, made by someone looking at
the release path.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: bound and retry apt, which is what actually keeps hanging

The timeouts in the previous commit did their job on the very next run — Check
and MSRV were cancelled at 20:19 on `Install system dependencies` — which
confirms the diagnosis and also shows that bounding alone is not enough. Three
separate runs have now stalled on that step, one of them for a full hour.

The failure mode matters for the fix: apt does not fail here, it *hangs* on an
unresponsive mirror and never returns. A bare retry loop is no use against
that, because it would wait forever on the first attempt. So each attempt is
bounded with `timeout`, which converts the hang into a failure the loop can
act on, and `Acquire::Retries=3` handles the ordinary transient case
underneath.

Three attempts, 90s for `update` and 120s for `install`, 10s between — a worst
case of about 11 minutes before the step gives up with a clear
`::error::` rather than sitting there. That fits inside the tightest job
ceiling this touches (20 minutes) while leaving room for the work itself,
which runs 3–4 minutes on these jobs.

Applied to all seven jobs carrying the step. Verified: the YAML parses, all 12
jobs still have `timeout-minutes`, no apt step is left unhardened, and the loop
body passes `bash -n` and retries as intended when the command fails.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: stop running the apt operation that is actually hanging

Bounding each attempt made the cause legible. On the last run MSRV and semver
checks failed at 09:18:38, 09:20:18 and 09:21:58 — exactly 90 seconds apart,
every one landing on the `timeout 90` guarding `apt-get update` and never on
the install. The mirror is unresponsive, and retrying it harder does not make
it responsive; it only decides how long we wait before saying so.

So the fix is to not run it unless it is needed. The runner image ships a
usable package index and already carries pkg-config, so the step now checks
what is actually missing, installs that straight from the shipped index, and
exits. `apt-get update` becomes the fallback for the case where the package
genuinely is not in the index — still bounded, still retried three times.

That turns the common case into a no-op instead of a network round trip
against a mirror that has failed four times today, and keeps a real path to
recovery if the index ever does lack the package.

Verified both branches by dry run: with the packages present the step reports
"already present; nothing to do" and exits 0 without invoking apt at all; with
nothing present and every apt call failing it degrades through the shipped
index, three bounded refreshes, and a clear `::error::`. `bash -n` clean, YAML
parses, all 12 jobs still carry `timeout-minutes`, and all 7 apt steps carry
the fast path.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: spec(vta): specify the context and webvh DID-lifecycle families
body:
## What

Adds JSON Schemas for 22 task families that the VTA already implements but
which had never been specified:

**`vta/contexts/*` (7)** — `list`, `get`, `create`, `update`, `update-did`,
`preview-delete`, `delete`
**`vta/webvh/*` (15)** — `dids/{list,get,create,update,rotate-keys,delete,log}`,
`servers/{list,add,update,remove,register,reconcile}`,
`agent-name/{set,remove,disable,enable,list,check}`

Plus two shared definition files: `_shared/0.1/context.schema.json`
(`ContextRecord`, `ContextPolicy`) and `_shared/0.1/webvh-records.schema.json`
(`WebvhDidRecord`, `WebvhServerRecord`, `AgentNameEntry`).

## Why

These were tracked debt (VTI #854). The families are live on the wire and have
consumers in both Rust and TypeScript, but with no schema each consumer
hand-transcribed the shapes from the Rust structs. That is how the casing drift
happened: a hand-written TS type has nothing to disagree with when the Rust side
changes, so it silently stays wrong until something round-trips.

Specifying them at the source means the generated bindings become the single
definition for both languages, and `check-bindings-conformance.mjs` fails the
build when they diverge.

## Notes for review

- Field naming follows SPEC §4.10 lowerCamelCase throughout. Externally-owned
  names are not in scope for these families.
- `unevaluatedProperties` is deliberately *not* used alongside `$ref` — it
  breaks the TS generator with a misleading resolution error. The house pattern
  is followed instead.
- The shared file is named `webvh-records` rather than `webvh` because
  `vta/_shared/0.1/webvh` and did-management's `webvh` both alias to
  `WebvhShared_v0_1` and collide.

## Test

Full generator run: **328 specs → 328 TS modules, 323 Rust modules**, all
agreeing. Conformance harness green.

## Checklist (stack guide §9, applicable items)

- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, schema registered, all consumers
      (incl. JS) updated (R3.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged explicitly — see the `unevaluatedProperties` note above

title: spec(vta): specify the context and webvh DID-lifecycle families (#240)
body:
spec(vta): specify the context and webvh DID-lifecycle families (#240)

* spec(vta/contexts): specify the context family — list, get, create, update, update-did, preview-delete, delete

A VTA *context* is the unit of separation: keys, DIDs, vault entries, policies
and memory each belong to exactly one, and an ACL entry's scopes are context
ids. Seven tasks manage them, all deployed at 1.0, and none of them had a
schema — so every consumer transcribed the shapes from the Rust by hand, and
each copy drifted on its own schedule. These are those seven, written down.

The shared `ContextRecord` and `ContextPolicy` live in `vta/_shared/0.1` since
five of the seven tasks return the record.

Decisions worth review, because they are inferred from an implementation
rather than handed down from a design:

- **`get` and `list` fail differently, and the pair is deliberate.** `get`
  answers `notFound` for an id the caller cannot reach — the same answer it
  gives for one that does not exist, so the task is not an existence oracle.
  `list` filters instead, and an empty array is a successful answer that says
  nothing about what the VTA holds.
- **`update` replaces `contextPolicy` whole rather than merging it.** Policy
  members mean *unrestricted* by absence, so a merge would make lifting a
  restriction impossible — the member's absence would read as "leave it" rather
  than "remove it". The spec says so, and says what that costs a caller who
  reads-modifies-writes one member.
- **`update-did` is its own task at a lower role than `update`.** Assigning an
  identity to a scope you administer is within that administration; changing
  what the scope permits is not. It also states plainly that nothing referencing
  the previous DID is migrated, because that is the surprise.
- **`delete` refuses a non-empty context unless `force`**, and `force` is an
  explicitness flag rather than a separate authority. `deleted: false` in a
  success response means the VTA declined — a consumer must read the member
  rather than infer from the status.
- **`preview-delete` carries the deletion's authorization, not the read's.** It
  is an inventory of a context's contents, and a caller who may not delete one
  may not enumerate it either.

Members are canonical lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 (`basePath`, `webvhDids`,
`aclEntriesRemoved`). **The current implementation emits snake_case for these**
— adopting this spec needs the same dual-accept migration the family's other
casing folds used.

Regenerated both binding sets: 313 specs, 313 TypeScript and 308 Rust modules,
all agreeing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(vta/webvh): specify the DID lifecycle — dids, hosting servers, agent names

Fifteen tasks, all deployed at 1.0 and none of them specified: creating and
retiring did:webvh DIDs, rotating their keys, registering the servers that
serve their logs, and binding agent names to them. Joins the three already
specified here (dids/update, servers/reconcile, servers/domains).

Shared `WebvhDidRecord`, `WebvhServerRecord` and `AgentNameEntry` live in
`vta/_shared/0.1/webvh-records` — named for the records rather than the family
because the generator derives a TS export alias from the basename, and plain
`webvh` collides with did-management's own shared schema. It says so loudly,
which is how this was caught.

The properties worth reviewing, each inferred from the implementation:

- **`create` commits two things permanently**: the SCID, and portability. A DID
  minted non-portable can never move domains, and the spec says so where an
  operator will read it rather than leaving it to be discovered.
- **`preRotationCount: 0` forfeits key-compromise recovery.** Without a
  committed successor, whoever steals the current key can rotate to their own as
  convincingly as the owner. Stated on create, on rotate-keys, and in both
  Security sections.
- **`delete` can half-succeed.** `daemonCleanupError` means the VTA dropped its
  record but the hosting server did not confirm removal — the DID may still
  resolve, and a consumer must surface that rather than report a clean delete.
- **`rotate-keys` never changes the SCID**, and when `serverless` is true the
  rotation exists only in the VTA until the caller publishes the entry.
- **`servers/remove` unpublishes nothing.** DIDs the server already serves keep
  resolving; what is lost is the VTA's route for updating them.
- **`servers/list` carries no credentials**, normatively — a hosting
  registration is the one place a VTA holds a long-lived secret for a third
  party, and a read that returned it would become an impersonation capability.
- **Agent names are authoritative in the DID→name direction only.** A name
  recorded here is half a claim; the DID document's `alsoKnownAs` is the other
  half. `remove` releases a name for anyone to take, so a published name should
  be disabled rather than removed.

Members are canonical lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10. The implementation is
mixed — did_management/delete is snake_case where its siblings are camelCase —
so adoption needs the same dual-accept migration as the contexts family.

328 specs, 328 TypeScript and 323 Rust modules, all agreeing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* fix(vta): spell out defaulted fields in the examples so they round-trip

Three conformance tests failed: `vta/contexts/delete`,
`vta/webvh/dids/list` and `vta/webvh/dids/register-with-server`.

A property carrying a `default` is generated as a plain (non-`Option`) member
with `#[serde(default)]` and no `skip_serializing_if`, so it is always emitted.
An example that leaves it out therefore does not survive its own round-trip —
deserialize materialises the default, re-serialize writes it, and the result no
longer matches the source. The examples were the wrong half: `force`,
`preRotationCount` and `nextFragmentId` are simply absent from them.

Spelling the defaults out matches the house pattern —
`did-management/did/register/0.1` carries `"force": false` in its example for
exactly this reason — and is better documentation besides, since a reader of
the example can now see what the default actually is rather than having to
find it in the schema.

Regenerated with `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`.
`trust-tasks-rs` is green at 408 passing.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

title: fix(sdk): carry Trust Tasks over the HTTPS binding on REST too
body:
> **Stacked on #1000.** Based on `fix/wire-casing-camel` so the diff shown here
> is just this change. GitHub will retarget to `main` when #1000 merges.
> I have not verified whether it strictly *requires* #1000 — `main` already
> camelCases the bodies these tests assert, so it may well apply standalone.
> Stacked for review clarity, not because a dependency is proven.

## What

`rpc_tt` forked on the transport: DIDComm and TSP dispatched a Trust Task,
while REST built a bespoke per-operation request from a `build_rest` closure
and parsed a bespoke response.

REST was therefore the one transport whose wire did not match the published
schemas — the same operation had two shapes depending on how you reached it,
and only one of them was specified. `dispatch_trust_task` already spoke the
HTTPS binding, so the fork wasn't buying anything.

Both `rpc_tt` and `rpc_tt_void` now dispatch the task on every transport, and
all three arms are identical.

## Checked before making the change

- **Path** — the service serves `/api/trust-tasks`
  (`vta-service/src/routes/mod.rs:398`), the SDK posts it, the plugin defaults
  to it. Nothing moves. Worth recording separately: the binding **spec** says
  `POST /trust-tasks`, so everything agrees with everything except the spec.
  That is a conformance item, not a break.
- **Coverage** — all 52 tasks referenced by `rpc_tt` call sites are dispatched
  by the service. Nothing was routed at a task the VTA doesn't implement.

## Two error-path defects fell out, both fixed here

**The REST arm decided on the status before reading the body.** A refused task
answers with a `trust-task-error` document carrying a machine-readable `code`
and a human `message`; throwing on the status alone reported it as
`unknown error: {raw json}`. It also swallowed `ConsentRequired` — turning a
question the caller could have answered into a dead end. The body is parsed
first now (R3.7). `vta-service`'s `client_round_trip` proves it.

**Truncation would have been lost.** `dispatch_trust_task` handed the whole
error body to `VtaError::from_http`, where the bespoke routes truncated at 256
characters. A server-controlled page of text reaching logs and CLI output is a
regression this fold would have introduced everywhere at once. Restored on the
shared path — `oversized_error_body_is_truncated` caught it.

## Tests move with the wire

Query-string assertions become task-payload assertions, which is strictly more
precise: the payload is what the VTA acts on. `list_acl` makes the point — the
filter is `scope` in the payload and was `context` in the query it replaced, so
these could not be translated mechanically.

Operations with **no task twin** keep their routes and get
`mount_rest_json` / `mount_rest_status`: backup blob streaming, the import
wrapping key, and the deprecated legacy-`rpc` DID verbs
(`update_did_webvh`, `rotate_did_webvh_keys`, both already superseded by their
canonical `*_by_did` twins).

## What this sets up, and does *not* do

All three arms of `rpc_tt` being identical makes the `match`, the `build_rest`
parameter, ~53 call-site closures, and the bespoke routes and body structs
behind them dead — the compiler already warns about the closures.

**Deleting them is deliberately not in this PR.** A client built before this
change still sends `GET /keys?offset=…`, and removing the route turns that into
a runtime 404 behind a green build on both sides. That needs a deprecation
window sized against what is actually deployed, which is a judgement call, not
a refactor.

## A note on one thing I got wrong

An earlier pass here concluded `get_key_secret` was mis-wired, because it
dispatches `TASK_SEEDS_EXPORT_MNEMONIC_1_0`. It isn't: the doc on that constant
records that the operation was `/keys/{id}/secret` in the legacy REST surface
and moved to the seeds slice because it acts on the seed identifier rather than
the individual key. `get_key_secret_via_didcomm` asserts the round-trip. The
change was reverted; `keys.rs` is untouched by this PR.

## Test

Full workspace: **144 suites, 4469 tests, 0 failures.**
`client_rest` 86/86, `auth_light_rest` 19/19, `client_didcomm` 49/49.

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` / bare `fetch()`; timeouts unchanged (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **New/changed wire types (R3.\*)** — REST now sends the *specified*
      document instead of a bespoke one; this removes a divergence rather than
      adding a type
- [x] **Errors matched on stable machine-readable codes, bodies parsed before
      throwing on status (R3.7)** — the substance of the two fixes above
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

title: fix(deps): take the patched h2, and document the line that has no patch (#241)
body:
fix(deps): take the patched h2, and document the line that has no patch (#241)

RUSTSEC-2026-0258: h2 accepts and queues empty DATA frames without limit, so a
peer that never drains can drive unbounded memory growth, or a panic if the
length overflows. Upstream rates it Low and patched it in 0.4.16.

The graph carried two h2 lines, and they end differently.

**0.4.14 → 0.4.16.** A straight bump to the patched release. The lockfile moves
exactly one package — `h2@0.4.14` → `h2@0.4.16` — and nothing else; the other
churn in the diff is dependency-list ordering inside packages that already had
both versions present.

**0.3.27 stays, and is now an explicit exception.** There is no version to move
to: 0.3.27 IS the newest 0.3, and upstream patched only the 0.4 line. It
arrives as hyper 0.14 → hyper-tls 0.5 → reqwest 0.11 → ssi-dids-core 0.1.3 →
affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk, reaching trust-tasks-tsp (via affinidi-tsp)
and trust-tasks-proof — the normal graph, not a dev-dependency, so crates we
publish link it.

Nothing here can shorten that chain. Our requirements are already open
(`affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk = "0.8"`, `affinidi-tsp = "0.1"`), and every
0.8.x of the resolver SDK up to the newest, 0.8.22, requires
`ssi-dids-core ^0.1` — which is what pins reqwest 0.11, hence hyper 0.14, hence
h2 0.3. Bumping the Affinidi crates was tried and changes nothing except
lockfile churn, so it is not in this commit.

The `deny.toml` entry says all of that, and says the part that matters for
judging it: reqwest is a *client* here, resolving DIDs, so reaching the flaw
needs a hostile or compromised resolution endpoint and costs availability only
— no confidentiality or integrity component. It is the first entry in that list
that is a real vulnerability rather than a maintenance notice, and it is
written to be removed: it clears when the resolver SDK moves to
ssi-dids-core 0.3+, which is on reqwest 0.12 / hyper 1.x.

`cargo deny check` is clean across advisories, bans, licenses and sources.
Workspace green at 493 passing.

title: chore(ts): declare the bindings side-effect free
body:
## What

Adds `"sideEffects": false` to `trust-tasks-ts/package.json`.

## Why

Every generated module is a pure `export const` / `export type` — there is no
module-level work anywhere in the package. Without this flag a bundler has to
assume otherwise and keeps every task family a consumer touches, because it
cannot prove that dropping one is safe.

The bindings are large and growing (328 modules at present) and consumers
typically import a handful of families. `@openvtc/pnm-core` is the immediate
beneficiary: it is heading for a browser extension bundle, where the MV3
service worker is a single Rollup output with no code splitting, so anything
tree-shaking cannot remove is carried at runtime.

## Risk

The claim is checkable and true today: the flag is a lie only if a module gains
an import with a side effect or does work at module scope. Nothing in the
generator emits either — it writes constants and types.

## Test

No behaviour to test; `npm run build` in `trust-tasks-ts` is unchanged.
author: stormer78

title: chore(ts): declare the bindings side-effect free (#239)
body:
chore(ts): declare the bindings side-effect free (#239)

Every generated module is data — payload interfaces, TYPE_URI / SPEC
constants — and the hand-written _runtime pipeline initialises nothing beyond
its own module-scoped Set and RegExp. Nothing here patches a global, so
importing a module a consumer never uses is safe to drop.

Without the declaration a bundler has to keep all of it. That matters for the
browser consumers this package is aimed at: a web console that imports one
task family should not ship the schema constants of the other 269. Verified
against the existing build and test suite.

title: feat(didcomm-v1-crate): implement binding 0.2 — the dedicated type, the omit rule, receivers move first (#238)
body:
feat(didcomm-v1-crate): implement binding 0.2 — the dedicated type, the omit rule, receivers move first (#238)

The reference crate lagged the specification it implements, on both rules
the binding gained since 0.1:

The carriage (0.2 §2): build_message now emits the binding's own message
type — the RFC 0020 URI …/trust-task/1.0/task — with the document in the
reserved ~attach entry and the advisory human-readable line moved from
basic-message's content to the dedicated type's comment member. Per §2.3
receivers move first: unpack_trust_task accepts BOTH carriages, the
dedicated type and 0.1's basic-message, while the producer emits only the
former.

The omit rule (§4, from #208): ~thread values must satisfy RFC 0008's
shape. A threadId, parentThreadId, or fallback id that cannot be
represented — urn:uuid: ids most prominently — is omitted, never
rewritten: a rewritten correlator contradicts the in-band member and
draws a guaranteed malformedRequest from the consumer's comparison. The
consumer side already read explicit_thid(), so a defaulted thid was
never treated as an assertion; the module docs now say why.

Version to 0.8.0 — producer output changes type, which is a behavioural
break for any consumer gating on basic-message. Tests 11 → 13: the omit
rule (member, fallback, and boundary cases), the dedicated-type shape,
the comment member, and the §2.3 legacy-acceptance gate.

Signed-off-by: Alberto L <aleon@law.harvard.edu>
author: albertoleon7794

title: feat(didcomm-v1-crate): implement binding 0.2 — dedicated type, omit rule, receivers move first
body:
The reference crate still implemented the binding as it stood at 0.1; the specification moved twice and this closes the gap — the follow-up offered in #173 ("still yours, as offered") after #208 and #216.

**The carriage (0.2 §2).** `build_message` now emits the binding's dedicated message type (`…/binding/didcomm-v1/0.2/trust-task/1.0/task`) with the document in the reserved `trust-task` attachment, and the advisory human-readable line moved from basic-message's `content` to the dedicated type's `comment`. Per §2.3 — receivers move first — `unpack_trust_task` accepts **both** carriages (the dedicated type and 0.1's basic-message) while the producer emits only the new one.

**The omit rule (§4, from #208).** `~thread` values must satisfy RFC 0008's shape; a `threadId`, `parentThreadId`, or fallback `id` that cannot be represented (`urn:uuid:` ids most prominently) is **omitted, never rewritten** — a rewritten correlator contradicts the in-band member and draws a guaranteed `malformedRequest` from the consumer's §3.1 comparison. The consumer side already compared `explicit_thid()` only, so a defaulted `thid` was never treated as an assertion; the docs now state that rule rather than leaving it implicit.

Version 0.7.0 → **0.8.0**: the producer's output changes message type, a behavioural break for any consumer gating on basic-message (per the workspace's semver-over-the-library rule). Tests 11 → 13 — the omit rule (member, fallback, boundaries), the dedicated-type shape, the `comment` member, and the §2.3 legacy-acceptance gate. `cargo test` / `clippy -D warnings` / `fmt` clean.

Validated against the deployed consumer side: the same carriage shape (type + `trust-task` attachment + omit rule) is what Credo 0.6.3 agents have been exercising in the Keyring reference ladder — [ref-06v1c](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06v1c-task-layer) runs it live including the §2.3 legacy check, and [ref-06x](https://github.com/berkmancenter/keyring-wallet/tree/doc/tsp-plan/tsp-reference/ref-06x-cypress-stack) end-to-end at the Cypress release.

**TL;DR: the reference crate now implements binding 0.2 as published — dedicated `@type` out, both carriages in (receivers move first), and the #208 omit rule for unrepresentable thread ids. 0.8.0, 13 tests, clippy/fmt clean.**
